<example number="2.21" title="Determining Validity of Biconditional Statements">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Construct a truth table to analyze all possible outcomes for each of the following statements, then determine whether they are valid.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left. p \land q\leftrightarrow p \land \right.\sim q$$</item>
        <item>$$\left. p \vee q\leftrightarrow \right.\sim p \vee q$$</item>
        <item>$$\left. p\rightarrow q\leftrightarrow \right.\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p$$</item>
        <item>$$\left. \left. p \land q\rightarrow \right.\sim r\leftrightarrow p \land q \land r \right.$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Applying the dominance of connectives, the statement $$\left. p \land q\leftrightarrow p \land \right.\sim q$$ is equivalent to $$\left. \left( {p \land q} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {p \land \left( {\sim q} \right)} \right). \right.$$ So, the columns of the truth table will include $$p$$ , $$q$$ , $$p \land q,$$ $$\sim q$$ , $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q$$ and $$\left. \left( {p \land q} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim q} \right). \right.$$ Because there are only two basic propositions, $$p$$ and $$q$$ , the table will have $$2(2) = 4$$ rows of truth values to account for all the possible outcomes. The statement is not valid because the last column is not all true. $$p$$ $$q$$ $$p \land q$$ $$\sim q$$ $$\left. p \land \right.\sim q$$ $$\left. \left( {p \land q} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim q} \right) \right.$$ T T T F F F T F F T T F F T F F F T F F F T F T</item>
        <item>Applying the dominance of connectives, the statement $$\left. p \vee q\leftrightarrow \right.\sim p \vee q$$ is equivalent to $$\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\left( {\sim p} \right) \vee q} \right). \right.$$ So, the columns of the truth table will include $$p$$ , $$q$$ , $$p \vee q,$$ $$\sim p$$ , $$\sim p \vee q,$$ and $$\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim p \vee q} \right). \right.$$ Because there are only two basic propositions, $$p$$ and $$q$$ , the table will have $$2(2) = 4$$ rows of truth values to account for all the possible outcomes. The statement is not valid because the last column is not all true. $$p$$ $$q$$ $$p \vee q$$ $$\sim p$$ $$\sim p \vee q$$ $$\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim p \vee q} \right) \right.$$ T T T F T T T F T F F F F T T T T T F F F T T F</item>
        <item>Applying the dominance of connectives, the statement $$\left. p\rightarrow q\leftrightarrow \right.\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p$$ is equivalent to $$\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right)\leftrightarrow\left( \left( {\sim q} \right)\rightarrow\left( {\sim p} \right) \right). \right.$$ So, the columns of the truth table will include $$p$$ , $$q$$ , $$\left. p\rightarrow q, \right.$$ $$\sim q$$ , $$\sim p$$ , $$\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p,$$ and $$\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p} \right). \right.$$ Because there are only two basic propositions, $$p$$ and $$q$$ the table will have $$2(2) = 4$$ rows of truth values to account for all the possible outcomes. The statement is valid because the last column is all true. $$p$$ $$q$$ $$\left. p\rightarrow q \right.$$ $$\sim q$$ $$\sim p$$ $$\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p$$ $$\left. \left( p\rightarrow\mathbf{q} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p} \right) \right.$$ T T T F F T T T F F T F F T F T T F T T T F F T T T T T</item>
        <item>Applying the dominance of connectives, the statement $$\left. \left. p \land q\rightarrow \right.\sim r\leftrightarrow p \land q \land r \right.$$ is equivalent to $$\left. \left( \left( {p \land q} \right)\rightarrow\left( {\sim r} \right) \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\left( {p \land q} \right) \land r} \right). \right.$$ So, the columns of the truth table will include $$p$$ , $$q$$ , $$r$$ , $$\sim r$$ , $$p \land q,$$ $$\left. \left( {p \land q} \right) \land \right.\sim r,$$ $$\left( {p \land q} \right) \land r,$$ and $$\left. \left( \left( {p \land q} \right)\rightarrow\left( {\sim r} \right) \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\left( {p \land q} \right) \land r} \right). \right.$$ Because there are three basic propositions, $$p$$ , $$q$$ , and $$r$$ , the table will have $$2(2)(2) = 8$$ rows of truth values to account for all the possible outcomes. The statement is not valid because the last column is not all true. $$p$$ $$q$$ $$r$$ $$\sim r$$ $$p \land q$$ $$\left. \left( {p \land q} \right)\rightarrow \right.\sim r$$ $$\left( {p \land q} \right) \land r$$ $$\left. \left( {\left. p \land q\rightarrow \right.\sim r} \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {p \land q \land r} \right) \right.$$ T T T F T F T T T T F T T T F T T F T F F T F F T F F T F T F F F T T F F T F F F T F T F T F F F F T F F T F F F F F T F T F F</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="2.22" title="Determining Logical Equivalence with a Truth Table">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Create a truth table to determine whether the following compound statements are logically equivalent.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left. p\rightarrow q; \right.$$ $$\sim\left. p\rightarrow \right.\sim q$$</item>
        <item>$$\left. p\rightarrow q; \right.$$ $$\sim p \vee q$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Construct a truth table for the biconditional formed by using the first statement as the hypothesis and the second statement as the conclusion, $$\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim\left. p\rightarrow \right.\sim q} \right). \right.$$ $$p$$ $$q$$ $$\left. p\rightarrow q \right.$$ $$\sim p$$ $$\sim q$$ $$\sim\left. p\rightarrow \right.\sim q$$ $$\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim\left. p\rightarrow \right.\sim q} \right) \right.$$ T T T F F T T T F F F T T F F T T T F F F F F T T T T T Because the last column it not all true, the biconditional is not valid and the statement $$\left. p\rightarrow q \right.$$ is not logically equivalent to the statement $$\sim\left. p\rightarrow \right.\sim q$$ .</item>
        <item>Construct a truth table for the biconditional formed by using the first statement as the hypothesis and the second statement as the conclusion, $$\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim p \vee q} \right). \right.$$ $$p$$ $$q$$ $$\left. p\rightarrow q \right.$$ $$\sim p$$ $$\sim p \vee q$$ $$\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right)\leftrightarrow\left( {\sim p \vee q} \right) \right.$$ T T T F T T T F F F F T F T T T T T F F T T T T Because the last column is true for every entry, the biconditional is valid and the statement $$\left. p\rightarrow q \right.$$ is logically equivalent to the statement $$\sim p \vee q$$ . Symbolically, $$\left. p\rightarrow q \equiv \right.\sim p \vee q.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

title: Writing the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive of a Conditional Statement
snippet: Writing the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive of a Conditional Statement: Use the statements, p : Harry is a wizard and q : Hermione is a witch, to write the following statements: Write the conditional statement, \left. p\rightarrow q...
body_xml:
<example number="2.23" title="Writing the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive of a Conditional Statement">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the statements, $$p$$ : Harry is a wizard and $$q$$ : Hermione is a witch, to write the following statements:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Write the conditional statement, $$\left. p\rightarrow q \right.$$ , in words.</item>
        <item>Write the converse statement, $$\left. q\rightarrow p \right.$$ , in words.</item>
        <item>Write the inverse statement, $$\sim\left. p\rightarrow \right.\sim q$$ , in words.</item>
        <item>Write the contrapositive statement, $$\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p$$ , in words.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The conditional statement takes the form, “if $$p$$ , then $$q$$ ,” so the conditional statement is: “If Harry is a wizard, then Hermione is a witch.” Remember the if … then … words are the connectives that form the conditional statement.</item>
        <item>The converse swaps or interchanges the hypothesis, $$p$$ , with the conclusion, $$q$$ . It has the form, “if $$q$$ , then $$p$$ .” So, the converse is: "If Hermione is a witch, then Harry is a wizard."</item>
        <item>To construct the inverse of a statement, negate both the hypothesis and the conclusion. The inverse has the form, “if $$\sim p$$ , then $$\sim q$$ ,” so the inverse is: "If Harry is not a wizard, then Hermione is not a witch."</item>
        <item>The contrapositive is formed by negating and interchanging both the hypothesis and conclusion. It has the form, “if $$\sim q$$ , then $$\sim p$$ ," so the contrapositive statement is: "If Hermione is not a witch, then Harry is not a wizard."</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Identifying the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive
snippet: Identifying the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive: Use the conditional statement, “If all dogs bark, then Lassie likes to bark,” to identify the following. Write the hypothesis of the conditional statement and label it with a p . Write...
body_xml:
<example number="2.24" title="Identifying the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the conditional statement, “If all dogs bark, then Lassie likes to bark,” to identify the following.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Write the hypothesis of the conditional statement and label it with a $$p$$ .</item>
        <item>Write the conclusion of the conditional statement and label it with a $$q$$ .</item>
        <item>Identify the following statement as the converse, inverse, or contrapositive: “If Lassie likes to bark, then all dogs bark.”</item>
        <item>Identify the following statement as the converse, inverse, or contrapositive: “If Lassie does not like to bark, then some dogs do not bark.”</item>
        <item>Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional statement?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The hypothesis is the phrase following the if. The answer is $$p$$ : All dogs bark. Notice, the word if is not included as part of the hypothesis.</item>
        <item>The conclusion of a conditional statement is the phrase following the then. The word then is not included when stating the conclusion. The answer is: $$q$$ : Lassie likes to bark.</item>
        <item>“Lassie likes to bark” is $$q$$ and “All dogs bark” is $$p$$ . So, “If Lassie likes to bark, then all dogs bark,” has the form “if $$q$$ , then $$p$$ ,” which is the form of the converse.</item>
        <item>“Lassie does not like to bark” is $$\sim q$$ and “Some dogs do not bark” is $$\sim p$$ . The statement, “If Lassie does not like to bark, then some dogs do not bark,” has the form “if $$\sim q$$ , then $$\sim p$$ ,” which is the form of the contrapositive.</item>
        <item>The contrapositive $$\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p$$ is logically equivalent to the conditional statement $$\left. p\rightarrow q. \right.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining the Truth Value of the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive
snippet: Determining the Truth Value of the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive: Assume the conditional statement, \left. p\rightarrow q: \right. “If Chadwick Boseman was an actor, then Chadwick Boseman did not star in the movie Black Panther” is...
body_xml:
<example number="2.25" title="Determining the Truth Value of the Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Assume the conditional statement, $$\left. p\rightarrow q: \right.$$ “If Chadwick Boseman was an actor, then Chadwick Boseman did not star in the movie Black Panther” is false, and use it to answer the following questions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Write the converse of the statement in words and determine its truth value.</item>
        <item>Write the inverse of the statement in words and determine its truth value.</item>
        <item>Write the contrapositive of the statement in words and determine its truth value.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The only way the conditional statement can be false is if the hypothesis, $$p$$ : Chadwick Boseman was an actor, is true and the conclusion, $$q$$ : Chadwick Boseman did not star in the movie Black Panther, is false. The converse is $$\left. q\rightarrow p, \right.$$ and it is written in words as: “If Chadwick Boseman did not star in the movie Black Panther, then Chadwick Boseman was an actor.” This statement is true, because false $$\rightarrow$$ true is true.</item>
        <item>The inverse has the form “ $$\sim\left. p\rightarrow \right.\sim q.$$ ” The written form is: “If Chadwick Boseman was not an actor, then Chadwick Boseman starred in the movie Black Panther.” Because $$p$$ is true, and $$q$$ is false, $$\sim p$$ is false, and $$\sim q$$ is true. This means the inverse is false $$\rightarrow$$ true, which is true. Alternatively, from Question 1, the converse is true, and because the inverse is logically equivalent to the converse it must also be true.</item>
        <item>The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the conditional. Because the conditional is false, the contrapositive is also false. This can be confirmed by looking at the truth values of the contrapositive statement. The contrapositive has the form “ $$\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p$$ .” Because $$q$$ is false and $$p$$ is true, $$\sim q$$ is true and $$\sim p$$ is false. Therefore, $$\sim\left. q\rightarrow \right.\sim p$$ is true $$\rightarrow$$ false, which is false. The written form of the contrapositive is “If Chadwick Boseman starred in the movie Black Panther, then Chadwick Boseman was not an actor.”</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>De Morgan’s Law for negation of a conjunction: $$\sim\left. \left( {p \land q} \right) \equiv \right.\sim\left. p \vee \right.\sim q$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>De Morgan’s Law for the negation of a disjunction: $$\sim\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right) \equiv \right.\sim\left. p \land \right.\sim q$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Negation of a conditional: $$\sim\left. \left( p\rightarrow q \right) \equiv p \land \right.\sim q$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Writing conditional as a disjunction: $$\left. p\rightarrow q \equiv \right.\sim p \vee q$$</paragraph>

<example number="2.26" title="Applying De Morgan’s Law for Negation of Conjunctions and Disjunctions">

<example number="2.29" title="Negating a Conditional Statement with a Conjunction or Disjunction">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write the negation of each conditional statement applying De Morgan’s Law.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>If mom needs to buy chips, then Mike had friends over and Bob was hungry.</item>
        <item>If Juan had pizza or Chris had wings, then dad watched the game.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The conditional has the form “If $$p$$ then $$q$$ or $$r$$ ,” where $$p$$ is “Mom needs to buy chips,” $$q$$ is “Mike had friends over,” and $$r$$ is “Bob was hungry.” The negation of $$\left. p\rightarrow(q \land r) \right.$$ is $$\left. p \land \right.\sim(q \land r).$$ Applying De Morgan’s Law to the statement $$\sim(q \land r)$$ the result is $$\sim\left. q \vee \right.\sim r$$ , so our conditional statement becomes $$\left. p \land ( \right.\sim\left. q \vee \right.\sim r).$$ By the distributive property for conjunction over disjunction, this statement is equivalent to $$\left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim q} \right) \vee \left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim r} \right).$$ Translating the statement $$\left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim q} \right) \vee \left( {\left. p \land \right.\sim r} \right)$$ into words, the solution is: “Mom needs to buy chips and Mike did not have friends over, or Mom needs to buy chips and Bob was not hungry.”</item>
        <item>The conditional has the form “If $$p$$ or $$q$$ , then $$r$$ ,” where $$p$$ is “Juan had pizza,” $$q$$ is “Chris had wings,” and $$r$$ is “Dad watched the game.” The negation of $$\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right)\rightarrow r \right.$$ is $$\left. \left( {p \vee q} \right) \land \right.\sim r.$$ By the distributive property for disjunction over conjuction, the statement is equivalent to $$\left( {\left. p \vee \right.\sim r} \right) \land \left( {\left. q \vee \right.\sim r} \right).$$ Translating the statement $$\left( {\left. p \vee \right.\sim r} \right) \land \left( {\left. q \vee \right.\sim r} \right)$$ into words, the solution is: “Juan had pizza or dad did not watch the game, and Chris had wings or dad did not watch the game.”</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine if 2,117 is prime or composite.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The square root of 2,117 is 46.0 (rounded to one decimal place). So, we need to check if 2,117 is divisible by any prime up to 46.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: First we’ll use the rules of divisibility we learned earlier:</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>We can tell 2,117 is not divisible by 2, as the last digit isn't even.</item>
        <item>2,117 is not divisible by 5 (the last digit isn't 0 or 5).</item>
        <item>Add the digits of 2,117 to get 11, which is not divisible by 3. So, 2,117 is also not divisible by 3.</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Now we repeat the process for all the primes up to 46.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using a calculator, we find that 2,117 divided by the prime numbers 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, and 23 results in a remainder, a decimal part. So, we know that 2,117 is not divisible by these prime numbers. (You should check these results yourself.)</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Moving on, we check the next prime: 29. Using the calculator to divide 2,117 by 29 results in 73. Since there is no decimal part, 2,117 is divisible by 29.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This means that 2,117 is not a prime number, but rather, a composite number. Writing 2,117 as the product of 29 and another natural number, $$2,117 = 29 \times 73$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>

Since 2 is a factor, that branch is done, and 2 is a leaf. Step 2: The 33, though, is divisible by 3, and is the product of 3 and 11. We attach that to the factor tree (Figure 3.6). Since the 2, 3 and 11 are all prime, the factor tree is done. The prime factorization of 66 is the product of the leaves, so $$66 = 2 \times 3 \times 11$$ . The factorization is complete.

title: Finding the Prime Factorization

body_xml: Find the prime factorization of 135. The number 135 is divisible by 3, and so 3 is a factor of 135. Step 1: Factor out the 3. The factorization is $$135 = 3 \times 45$$ . Using the factor tree (Figure 3.7), 45 is also divisible by 3. Step 2: Factor out a 3 from 45. The other factor is 15. The factor tree is shown in Figure 3.8. 15 is also divisible by 3. Step 3: The factors of 15 are 3 and 5. The factor tree is shown in Figure 3.9. All the leaves are prime, so the process is complete. The prime factorization of 135 is $$3^{3} \times 5$$ .

title: Identifying Prime Factors
snippet: Identifying Prime Factors: How many different prime factors does 10,241 have? To know how many different prime factors 10,241 has, we need the prime factorization of 10,241. Step 1: Use divisibility rules, to see that the number 10,241 is...
body_xml:
<example number="3.14" title="Identifying Prime Factors">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>How many different prime factors does 10,241 have?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To know how many different prime factors 10,241 has, we need the prime factorization of 10,241.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Use divisibility rules, to see that the number 10,241 is not divisible by 2 or by 3 (the sum of the digits is 8), or by 5. However, it is divisible by 7.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: After factoring the 7, the factorization is $$10,241 = 7 \times 1463$$ ; 1,463 is also divisible by 7.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: After factoring the 7, the factorization is $$10,241 = 7 \times 7 \times 209 = 7^{2} \times 209$$ . The number 209 is not divisible by 7.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Check the next prime number: 11; 11 does divide 1,463.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: After factoring the 11, the factorization is $$10,241 = 7^{2} \times 11 \times 19$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since 19 is prime, the prime factorization of 10,241 is complete. We see that 10,241 has three different prime factors: 7, 11, and 19.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.15" title="Finding the Greatest Common Divisor Using Lists">

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We create a list of all the divisors of 1,400 and of 250, and choose the largest one.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The divisors of 1,400 are</paragraph>
      <paragraph>1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 14, 20, 25, 28, 35, 40, 50, 56, 70, 100, 140, 175, 200, 280, 350, 700, 1,400.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The divisors of 250 are</paragraph>
      <paragraph>1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 125, 250.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The largest value that appears on both lists is 50, so the greatest common divisor of 1,400 and 250 is 50.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Greatest Common Divisor Using Prime Factorization
snippet: Finding the Greatest Common Divisor Using Prime Factorization: Find the greatest common divisor of 1,400 and 250 by using their prime factorizations. Step 1: Find the prime factorizations of the numbers. The prime factorization of 1,400 is...
body_xml:
<example number="3.16" title="Finding the Greatest Common Divisor Using Prime Factorization">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the greatest common divisor of 1,400 and 250 by using their prime factorizations.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Find the prime factorizations of the numbers.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 1,400 is $$2^{3} \times 5^{2} \times 7$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 250 is $$250 = 2 \times 5^{3}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Identify the prime factors that appear in every number’s prime factorization.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The common prime factors are 2 and 5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Identify the smallest exponent of each prime identified in Step 2 in the prime factorizations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The exponent of common prime factor 2 in the prime factorization of 1,400 is 3, and in the prime factorization of 250 is 1. The smallest of those exponents is 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The exponent of the common prime factor 5 in the prime factorization of 1,400 is 2 and is in the prime factorization of 250 is 3. The smallest of these exponents is 2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Multiply the prime factors identified in Step 2 raised to the powers identified in Step 3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives $$2^{1} \times 5^{2} = 50$$ . The greatest common divisor of 1,400 and 250 is $$2 \times 5^{2} = 50$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that the answer matches the one we found in Example 3.15.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Find the prime factorizations of the numbers.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 600 is $$2^{3} \times 3 \times 5^{2}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 784 is $$2^{4} \times 7^{2}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Identify the prime factors that appear in every number’s prime factorization.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>There is only one common prime factor, 2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Identify the smallest exponent of each prime from identified in Step 2 in the prime factorizations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The exponent of 2 in the prime factorization of 600 is 3. The exponent of 2 in the prime factorization of 784 is 4. So, the smallest exponent of 2 is 3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Multiply the prime factors identified in Step 2 raised to the powers identified in Step 3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives $$2^{3} = 8$$ . The greatest common divisor of 600 and 784 is 8.</paragraph>

title: Calculating Floor Tile Size
snippet: Calculating Floor Tile Size: Suppose you have a rectangular room that is 570 cm wide and 450 cm long. You wish to cover the floor of the room with square tiles. What’s the largest size square tile that can be used to cover this floor?...
body_xml:
<example number="3.18" title="Calculating Floor Tile Size">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose you have a rectangular room that is 570 cm wide and 450 cm long. You wish to cover the floor of the room with square tiles. What’s the largest size square tile that can be used to cover this floor?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using squares means that the length and width of the tiles are equal. To ensure we are using full tiles, the side length of the square tiles must divide the length of the room and the width of the room. Since we want the largest square tiles, we need the GCD of the width and length of the room or the GCD of 570 and 450.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Find the prime factorizations of the numbers.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 570 is $$2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 19$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 450 is $$2 \times 3^{2} \times 5^{2}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Identify the prime factors that appear in every number’s prime factorization.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The common prime factors are 2, 3, and 5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Identify the smallest exponent of each prime identified in Step 2 in the prime factorizations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The exponents of 2 in the prime factorizations of 570 and 450 are 1 and 1. So the smallest exponent for 2 is 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The exponents of 3 in the prime factorizations of 570 and 450 are 1 and 2, so the smallest exponent for 3 is 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The exponents of 5 in the prime factorizations of 570 and 450 are 1 and 2, so the smallest exponent for 5 is 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Multiply the prime factors identified in Step 2 raised to the powers identified in Step 3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives $$2^{1} \times 3^{1} \times 5^{1} = 30$$ . The GCD of 450 and 570 is 30, so the largest size square tile that can be used to cover the floor is 30 cm by 30 cm.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Organizing Books Per Shelf
snippet: Organizing Books Per Shelf: Suppose you want to organize books onto shelves, and you want the shelves to hold the same number of books. Each shelf will only contain one genre of book. You have 24 sci-fi, 42 fantasy, and 30 horror books....
body_xml:
<example number="3.19" title="Organizing Books Per Shelf">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose you want to organize books onto shelves, and you want the shelves to hold the same number of books. Each shelf will only contain one genre of book. You have 24 sci-fi, 42 fantasy, and 30 horror books. How many books can go on each shelf?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since we want shelves that hold an equal number of books, and a shelf can only hold one genre of book, we need a number that will equally divide 24, 42, and 30. So, we need the GCD of the number of books of each genre or the GCD of 24, 42, and 30.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Find the prime factorizations of the numbers.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 24 is $$2^{3} \times 3$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 42 is $$2 \times 3 \times 7$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The prime factorization of 30 is $$2 \times 3 \times 5$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Identify the prime factors that appear in every number’s prime factorization.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The common prime factors are 2 and 3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Identify the smallest exponent of each prime identified in Step 2 in the prime factorizations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The smallest exponent of 2 and 3 in the factorizations is 1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Multiply the prime factors identified in Step 2 raised to the powers identified in Step 3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives $$2^{1} \times 3^{1} = 6$$ . The GCD of 24, 42, and 30 is 6, so the largest number of books that can go on a shelf is 6.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Finding the Least Common Multiple Using Prime Factorization: Use the prime factorizations of 24 and 90 to identify their LCM. Step 1: Find the prime factorization of each number. 24 = 2^{3} \times 3 90 = 2 \times 3^{2} \times 5 Step 2:...
body_xml:
Use the prime factorizations of 24 and 90 to identify their LCM. Step 1: Find the prime factorization of each number. $$24 = 2^{3} \times 3$$ $$90 = 2 \times 3^{2} \times 5$$ Step 2: Identify each prime that is present in any of the prime factorizations. The prime numbers present in the prime factorizations are 2, 3, and 5. Step 3: Identify the largest exponent of each prime identified in Step 2 in the prime factorizations. Prime 2 3 5 Largest exponent 3 2 1
Step 4: Compute the LCM by multiplying the prime factors identified in Step 2 raised to the powers identified in Step 3. The LCM for 24 and 90 is $$2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 = 2^{3} \times 3^{2} \times 5^{1} = 360$$ .

title: Finding the Least Common Multiple Using Prime Factorization
snippet: Finding the Least Common Multiple Using Prime Factorization: Use the prime factorizations of 36, 66, and 250 to identify the LCM. Step 1: Find the prime factorization of each number. 36 = 2^{2} \times 3^{2} 66 = 2 \times 3 \times 11 250 =...
body_xml:
Use the prime factorizations of 36, 66, and 250 to identify the LCM. Step 1: Find the prime factorization of each number. $$36 = 2^{2} \times 3^{2}$$ $$66 = 2 \times 3 \times 11$$ $$250 = 2 \times 5^{3}$$ Step 2: Identify each prime that is present in any of the prime factorizations. The prime numbers present in the prime factorizations are 2, 3, 5, and 11. Step 3: Identify the largest exponent of each prime identified in Step 2 in the prime factorizations. Prime 2 3 5 11 Largest exponent 2 2 3 1
Step 4: Compute the LCM by multiplying the prime factors identified in Step 2 raised to the powers identified in Step 3. The LCM for 36, 66, and 250 is $$2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 5 \times 5 \times 11 = 2^{2} \times 3^{2} \times 5^{3} \times 11^{1} = 49,500$$ .

title: Finding the Least Common Multiple Using Both Methods
snippet: Finding the Least Common Multiple Using Both Methods: Find the LCM of 20, 36, and 45 using lists and prime factorization. Step 1: Use listing. List the multiples: 20 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200, 220 36 36, 72, 108, 144,...
body_xml:
Find the LCM of 20, 36, and 45 using lists and prime factorization. Step 1: Use listing. List the multiples: 20 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200, 220 36 36, 72, 108, 144, 180, 216, 252, 288, 324, 360 45 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, 315, 360, 405, 450, 495, 540
The smallest value that appears on all the lists is 180, so 180 is the LCM of 20, 36, and 45. Step 2: Find the prime factorization of each number. $$20 = 2^{2} \times 5$$ $$36 = 2^{2} \times 3^{2}$$ $$45 = 3^{2} \times 5$$ Step 3: Identify each prime that is present in any of the prime factorizations. The prime numbers present in the prime factorizations are 2, 3, 5. Step 4: Identify the largest exponent of each prime identified in Step 3 in the prime factorizations. Prime 2 3 5 Largest exponent 2 2 1
Step 5: Compute the LCM by multiplying the prime factors identified in Step 3 raised to the powers identified in Step 4. The LCM for 20, 36, and 45 is $$2^{2} \times 3^{2} \times 5^{1} = 180$$ . Both listing and prime factorization produced the same result: the LCM is 180.

<example number="3.24" title="Determining Scheduling Overlap Using the Least Common Multiple">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Two students, João, and Amelia, meet one day at an assisted living facility where they volunteer. João volunteers every 6 days. Amelia volunteers every 10 days. How many days will it be until they are both volunteering on the same day again?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>If we list the days that each student will volunteer, it becomes clear that we could solve this problem using the LCM of 6 and 10.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>João will be at the assisted living facility 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, and 48 days later.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Amelia will be at the assisted living facility 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 days later.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The smallest number appearing on both lists is 30. João and Amelia will once more be volunteering together 30 days later.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.25" title="Determining the Minimum Height Using the LCM">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A team-building exercise has teams build a house of cards as high as possible. However, the cards for different teams are of different sizes. Team 1 uses 10 cm × 10 cm cards, while Team 2 uses 8 cm × 8 cm cards. What is the minimum height when the two teams will be tied? Ignore the width of the cards.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This is an example where we want to put together objects with different sizes. We want to know the minimum height when they are tied, or when the houses of cards line up the first time. The heights of the towers built using the 10 cm × 10 cm cards will be 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 cm tall. When the 8 cm × 8 cm cards are used, the tower will be 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, and 56 cm tall. The smallest number appearing on both lists is 40. The first time they are tied is when the two towers are 40 cm tall.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml: Which of the following are integers and which are not? −3 Is an integer, as it is the negative of a counting number $$\sqrt{24}$$ This is not written as an integer. Entering the square root of 24 in a calculator, such as desmos, the result is 4.899 (rounded off). Since this is not an integer, then $$\sqrt{24}$$ is not an integer. 36/4 Since 36 divided by 4 is 9, and 9 is an integer, then 36/4 is an integer. 45 Is an integer, as it is a counting number 63.9 Is not an integer, because it is not a counting number and not the negative of a counting number. 2/7 Dividing 2 by 7 results in a number less than 1, but greater than 0, so is between two consecutive integers. So, 2/7 is not an integer. −16.0 Is an integer, since the decimal part is 0

<example number="3.42" title="Finding the Average of a Set of Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The daily low temperatures in Barrie, Ontario, for the week of February 14, 2021, were −20°, −12°, −15°, −23°, −17°, −13°, and −19° degrees Celsius. What was the average daily temperature for the week of February 14, 2021, in Barrie?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: To find the average daily temperature, we first need to add the temperatures.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>(−20) + (−12) + (−15) + (−23) + (−17) + (−13) + (−19) = −119</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: That sum will then be divided by 7 since we are averaging over seven days, giving −119/7 = −17. So, the average daily temperature in Barrie, Ontario the week of February 14, 2021, was −17° Celsius.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.43" title="Using Two Order of Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate $$21 - 4 \times 13$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>There are no exponents in this expression, so the next operations to check are multiplication and division.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Moving left to right, the first multiplication encountered is 4 multiplied by 13. We perform that operation first.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {21 - \mathbf{4 \times 13}} \\ {= 21\mathbf{- 52}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: The only operation remaining is the subtraction.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$21 - 52 = - 31$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, $$21 - 4 \times 13 = - 31$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.45" title="Using Three Order of Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate $$2 + 3^{2} \times 4$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: To calculate this, move left to right, and compute all the exponents first. The only exponent we see is the squaring of the 3, so that is calculated first.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$2 + 3^{2} \times 4 = 2 + \mathbf{\left( {3 \times 3} \right)} \times 4 = 2 + \mathbf{9} \times 4$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Since the exponents are all calculated, now calculate all the multiplications and divisions moving left to right. The only multiplication or division present is 9 times 4.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$2 + 9\mathbf{\times}4 = 2 + \mathbf{36}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Moving left to right, perform the additions and subtractions. There is only one such operation, 2 plus 36.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$2 + 36 = 38$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, $$2 + 3^{2} \times 4 = 38$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Eight Order of Operations
snippet: Using Eight Order of Operations: Correctly apply the order of operations to compute the following: 4 - 25 \times 6/10 \times 3^{2} + 7 \times 2^{3} . Step 1: To do so, calculate the exponents first, moving left to right. There are two...
body_xml:
<example number="3.46" title="Using Eight Order of Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Correctly apply the order of operations to compute the following:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$4 - 25 \times 6/10 \times 3^{2} + 7 \times 2^{3}$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: To do so, calculate the exponents first, moving left to right. There are two occurrences of exponents in the expression, 3 squared and 2 cubed.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$4 - 25 \times 6/10 \times \mathbf{3^{2}} + 7 \times \mathbf{2^{3}} = 4 - 25 \times 6/10 \times \mathbf{9} + 7 \times \mathbf{8}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Now that the exponents are calculated, perform the multiplication and division, moving left to right. The first is the product of 25 and 6.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 - \mathbf{25 \times 6}/10 \times 9 + 7 \times 8} \\ {= 4 - \mathbf{150}/10 \times 9 + 7 \times 8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Next is the 150 divided by 10.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 - \mathbf{150/10} \times 9 + 7 \times 8} \\ {= 4 - \mathbf{15} \times 9 + 7 \times 8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Next is 15 multiplied by 9.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 - \mathbf{15 \times 9} + 7 \times 8} \\ {= 4 - \mathbf{135} + 7 \times 8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: Finally, multiply the 7 and 8.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 - 135 + \mathbf{7 \times 8}} \\ {= 4 - 135 + \mathbf{56}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>As all the multiplications and divisions have been calculated, the additions and subtractions are performed, moving left to right.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{4 - 135} + 56} \\ {= \mathbf{- 131} + 56} \\ {= \mathbf{- 131 + 56}} \\ {= \mathbf{- 75}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The computed value is −75.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.47" title="Using Six Order of Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Correctly apply the rules for the order of operations to accurately compute the following:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$10 - 3 \times 5^{3}/15 + 56/4$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Calculate exponents first, moving left to right:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {10 - 3 \times \mathbf{5^{3}}/15 + 56/4} \\ {= 10 - 3 \times \mathbf{125}/15 + 56/4} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Multiply and divide, moving left to right:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {10 - \mathbf{3 \times 125}/15 + 56/4} \\ {= 10 - \mathbf{375/15} + 56/4} \\ {= 10 - 25 + \mathbf{56/4}} \\ {= 10 - 25 + \mathbf{14}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Add and subtract, moving left to right:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{10 - 25} + 14} \\ {= \mathbf{- 15 + 14}} \\ {= - 1} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Order of Operations
snippet: Using Order of Operations: Correctly apply the rules for the order of operations to accurately compute the following: ( - 8)/2 \times 3 - 9 \times 2^{4}/12 + 9 \times {( - 4)}^{2}/2^{3} . Step 1: Calculate the exponents first, moving left...

<example number="3.48" title="Using Order of Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Correctly apply the rules for the order of operations to accurately compute the following: $$( - 8)/2 \times 3 - 9 \times 2^{4}/12 + 9 \times {( - 4)}^{2}/2^{3}$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Calculate the exponents first, moving left to right:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {( - 8)/2 \times 3 - 9 \times \mathbf{2^{4}}/12 + 9 \times {( - 4)}^{2}/2^{3}} \\ {= ( - 8)/2 \times 3 - 9 \times 16/12 + 9 \times \mathbf{12^{2}}/2^{3}} \\ {= ( - 8)/2 \times 3 - 9 \times 16/12 + 9 \times 144/\mathbf{2^{3}}} \\ {= ( - 8)/2 \times 3 - 9 \times 16/12 + 9 \times 144/8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Multiply and divide, moving left to right:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {= \mathbf{( - 8)/2} \times 3 - 9 \times 16/12 + 9 \times 144/8} \\ {= \mathbf{( - 4) \times 3} - 9 \times 16/12 + 9 \times 144/8} \\ {= ( - 12) - \mathbf{9 \times 16}/12 + 9 \times 144/8} \\ {= ( - 12) - \mathbf{144/12} + 9 \times 144/8} \\ {= ( - 12) - 12 + \mathbf{9 \times 144}/8} \\ {= ( - 12) - 12 + \mathbf{1,296/8}} \\ {= ( - 12) - 12 + 162} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Add and subtract, moving left to right:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$= \mathbf{( - 12) - 12} + 162 = \mathbf{( - 24) + 162} = 138$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Working Innermost Parentheses in the Order of Operations
snippet: Working Innermost Parentheses in the Order of Operations: Correctly apply the rules for order of operations to accurately compute the following: 4 + 2 \times (3^{2} - {(2 + 5)}^{2} \times 4)/(3 + 8) . Step 1: Perform all calculations...
body_xml:
<example number="3.50" title="Working Innermost Parentheses in the Order of Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Correctly apply the rules for order of operations to accurately compute the following:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$4 + 2 \times (3^{2} - {(2 + 5)}^{2} \times 4)/(3 + 8)$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Perform all calculations within the parentheses before other operations. Evaluate the innermost parentheses first. We can work separate parentheses expressions at the same time. The innermost set of parentheses has the 2 + 5 inside. The 3 + 8 is in a separate set of parentheses, so that addition can occur at the same time as the 2 + 5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 + 2 \times (3^{2} - {(\mathbf{2 + 5})}^{2} \times 4)/(\mathbf{3 + 8})} \\ {= 4 + 2 \times (3^{2} - {(\mathbf{7})}^{2} \times 4)/(\mathbf{11})} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Now that those parentheses have been handled, move on to the next set of parentheses. Applying the order of operation rules inside that set of parentheses, the exponent is evaluated first, then the multiplication, and then the addition.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 + 2 \times (\mathbf{3^{2} - 7^{2} \times 4})/11} \\ {= 4 + 2 \times (\mathbf{3^{2} - 49 \times 4})/11} \\ {= 4 + 2 \times \left( \mathbf{- 187} \right)/11} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Since all parentheses have been cleared, apply the EMDAS rules to finish the calculation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$4 + \mathbf{2 \times ( - 187)}/11 = 4 - \mathbf{374/11} = \mathbf{4 - 34} = - 30$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Identifying Perfect Squares: Which of the following are perfect squares? 45 144 We could attempt to find the perfect square by factoring. Writing all the factor pairs of 45 results in 1 \times 45,3 \times 15 , and 5 \times 9 . None of the...

<example number="3.51" title="Identifying Perfect Squares">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Which of the following are perfect squares?</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>45</item>
        <item>144</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>We could attempt to find the perfect square by factoring. Writing all the factor pairs of 45 results in $$1 \times 45,3 \times 15$$ , and $$5 \times 9$$ . None of the pairs is a square, so 45 is not a perfect square. Using a calculator to find the square root of 45, we obtain 6.708 (rounded to three decimal places). Since this was not an integer, the original number was not a perfect square.</item>
        <item>We could attempt to find the perfect square by factoring. Writing all the factor pairs of 144 results in $$1 \times 144,2 \times 72,3 \times 48,6 \times 24,8 \times 18$$ , and $$12 \times 12$$ . Since the last pair is an integer multiplied by itself, 144 is a perfect square. Alternately, using Desmos to find the square root of 144, we obtain 12. Since the square root of 144 is an integer, 144 is a perfect square.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.52" title="Identifying Rational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine which of the following are rational numbers:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\sqrt{73}$$</item>
        <item>$$4.556$$</item>
        <item>$$3\frac{1}{5}$$</item>
        <item>$$\frac{41}{17}$$</item>
        <item>$$5.\overline{64}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Since 73 is not a perfect square, its square root is not a rational number. This can also be seen when a calculator is used. Entering $$\sqrt{73}$$ into a calculator results in 8.544003745317 (and then more decimal values after that). There is no repeated pattern, so this is not a rational number.</item>
        <item>Since 4.556 is a decimal that terminates, this is a rational number.</item>
        <item>$$3\frac{1}{5}$$ is a mixed number, so it is a rational number.</item>
        <item>$$\frac{41}{17}$$ is an integer divided by an integer, so it is a rational number.</item>
        <item>$$5.646464...$$ is a decimal that repeats a pattern, so it is a rational number.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Reducing Fractions to Lowest Terms
snippet: Reducing Fractions to Lowest Terms: Express the following rational numbers in lowest terms: \frac{36}{48} \frac{100}{250} \frac{51}{136} One process to reduce \frac{36}{48} to lowest terms is to identify the GCD of 36 and 48 and divide out...
body_xml:
<example number="3.54" title="Reducing Fractions to Lowest Terms">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Express the following rational numbers in lowest terms:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\frac{36}{48}$$</item>
        <item>$$\frac{100}{250}$$</item>
        <item>$$\frac{51}{136}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>One process to reduce $$\frac{36}{48}$$ to lowest terms is to identify the GCD of 36 and 48 and divide out the GCD. The GCD of 36 and 48 is 12. Step 1: We can then rewrite the numerator and denominator by factoring 12 from both. $$\frac{36}{48} = \frac{12 \times 3}{12 \times 4}$$ Step 2: We can now divide out the 12s from the numerator and denominator. $$\frac{36}{48} = \frac{12 \times 3}{12 \times 4} = \frac{3}{4}$$ So, when $$\frac{36}{48}$$ is reduced to lowest terms, the result is $$\frac{3}{4}$$ . Alternately, you could identify a common factor, divide out that common factor, and repeat the process until the remaining fraction is in lowest terms. Step 1: You may notice that 4 is a common factor of 36 and 48. Step 2: Divide out the 4, as in $$\frac{36}{48} = \frac{4 \times 9}{4 \times 12} = \frac{4 \times 9}{4 \times 12} = \frac{9}{12}$$ . Step 3: Examining the 9 and 12, you identify 3 as a common factor and divide out the 3, as in $$\frac{9}{12} = \frac{3 \times 3}{3 \times 4} = \frac{3}{4}$$ . The 3 and 4 have no common positive factors other than 1, so it is in lowest terms. So, when $$\frac{36}{48}$$ is reduced to lowest terms, the result is $$\frac{3}{4}$$ .</item>
        <item>Step 1: To reduce $$\frac{100}{250}$$ to lowest terms, identify the GCD of 100 and 250. This GCD is 50. Step 2: We can then rewrite the numerator and denominator by factoring 50 from both. $$\frac{100}{250} = \frac{50 \times 2}{50 \times 5}$$ . Step 3: We can now divide out the 50s from the numerator and denominator. $$\frac{100}{250} = \frac{50 \times 2}{50 \times 5} = \frac{2}{5}$$ So, when $$\frac{100}{250}$$ is reduced to lowest terms, the result is $$\frac{2}{5}$$ .</item>
        <item>Step 1: To reduce $$\frac{51}{136}$$ to lowest terms, identify the GCD of 51 and 136. This GCD is 17. Step 2: We can then rewrite the numerator and denominator by factoring 17 from both. $$\frac{51}{136} = \frac{17 \times 3}{17 \times 8}$$ Step 3: We can now divide out the 17s from the numerator and denominator. $$\frac{51}{136} = \frac{17 \times 3}{17 \times 8} = \frac{3}{8}$$ So, when $$\frac{51}{136}$$ is reduced to lowest terms, the result is $$\frac{3}{8}$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.56" title="Adding Rational Numbers with the Same Denominator">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate $$\frac{13}{28} + \frac{7}{28}$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the rational numbers have the same denominator, we perform the addition of the numerators, $$13 + 7$$ , and then place the result in the numerator and the common denominator, 28, in the denominator. $$\frac{13}{28} + \frac{7}{28} = \frac{13 + 7}{28} = \frac{20}{28}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Once we have that result, reduce to lowest terms, which gives $$\frac{20}{28} = \frac{4 \times 5}{4 \times 7} = \frac{4 \times 5}{4 \times 7} = \frac{5}{7}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the rational numbers have the same denominator, we perform the subtraction of the numerators, $$45 - 17$$ , and then place the result in the numerator and the common denominator, 136, in the denominator. $$\frac{45}{136} - \frac{17}{136} - \frac{45 - 17}{136} = \frac{28}{136}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Once we have that result, reduce to lowest terms, this gives $$\frac{28}{136} = \frac{4 \times 7}{4 \times 34} = \frac{4 \times 7}{4 \times 34} = \frac{7}{34}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.58" title="Adding Rational Numbers with Unequal Denominators">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate $$\frac{11}{18} + \frac{2}{15}$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The denominators of the fractions are 18 and 15, so we label $$b = 18$$ and $$d = 15$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Find LCM(18,15). This is 90.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Calculate $$n$$ and $$m$$ . $$n = \frac{90}{18} = 5$$ and $$m = \frac{90}{15} = 6$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Multiplying the numerator and denominator of $$\frac{11}{18}$$ by $$n = 5$$ yields $$\frac{11 \times 5}{18 \times 5} = \frac{55}{90}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Multiply the numerator and denominator of $$\frac{2}{15}$$ by $$m = 6$$ yields $$\frac{2 \times 6}{15 \times 6} = \frac{12}{90}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: Now we add the values from Steps 3 and 4: $$\frac{55}{90} + \frac{12}{90} = \frac{67}{90}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This is in lowest terms, so we have found that $$\frac{11}{18} + \frac{2}{15} = \frac{67}{90}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <problem>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>The denominators of the fractions are 25 and 70, so we label $$b = 25$$ and $$d = 70$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Find LCM(25,70). This is 350.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Calculate $$n$$ and $$m$$ : $$n = \frac{350}{25} = 14$$ and $$m = \frac{350}{70} = 5$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Multiplying the numerator and denominator of $$\frac{14}{25}$$ by $$n = 14$$ yields $$\frac{14 \times 14}{25 \times 14} = \frac{196}{350}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Multiplying the numerator and denominator of $$\frac{9}{70}$$ by $$m = 5$$ yields $$\frac{9 \times 5}{70 \times 5} = \frac{45}{350}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: Now we subtract the value from Step 4 from the value in Step 3: $$\frac{196}{350} - \frac{45}{350} = \frac{151}{350}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This is in lowest terms, so we have found that $$\frac{14}{25} - \frac{9}{70} = \frac{151}{350}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.68" title="Dividing Rational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Calculate $$\frac{4}{21} \div \frac{6}{35}$$ .</item>
        <item>Calculate $$\frac{1}{8} \div \frac{5}{28}$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Step 1: Find the reciprocal of the number being divided by $$\frac{6}{35}$$ . The reciprocal of that is $$\frac{35}{6}$$ . Step 2: Multiply the first fraction by that reciprocal. $$\frac{4}{21} \div \frac{6}{35} = \frac{4}{21} \times \frac{35}{6} = \frac{140}{126}$$ The answer, $$\frac{140}{126}$$ is not in lowest terms. The GCD of 140 and 126 is 14. Factoring and canceling gives $$\frac{140}{126} = \frac{14 \times 10}{14 \times 9} = \frac{10}{9}$$ .</item>
        <item>Step 1: Find the reciprocal of the number being divided by, which is $$\frac{5}{28}$$ . The reciprocal of that is $$\frac{28}{5}$$ . Step 2: Multiply the first fraction by that reciprocal: $$\frac{1}{8} \div \frac{5}{28} = \frac{1}{8} \times \frac{28}{5} = \frac{28}{40}$$ The answer, $$\frac{28}{40}$$ , is not in lowest reduced form. The GCD of 28 and 40 is 4. Factoring and canceling gives $$\frac{28}{40} = \frac{4 \times 7}{4 \times 10} = \frac{7}{10}$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph>Step 1: To calculate this, perform all calculations within the parentheses before other operations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\left( \frac{5}{7} - \frac{2}{7} \right) \times 2^{3} = \left( \frac{3}{7} \right) \times 2^{3}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Since all parentheses have been cleared, we move left to right, and compute all the exponents next.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\left( \frac{3}{7} \right) \times 2^{3} = \left( \frac{3}{7} \right) \times 8$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Now, perform all multiplications and divisions, moving left to right.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\left( \frac{3}{7} \right) \times 8 = \frac{24}{7}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="3.70" title="Applying the Order of Operations with Rational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Correctly apply the rules for the order of operations to accurately compute $$4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( {\left( \frac{5}{9} \right)^{2} - \left( {\frac{2}{3} + 5} \right)} \right)^{2}$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To calculate this, perform all calculations within the parentheses before other operations. Evaluate the innermost parentheses first. We can work separate parentheses expressions at the same time.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: The innermost parentheses contain $$\frac{2}{3} + 5$$ . Calculate that first, dividing after finding the common denominator.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( {\left( \frac{5}{9} \right)^{2} - \left( \mathbf{\frac{2}{3} + 5} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {= 4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( {\left( \frac{5}{9} \right)^{2} - \left( \mathbf{\frac{2}{3} + \frac{5}{1}} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {= 4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( {\left( \frac{5}{9} \right)^{2} - \left( \mathbf{\frac{2}{3} + \frac{15}{3}} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {= 4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( {\left( \frac{5}{9} \right)^{2}\mathbf{- \left( \frac{17}{3} \right)}} \right)^{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Calculate the exponent in the parentheses, $$\left( \frac{5}{9} \right)^{2}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( {\mathbf{\left( \frac{5}{9} \right)^{2}} - \left( \frac{17}{3} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {= 4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( {\mathbf{\left( \frac{25}{81} \right)} - \left( \frac{17}{3} \right)} \right)^{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Subtract inside the parentheses is done, using a common denominator.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( \mathbf{\left( \frac{25}{81} \right) - \left( \frac{17}{3} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( \mathbf{\left( \frac{25}{81} \right) - \left( \frac{17 \times 27}{3 \times 27} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( \mathbf{\left( \frac{25}{81} \right) - \left( \frac{459}{81} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( \mathbf{\left( \frac{- 434}{81} \right)} \right)^{2}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: At this point, evaluate the exponent and divide.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \left( \mathbf{\left( \frac{- 434}{81} \right)} \right)^{2}} \\ {4 + \frac{2}{3} \div \mathbf{\left( \frac{188,356}{6,561} \right)}} \\ {= 4 + \mathbf{\frac{2}{3} \times \left( \frac{6,561}{188,356} \right)}} \\ {= \mathbf{4 + \frac{2,187}{94,178}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: Add.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} \mathbf{4 + \frac{2,187}{94,178}} \\ {= \frac{378,899}{94,178}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Had this been done on a calculator, the decimal form of the answer would be 4.0232 (rounded to four decimal places).</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying the Density Property of Rational Numbers
snippet: Applying the Density Property of Rational Numbers: Demonstrate the density property of rational numbers by finding a rational number between \frac{4}{11} and \frac{7}{12} . To find a rational number between \frac{4}{11} and \frac{7}{12} :...
body_xml:
<example number="3.71" title="Applying the Density Property of Rational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Demonstrate the density property of rational numbers by finding a rational number between $$\frac{4}{11}$$ and $$\frac{7}{12}$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find a rational number between $$\frac{4}{11}$$ and $$\frac{7}{12}$$ :</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Add the fractions.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\frac{4}{11} + \frac{7}{12} = \frac{4 \times 12}{11 \times 12} + \frac{7 \times 11}{12 \times 11} = \frac{48}{132} + \frac{77}{132} = \frac{125}{132}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Divide the result by 2. Recall that to divide by 2, you multiply by the reciprocal of 2. The reciprocal of 2 is $$\frac{1}{2}$$ , as seen below.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\frac{125}{132} \div 2 = \frac{125}{132} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{125}{264}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, one rational number between $$\frac{4}{11}$$ and $$\frac{7}{12}$$ is $$\frac{125}{264}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We could check that the number we found is between the other two by finding the decimal representation of the numbers. Using a calculator, the decimal representations of the rational numbers are 0.363636…, 0.473484848…, and 0.5833333…. Here it is clear that $$\frac{125}{264}$$ is between $$\frac{4}{11}$$ and $$\frac{7}{12}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Mixing Soil for Vegetables
snippet: Mixing Soil for Vegetables: James is mixing soil for a raised garden, in which he plans to grow a variety of vegetables. For the soil to be suitable, he determines that \frac{2}{5} of the soil can be topsoil, but \frac{2}{5} needs to be...
body_xml:
<example number="3.72" title="Mixing Soil for Vegetables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>James is mixing soil for a raised garden, in which he plans to grow a variety of vegetables. For the soil to be suitable, he determines that $$\frac{2}{5}$$ of the soil can be topsoil, but $$\frac{2}{5}$$ needs to be peat moss and $$\frac{1}{5}$$ has to be compost. To fill the raised garden bed with 60 cubic feet of soil, how much of each component does James need to use?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>In this example, we know the proportion of each component to mix, and we know the total amount of the mix we need. In this kind of situation, we need to determine the appropriate amount of each component to include in the mixture. For each component of the mixture, multiply 60 cubic feet, which is the total volume of the mixture we want, by the fraction required of the component.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: The required fraction of topsoil is $$\frac{2}{5}$$ , so James needs $$60 \times \frac{2}{5}$$ cubic feet of topsoil. Performing the multiplication, James needs $$60 \times \frac{2}{5} = \frac{120}{5} = 24$$ (found by treating the fraction as division, and 120 divided by 5 is 24) cubic feet of topsoil.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: The required fraction of peat moss is also $$\frac{2}{5}$$ , so he also needs $$60 \times \frac{2}{5}$$ cubic feet, or $$60 \times \frac{2}{5} = \frac{120}{5} = 24$$ cubic feet of peat moss.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: The required fraction of compost is $$\frac{1}{5}$$ . For the compost, he needs $$60 \times \frac{1}{5} = \frac{60}{5} = 12$$ cubic feet.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph>One-third of the whole are specialty pizzas, so we need one-third of 273, which gives $$\frac{1}{3} \times 273 = \frac{273}{3} = 91$$ , found by dividing 273 by 3. So, 91 of the pizzas that were ordered were specialty pizzas.</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>We know that 1 liter = 0.264172 gal. Since we are converting from liters, when we create the fraction we use, make sure the liter part of the equivalence is in the denominator. So, to convert the 14 liters to gallons, we multiply 14 by $$\frac{1{gal}}{0.264172{gal}/1{liter}}$$ . Notice the gallon part is in the numerator since we’re converting to gallons, and the liter part is in the denominator since we are converting from liters. Performing this and rounding to three decimal places, we find that 14 liters is $$14{liter} \times \frac{0.264172{gal}}{1{liter}} = 3.69841{gal}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>

<example number="3.79" title="Finding the Total When the Percentage and Percentage of the Total Are Known">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>What is the total if 28% of the total is 140?</item>
        <item>What is the total if 6% of the total is 91?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>28 is the percentage, so $$n = 28$$ . 28% of the total is 140, so $$x = 140$$ . Using those we find that the total was $$\frac{100 \times \text{140} }{ \text{28} } = 500$$ .</item>
        <item>6 is the percentage, so $$n = 6$$ . 6% of the total is 91, so $$x = 91$$ . Using those we find that the total was $$\frac{100 \times \text{91} }{ \text{6} } = 1,516.6$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.82" title="Amazon Prime Subscribers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>There are 126 million users who are U.S. Amazon Prime subscribers. If there are 328.2 million residents in the United States, what percentage of U.S. residents are Amazon Prime subscribers?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We are asked to find the percentage. To do so, we divide the percentage of the total, which is 126 million, by the total, which is 328.2 million. Performing this division and rounding to three decimal places yields $$\frac{126}{328.2} = 0.384$$ . The decimal is moved to the right by two places, and a % sign is appended to the end. Doing this shows us that 38.4% of U.S. residents are Amazon Prime subscribers.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evander plays on the basketball team at their university and 73% of the athletes at their university receive some sort of scholarship for attending. If they know 219 of the student-athletes receive some sort of scholarship, how many student-athletes are at the university?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We need to find the total number of student-athletes at Evander’s university.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Identify what we know. We know the percentage of students who receive some sort of scholarship, 73%. We also know the number of athletes that form the part of the whole, or 219 student-athletes.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: To find the total number of student-athletes, use $$\frac{100 \times x}{n}$$ , with $$x = 219$$ and $$n = 73$$ . Calculating with those values yields $$\frac{100 \times 219}{73} = 300$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, there are 300 total student-athletes at Evander’s university</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Identifying Perfect Squares
snippet: Identifying Perfect Squares: Determine which of the following are perfect squares. 45 81 \frac{9}{28} \frac{144}{400} The prime factorization of 45 is 45 = 3^{2} \times 5 . Since the 5 is not raised to an even power, 45 is not a perfect...
body_xml:
<example number="3.84" title="Identifying Perfect Squares">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine which of the following are perfect squares.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>45</item>
        <item>81</item>
        <item>$$\frac{9}{28}$$</item>
        <item>$$\frac{144}{400}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The prime factorization of 45 is $$45 = 3^{2} \times 5$$ . Since the 5 is not raised to an even power, 45 is not a perfect square.</item>
        <item>The prime factorization of 81 is $$3^{4}$$ . All the prime factors are raised to even powers, so 81 is a perfect square.</item>
        <item>We must determine if both the numerator and denominator of $$\frac{9}{28}$$ are perfect squares for the rational number to be a perfect square. The numerator is 9, and as mentioned above, 9 is a perfect square (it is 3 squared). Now we check the prime factorization of the denominator, 28, which is $$28 = 2^{2} \times 7$$ . Since 7 is not raised to an even power, 28 is not a perfect square. Since the denominator is not a perfect square, $$\frac{9}{28}$$ is not a perfect square.</item>
        <item>We must determine if both the numerator and denominator of $$\frac{144}{400}$$ are perfect squares for the rational number to be a perfect square. The numerator is 144. The prime factorization of 144 is $$144 = 2^{4} \times 3^{2}$$ . Since all the prime factors of 144 are raised to even powers, 144 is a perfect square. Now we check the prime factorization of the denominator, 400, which is $$400 = 2^{4} \times 5^{2}$$ . Since all the prime factors of 400 are raised to even powers, 400 is a perfect square. Since the numerator and denominator of $$\frac{144}{400}$$ are perfect squares, $$\frac{144}{400}$$ is a perfect square.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.85" title="Identifying Irrational Numbers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify which of the following numbers are irrational.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\sqrt{35}$$</item>
        <item>$$\text{0.} \overline{15}$$</item>
        <item>$$\sqrt{121}$$</item>
        <item>$$4\pi$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>35 can be factored as $$5 \times 7$$ , showing that 35 is not the square of an integer or a rational number. This mean its square root is an irrational number.</item>
        <item>Since $$0.\overline{15}$$ is a decimal with a repeating pattern, it is rational, so it is not an irrational number.</item>
        <item>$$121 = 11^{2}$$ . Since 121 is the square of an integer, its square root is a rational number.</item>
        <item>Since $$4\pi$$ is a multiple of pi, it is irrational. In this case, the rational part of the number is 4, while the irrational part is $$\pi$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Simplifying a Square Root

<example number="3.86" title="Simplifying a Square Root">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Simplify the irrational number $$\sqrt{180}$$ and express in lowest terms. Identify the rational and irrational parts.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Begin by finding the largest perfect square that is a factor of 180. We can do this by writing out the factor pairs of 180:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {1 \times 180 2 \times 90 3 \times 60 4 \times 45 5 \times 36 6 \times 30 9 \times 20 10 \times 18 12 \times 15} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Looking at the list of factors, the perfect squares are 4, 9, and 36. The largest is 36, so we factor the into $$36 \times 5 = 6^{2} \times 5$$ . In the formula, $$a = 6$$ and $$b = 5$$ . Apply $$\sqrt{a^{2} \times b} = \sqrt{a^{2}} \times \sqrt{b}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\sqrt{6^{2} \times 5} = \sqrt{6^{2}} \times \sqrt{5}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The simplified form of $$\sqrt{180}$$ is $$6\sqrt{5}$$ . In this example, the 6 is the rational part, and the $$\sqrt{5}$$ is the irrational part.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since these two irrational numbers have the same irrational part, $$\sqrt{7}$$ , we can subtract without using a calculator. The rational part of the first number is 3. title: Dividing Irrational Numbers with Similar Irrational Parts
snippet: Dividing Irrational Numbers with Similar Irrational Parts: Perform the following operations without a calculator. Simplify if possible. 3\sqrt{15} \div \left( 8\sqrt{3} \right) 14.7\sqrt{135} \div \left( 3\sqrt{5} \right) . In this...
body_xml:
<example number="3.92" title="Dividing Irrational Numbers with Similar Irrational Parts">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Perform the following operations without a calculator. Simplify if possible.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$3\sqrt{15} \div \left( 8\sqrt{3} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$14.7\sqrt{135} \div \left( 3\sqrt{5} \right)$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>In this division problem, $$3\sqrt{15} \div \left( 8\sqrt{3} \right)$$ , notice that the irrational parts of these numbers are similar. They are both square roots, so follow the steps given above. Step 1: Divide the rational parts. $$3 \div 8 = \frac{3}{8}$$ Step 2: If necessary, reduce the result of Step 1 to lowest terms. The 3 and 8 have no common factors, so $$\frac{3}{8}$$ is already in lowest terms. Step 3: Divide the irrational parts. $$\sqrt{15} \div \sqrt{3} = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{\frac{15}{3}}$$ Step 4: If necessary, reduce the result from Step 3 to lowest terms. The radicand can be reduced, which yields $$\sqrt{5}$$ . Step 5: The result is the product of the rational and irrational parts, which is $$\frac{3}{8}\sqrt{5}$$ .</item>
        <item>In this division problem, $$14.7\sqrt{135} \div \left( 3\sqrt{5} \right)$$ , notice that the irrational parts of these numbers are similar. They are both square roots, so follow the steps given above. Step 1: Divide the rational parts. $$14.7 \div 3 = 4.9$$ Step 2: If necessary, reduce the result of Step 1 to lowest terms. This rational number is expressed as a decimal so will not be reduced. Step 3: Divide the irrational parts. $$\sqrt{135} \div \sqrt{5} = \frac{\sqrt{135}}{\sqrt{5}} = \sqrt{\frac{135}{5}}$$ Step 4: If necessary, reduce the result from Step 3 to lowest terms. The radicand can be reduced, which yields $$\sqrt{\frac{135}{5}} = \sqrt{27} = \sqrt{9 \times 3} = 3\sqrt{3}$$ . Step 5: The result is the product of the rational and irrational parts, which is $$4.9 \times 3\sqrt{3} = 14.7\sqrt{3}$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Multiplying Irrational Numbers with Similar Irrational Parts
snippet: Multiplying Irrational Numbers with Similar Irrational Parts: Perform the following operations without a calculator. Simplify if possible. \left( {19\sqrt{3}} \right) \times \left( {5.6\sqrt{12}} \right) 13\pi \times 8\pi In this...

<example number="3.93" title="Multiplying Irrational Numbers with Similar Irrational Parts">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Perform the following operations without a calculator. Simplify if possible.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left( {19\sqrt{3}} \right) \times \left( {5.6\sqrt{12}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$13\pi \times 8\pi$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>In this multiplication problem, $$\left( {19\sqrt{3}} \right) \times \left( {5.6\sqrt{12}} \right)$$ , notice that the irrational parts of these numbers are similar. They are both square roots. Follow the process above. Step 1: Multiply the rational parts. $$19 \times 5.6 = 106.4$$ Step 2: If necessary, reduce the result of Step 1 to lowest terms. This rational number is expressed as a decimal and will not be reduced. Step 3: Multiply the irrational parts. $$\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{12} = \sqrt{3 \times 12} = \sqrt{36}$$ Step 4: If necessary, reduce the result from Step 3 to lowest terms. The radicand is 36, which is the square of 6. The irrational part reduces to $$\sqrt{36} = 6$$ . Step 5: The result is the product of the rational and irrational parts, which is $$106.4 \times 6 = 638.4$$ . Notice that sometimes multiplying or dividing irrational numbers can result in a rational number.</item>
        <item>In this multiplication problem, $$13\pi \times 8\pi$$ , notice that the irrational parts of these numbers are the same, $$\pi$$ . Follow the process above. Step 1: Multiply the rational parts. $$13 \times 8 = 104$$ Step 2: If necessary, reduce the result of Step 1 to lowest terms. That result is an integer. Step 3: Multiply the irrational parts. $$\pi \times \pi = \pi^{2}$$ Step 4: If necessary, reduce the result from Step 3 to lowest terms. This cannot be reduced. Step 5: The result is the product of the rational and irrational parts, which is $$104\pi^{2}$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Rationalizing the Denominator
snippet: Rationalizing the Denominator: Rationalize the denominator of the following: \frac{5}{\sqrt{7}} \frac{3\sqrt{6}}{2\sqrt{10}} The square root in the denominator is \sqrt{7} . In order to rationalize the denominator of \frac{5}{\sqrt{7}} ,...
body_xml:
<example number="3.94" title="Rationalizing the Denominator">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Rationalize the denominator of the following:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\frac{5}{\sqrt{7}}$$</item>
        <item>$$\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{2\sqrt{10}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The square root in the denominator is $$\sqrt{7}$$ . In order to rationalize the denominator of $$\frac{5}{\sqrt{7}}$$ , we need to multiply the numerator and denominator by $$\sqrt{7}$$ and simplify. $$\frac{5}{\sqrt{7}} = \frac{5\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{7}} = \frac{5\sqrt{7}}{7}$$ The square root is in simplified form, so the final answer is $$\frac{5\sqrt{7}}{7}$$ .</item>
        <item>The square root in the denominator is $$\sqrt{10}$$ .Step 1: In order to rationalize the denominator of $$\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{2\sqrt{10}}$$ , we need to multiply the numerator and denominator by $$\sqrt{10}$$ and simplify. $$\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{2\sqrt{10}} = \frac{3\sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{10}}{2\sqrt{10} \times \sqrt{10}} = \frac{3\sqrt{60}}{2 \times 10} = \frac{3\sqrt{60}}{20}$$ Step 2: The 60 under the square root can be factored into the following factor pairs: $$1 \times 60 2 \times 30 3 \times 20 4 \times 15 5 \times 12 6 \times 10$$ Step 3: The largest square factor of 60 is 4, so we simplify the $$\sqrt{60}$$ in the numerator into $$2\sqrt{15}$$ . We also cancel any common factors. $$\frac{3\sqrt{60}}{20} = \frac{3 \times 2\sqrt{15}}{20} = \frac{6\sqrt{15}}{20} = \frac{3\sqrt{15}}{10}$$ This is completely simplified.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>
