snippet: Determining Points on a Line: Figure 5.24 is the graph of y = 2x - 3 . For each ordered pair, decide: Is the ordered pair a solution to the equation? Is the point on the line? \begin{matrix} { \text{A:} \left( {0,-3} \right)} & { \text{B:}...
body_xml: Figure 5.24 is the graph of $$y = 2x - 3$$ . For each ordered pair, decide: Is the ordered pair a solution to the equation? Is the point on the line? $$\begin{matrix} { \text{A:} \left( {0,-3} \right)} & { \text{B:} \left( {3,3} \right)} & { \text{C:} \left( {2,-3} \right)} & { \text{D:} \left( {-1,-5} \right)} \end{matrix}$$ Substitute the $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -values into the equation to check if the ordered pair is a solution to the equation. $$\begin{matrix} {A:(0, - 3)} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ {- 3} & \overset{?}{=} & {2(0) - 3} \\ {- 3} & = & {- 3✓} \end{array} \\ {(0, - 3) \text{is a solution.} } \end{matrix}\begin{matrix} {B:(3,3)} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ 3 & \overset{?}{=} & {2(3) - 3} \\ 3 & = & {3✓} \end{array} \\ {(3,3) \text{is a solution.} } \end{matrix}\begin{matrix} {C:(2, - 3)} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ {- 3} & \overset{?}{=} & {2(2) - 3} \\ {- 3} & \neq & 1 \end{array} \\ {(2, - 3) \text{is not a solution.} } \end{matrix}\begin{matrix} {D:( - 1, - 5)} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ {- 5} & \overset{?}{=} & {2( - 1) - 3} \\ {- 5} & = & {- 5✓} \end{array} \\ {( - 1, - 5) \text{is a solution.} } \end{matrix}$$ Plot the points $$(0, - 3)$$ , $$(3,3)$$ , $$(2, - 3)$$ , and $$( - 1, - 5)$$ . In Figure 5.25, the points $$(0,3)$$ , $$(3, - 3)$$ , and $$( - 1, - 5)$$ are on the line $$y = 2x - 3$$ , and the point $$(2, - 3)$$ is not on the line. The points that are solutions to $$y = 2x - 3$$ are on the line, but the point that is not a solution is not on the line.

title: Graphing a Line by Plotting Points
snippet: Graphing a Line by Plotting Points: Graph the equation: y = \frac{1}{2}x + 3 . Find three points that are solutions to the equation. Since this equation has the fraction \frac{1}{2} as a coefficient of x , we will choose values of x...
body_xml:
Graph the equation: $$y = \frac{1}{2}x + 3$$ . Find three points that are solutions to the equation. Since this equation has the fraction $$\frac{1}{2}$$ as a coefficient of $$x$$ , we will choose values of $$x$$ carefully. We will use zero as one choice and multiples of 2 for the other choices. Why are multiples of two a good choice for values of $$x$$ ? By choosing multiples of 2, the multiplication by $$\frac{1}{2}$$ simplifies to a whole number. $$\begin{array}{lll} {x = 0} & {x = 2} & {x = 4} \\ {y = \frac{1}{2}x + 3} & {y = \frac{1}{2}x + 3} & {y = \frac{1}{2}x + 3} \\ {y = \frac{1}{2}(0) + 3} & {y = \frac{1}{2}(2) + 3} & {y = \frac{1}{2}(4) + 3} \\ {y = 0 + 3} & {y = 1 + 3} & {y = 2 + 3} \\ {y = 3} & {y = 4} & {y = 5} \end{array}$$ $$\mathbf{x}$$ $$\mathbf{y}$$ ( $$x$$ , $$y$$ ) 0 3 $$\left( {0,3} \right)$$ 2 4 $$\left( {2,4} \right)$$ 4 5 $$\left( {4,5} \right)$$
Plot the points, check that they line up, and draw the line (Figure 5.26).

title: Pumping Gas
snippet: Pumping Gas: Gasoline costs \$3.53 per gallon. You put 10 gallons of gasoline in your car, and pay \$35.30. Your friend puts 15 gallons of gasoline in their car and pays \$52.95. Your neighbor needs 5 gallons of gasoline, how much will...
body_xml: Gasoline costs \$3.53 per gallon. You put 10 gallons of gasoline in your car, and pay \$35.30. Your friend puts 15 gallons of gasoline in their car and pays \$52.95. Your neighbor needs 5 gallons of gasoline, how much will they pay? Let $$x = \text{the number of gallons of gasoline}$$ and let $$y = \text{the total cost}$$ . If gas is \$3.53 per gallon, then $$y = 3.53x$$ . The two points given are (10, 35.30) and (15, 52.95). Plot the points, check that they line up, and draw the line (Figure 5.27). We can see the point at $$x = 5$$ . The $$y$$ -value is found by multiplying 5 by \$3.53 to get \$17.65. Your neighbor will pay \$17.65.

title: Determining Solutions to an Inequality
snippet: Determining Solutions to an Inequality: Determine whether each ordered pair is a solution to the inequality y > x + 4 : (0,0) (1,6) \left( {2,6} \right) \left( {-5,-15} \right) \left( {- 8,12} \right) \begin{array}{ll} {(0,0)} & {y > x +...
body_xml:
<example number="5.43" title="Determining Solutions to an Inequality">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether each ordered pair is a solution to the inequality $$y > x + 4$$ :</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$(0,0)$$</item>
        <item>$$(1,6)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {2,6} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {-5,-15} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {- 8,12} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\begin{array}{ll} {(0,0)} & {y > x + 4} \\ { \text{Substitute} 0 \text{for} x \text{and} 0 \text{for} y} & {0\overset{?}{>}0 + 4} \\ { \text{Simplify} .} & {0 > 4} \\ & {(0,0) \text{is not a solution to} y > x + 4.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>$$\begin{array}{ll} {(1,6)} & {y > x + 4} \\ { \text{Substitute} 1 \text{for} x \text{and} 6 \text{for} y} & {6\overset{?}{>}1 + 4} \\ { \text{Simplify} .} & {6 > 5} \\ & {(1,6) \text{is a solution to} y > x + 4.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>$$\begin{array}{ll} {(2,6)} & {y > x + 4} \\ { \text{Substitute} 2 \text{for} x \text{and} 6 \text{for} y} & {6\overset{?}{>}2 + 4} \\ { \text{Simplify} .} & {6 > 6} \\ & {(2,6) \text{is not a solution to} y > x + 4.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>$$\begin{array}{ll} {( - 5, - 15)} & {y > x + 4} \\ { \text{Substitute} - 5 \text{for} x \text{and} - 15 \text{for} y} & {- 15\overset{?}{>} - 5 + 4} \\ { \text{Simplify} .} & {- 15 > - 1} \\ & { \text{So} ,( - 5, - 15) \text{is not a solution to} y > x + 4.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>$$\begin{array}{ll} {( - 8,12)} & {y > x + 4} \\ { \text{Substitute} - 8 \text{for} x \text{and} 12 \text{for} y} & {12\overset{?}{>} - 8 + 4} \\ { \text{Simplify} .} & {12 > - 4} \\ & { \text{So} ,( - 8,12) \text{is a solution to} y > x + 4.} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Writing a Linear Inequality Shown by a Graph
snippet: Writing a Linear Inequality Shown by a Graph: The boundary line shown in this graph is y = 2x - 1 . Write the inequality shown in Figure 5.35. The line y = 2x - 1 is the boundary line. On one side of the line are the points with y > 2x - 1...
body_xml:
The boundary line shown in this graph is $$y = 2x - 1$$ . Write the inequality shown in Figure 5.35. The line $$y = 2x - 1$$ is the boundary line. On one side of the line are the points with $$y > 2x - 1$$ and on the other side of the line are the points with $$y < 2x - 1$$ . Let us test the point $$(0,0)$$ and see which inequality describes its position relative to the boundary line. At $$(0,0)$$ , which inequality is true: $$y > 2x - 1$$ or $$y < 2x - 1$$ ? $$0 > 2(0) - 1$$ $$0 < 2(0) - 1$$ $$0 > 0 - 1$$ $$0 < 0 - 1$$ $$0 > - 1$$ $$0 < - 1$$ True False
Since $$y > 2x - 1$$ is true, the side of the line with $$(0,0)$$ , is the solution. The shaded region shows the solution of the inequality $$y > 2x - 1$$ . Since the boundary line is graphed with a dashed line, the inequality does not include the equal sign. The graph shows the inequality $$y > 2x - 1$$ . We could use an $$y$$ point as a test point, provided it is not on the line. Why did we choose $$(0,0)$$ ? Because it is the easiest to evaluate. You may want to pick a point on the other side of the boundary line and check that $$y < 2x - 1$$ .

title: Graphing a Linear Inequality
snippet: Graphing a Linear Inequality: Graph the linear inequality y \geq \frac{3}{4}x - 2 . Step 1. Identify and graph the boundary line (Figure 5.36). If the inequality is ≤ or ≥, the boundary line is solid. If the inequality is < or >, the...
body_xml: Graph the linear inequality $$y \geq \frac{3}{4}x - 2$$ . Step 1. Identify and graph the boundary line (Figure 5.36). If the inequality is ≤ or ≥, the boundary line is solid. If the inequality is < or >, the boundary line is dashed. Replace the inequality sign with an equal sign to find the boundary line. Graph the boundary line $$y = \frac{3}{4}x - 2$$ . The inequality sign is ≥, so we draw a solid line. Figure 5.36 Step 2. Test a point that is not on the boundary line. Is it a solution of the inequality? We’ll test $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Is it a solution of the inequality? At $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , is $$y \geq \frac{3}{4}x - 2$$ ? $$\begin{array}{l} {0\overset{?}{\geq}\frac{3}{4}(0) - 2} \\ {0 \geq - 2} \end{array}$$ So, $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is a solution. Step 3. Shade in one side of the boundary line (Figure 5.37). If the test point is a solution, shade in the side that includes the point. If the test point is not a solution, shade in the opposite side. The test point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is a solution to $$y \geq \frac{3}{4}x - 2$$ . So we shade in that side. Figure 5.37 All points in the shaded region and on the boundary line represent the solution to $$y \geq \frac{3}{4}x - 2$$ .

title: Working Multiple Jobs
snippet: Working Multiple Jobs: Hilaria works two part time jobs to earn enough money to meet her obligations of at least \$240 a week. Her job in food service pays \$10 an hour and her tutoring job on campus pays \$15 an hour. How many hours does...
body_xml:
<example number="5.46" title="Working Multiple Jobs">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Hilaria works two part time jobs to earn enough money to meet her obligations of at least \$240 a week. Her job in food service pays \$10 an hour and her tutoring job on campus pays \$15 an hour. How many hours does Hilaria need to work at each job to earn at least \$240?</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let $$x$$ be the number of hours she works at the job in food service and let $$y$$ be the number of hours she works tutoring. Write an inequality that would model this situation.</item>
        <item>Graph the inequality.</item>
        <item>Find three ordered pairs ( $$\mathit{x,y}$$ ) that would be solutions to the inequality. Then, explain what that means for Hilaria.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let $$x$$ be the number of hours she works at the job in food service and let $$y$$ be the number of hours she works tutoring. She earns \$10 per hour at the job in food service and \$15 an hour tutoring. At each job, the number of hours multiplied by the hourly wage will give the amount earned at that job. $$\underset{ \text{10} x}{\underset{︸}{ \text{Amount earned at the food service job} }}\underset{+}{ \text{plus} }\underset{ \text{15} y}{\underset{︸}{ \text{the amount earned tutoring} }}\underset{\geq \text{240} }{\underset{︸}{ \text{is at least} }}$$</item>
        <item>Graph the inequality: Step 1: Graph the boundary line $$10x + 15y = 240$$ Create a table of values $$x$$ $$y$$ 0 $$10(0) + 15y = 240 - > y = 16$$ 6 $$10(6) + 15y = 240 - > y = 12$$ 12 $$10(12) + 15y = 240 - > y = 8$$ Step 2: Pick a test point. Let us pick $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ again: $$10(0) + 15(0) \geq 240$$ ? $$0 \geq 240$$ is false and not a solution so the shading happens on the other side of the boundary line (Figure 5.38). Figure 5.38</item>
        <item>From the graph, we see that the ordered pairs $$\left( {15,10} \right)$$ , $$\left( {0,16} \right)$$ , $$\left( {24,0} \right)$$ represent three of infinitely many solutions. Check the values in the inequality. $$\begin{matrix} {(15,10)} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} {10x + 15y} & \geq & 240 \\ {10(15) + 15(10)} & \overset{?}{\geq} & 240 \\ 300 & \geq & {240 \text{True} } \end{array} \end{matrix}\begin{matrix} {(0,16)} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} {10x + 15y} & \geq & 240 \\ {10(0) + 15(16)} & \overset{?}{\geq} & 240 \\ 240 & \geq & {240 \text{True} } \end{array} \end{matrix}\begin{matrix} {(24,0)} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} {10x + 15y} & \geq & 240 \\ {10(24) + 15(0)} & \overset{?}{\geq} & 240 \\ 240 & \geq & {240 \text{True} } \end{array} \end{matrix}$$</item>
      </list>
      <paragraph>For Hilaria, it means that to earn at least \$240, she can work 15 hours tutoring and 10 hours at her food service job, earn all her money tutoring for 16 hours, or earn all her money while working 24 hours at the job in food service.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Multiply Binomials: Multiply \left( {x + 2} \right)\left( {x + 3} \right) . Step 1: Use the distributive property: (x)(x) + (x)(3) + (2)(x) + (2)(3) In the area model (Figure 5.40) multiply each term on the side by each term on the top...
body_xml: Multiply $$\left( {x + 2} \right)\left( {x + 3} \right)$$ . Step 1: Use the distributive property: $$(x)(x) + (x)(3) + (2)(x) + (2)(3)$$ In the area model (Figure 5.40) multiply each term on the side by each term on the top (think of it as a multiplication table). Step 2: After we multiply, we get the following equation: $$x^{2} + 3x + 2x + 6$$ Step 3: Combine the like terms to arrive at: $$x^{2} + 5x + 6$$

body_xml:
Factor $$x^{2} + 7x + 12$$ . The numbers that must have a product of 12 will need a sum of 7. We will summarize the results in a table below. Factors of 12 Sum of Factors 1, 12 $$1 + 12 = 13$$ 2, 6 $$2 + 6 = 8$$ 3, 4 $$3 + 4 = 7$$
We see that 3 and 4 are the numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7. The factors of $$x^{2} + 7x + 12$$ are $$\left( {x + 3} \right)\left( {x + 4} \right)$$ .

snippet: Factoring More Complex Trinomials: Factor x^{2} - 11x + 28 . The numbers that must have a product of 28 will need a sum of - 11 . We will summarize the results in a table. Factors of 28 Sum of Factors 1,28 1 + 28 = 29 2,14 2 + 14 = 16 4,7...
body_xml:
Factor $$x^{2} - 11x + 28$$ . The numbers that must have a product of 28 will need a sum of $$- 11$$ . We will summarize the results in a table. Factors of 28 Sum of Factors $$1,28$$ $$1 + 28 = 29$$ $$2,14$$ $$2 + 14 = 16$$ $$4,7$$ $$4 + 7 = 11$$
We see that 4 and 7 are the numbers that multiply to 28 and add to 11. But we needed $$- 11$$ , so we will need to use $$- 4$$ and $$- 7$$ because $$\left( {- 4} \right)\left( {- 7} \right) = 28$$ and $$\left( {- 4} \right) + \left( {- 7} \right) = - 11$$ . The factors of $$x^{2} - 11x + 28$$ are $$\left( {x - 4} \right)\left( {x - 7} \right)$$ .

title: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factoring
snippet: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factoring: Solve y = x^{2} + x - 6 . Step 1. Set each factor equal to zero. The product equals zero, so at least one factor must equal zero. \left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 4} \right) = 0 Step 2. Solve the...
body_xml: Solve $$y = x^{2} + x - 6$$ . Step 1. Set each factor equal to zero. The product equals zero, so at least one factor must equal zero. $$\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 4} \right) = 0$$ Step 2. Solve the linear equations. Solve each equation. $$\begin{matrix} {(x + 1)(x - 4) = 0} \\ {x + 1 = 0 \text{or} x - 4 = 0} \end{matrix}$$ Step 3. Check. Substitute each solution separately into the original equation. $$x = - 1 \text{or} x = 4$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} x & = & {- 1} \\ {(x + 1)(x - 4)} & = & 0 \\ {( - 1 + 1)( - 1 - 4)} & \overset{?}{=} & 0 \\ {(0)( - 5)} & \overset{?}{=} & 0 \\ 0 & = & {0✓} \end{array}$$

title: Solve Another Quadratic Equation by Factoring
snippet: Solve Another Quadratic Equation by Factoring: Solve (x - 2)(x + 5) = 0 . Step 1. Write the quadratic equation in standard form, x^{2} + 2x - 8 = 0 . The equation is already in standard form. \mathit{ax}^{2} + \mathit{bx} + c = 0 Step 2....
body_xml: Solve $$(x - 2)(x + 5) = 0$$ . Step 1. Write the quadratic equation in standard form, $$x^{2} + 2x - 8 = 0$$ . The equation is already in standard form. $$\mathit{ax}^{2} + \mathit{bx} + c = 0$$ Step 2. Factor the quadratic expression. Factor $$x^{2} + 2x - 8 = 0$$ $$\begin{array}{l} {x^{2} + 2x - 8} \\ {(x + 4)(x - 2)} \end{array}$$ Step 3. Use the Zero Product Property. Set each factor equal to zero. $$(x + 4)(x - 2) = 0$$ Step 4. Solve the linear equations. We have two linear equations. $$x + 4 = 0 \text{or} x - 2 = 0$$ Step 5. Check. Substitute each solution separately into the original equation. $$x = - 4 \text{or} x = 2$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x^{2} + 2x - 8} & = & 0 \\ x & = & {- 4} \\ {( - 4)^{2} - 2( - 4) - 8} & \overset{?}{=} & 0 \\ {16 + ( - 8) - 8} & \overset{?}{=} & 0 \\ 0 & = & {0✓} \end{array}$$

<example number="5.57" title="Solving a Quadratic Equation Using the Quadratic Formula">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve using the quadratic formula: $$c$$ .</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>$$x^{2} - 6x + 5 = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This equation is in standard form.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x^{2} - 6x + 5 = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Identify the $$\begin{array}{rcl} {ax^{2} + bx + c} & = & 0 \\ {x^{2} - 6x + 5} & = & 0 \end{array}$$ , $$a$$ , and $$b$$ values.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$c$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Write the quadratic formula.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$a = 1,b = - 6,c = 5$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Substitute in the values of $$x = \frac{- b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a}$$ , $$a$$ , $$b$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$c$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Simplify.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x = \frac{( - 6) \pm \sqrt{{( - 6)}^{2} - 4(1)(5)}}{2.1}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 20}}{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{16}}{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: Rewrite to show two solutions.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x = \frac{6 \pm 4}{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 6: Simplify.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x = \frac{6 + 4}{2},x = \frac{6 - 4}{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x = \frac{10}{2},x = \frac{2}{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 7: Check.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x = 5,x = 1$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml: Solve using the quadratic formula: $$a^{2} - 2a - 15 = 0$$ . Step 1. Write the quadratic equation in standard form. Identify the $$2x^{2} + 9x - 5 = 0$$ , $$a$$ , $$b$$ values. This equation is in standard form. $$c$$ Step 2. Write the quadratic formula. Then substitute in the values of $$\begin{matrix} \mathbf{\mathbf{ax}^{2} + \mathbf{bx} + \mathbf{c} = 0} \\ {2x^{2} + 9x - 5 = 0} \\ {a = 2, b = 9, c = - 5} \end{matrix}$$ , $$a$$ , $$b$$ . Substitute in $$c$$ , $$\mathbf{\mathbf{a} = 2}$$ , $$\mathbf{\mathbf{b} = 9}$$ $$\mathbf{\mathbf{c} = - 5}$$ Step 3. title: Finding Consecutive Integers
snippet: Finding Consecutive Integers: The product of two consecutive integers is 132. Find the integers. Step 1: Read the problem. Step 2: Identify what we are looking for. We are looking for two consecutive integers. Step 3: Name what we are...
body_xml:
<example number="5.59" title="Finding Consecutive Integers">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The product of two consecutive integers is 132. Find the integers.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Read the problem.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Identify what we are looking for.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We are looking for two consecutive integers.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Name what we are looking for.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let $$3y^{2} - 5y + 2 = 0$$ the first integer</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let $$n =$$ the next consecutive integer.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Translate into an equation. Restate the problem in a sentence.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$n + 1 =$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The product of the two consecutive integers is 132. The first integer times the next integer is 132.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: Solve the equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$n\left( {n + 1} \right) = 132$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Bring all the terms to one side.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$n^{2} + n = 132$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Factor the trinomial.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$n^{2} + n - 132 = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Use the zero product property.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\left( {n - 11} \right)\left( {n + 12} \right) = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Solve the equations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$n - 11 = 0 \text{or} n + 12 = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>There are two values for $$n = 11,n = - 12$$ that are solutions to this problem. So, there are two sets of consecutive integers that will work.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>If the first integer is $$n$$ , then the next integer is 12. If the first integer is $$n = 11$$ , then the next integer is $$n = - 12$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 6: Check the answer.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The consecutive integers are 11, 12 and $$- 11$$ , $$- 11$$ . The product of 11 and $$- 12$$ and the product of $$12 = 132$$ . Both pairs of consecutive integers are solutions.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 7: Answer the question.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The consecutive integers are 11, 12, and $$- 11\left( {- 12} \right) = 132$$ , $$- 11$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

Step 3: Name what you are looking for. The length is 2 feet more than width. Let $$- 12$$ the width of the garden. $$W =$$ the length of the garden. Step 4: Translate into an equation. Restate the important information in a sentence. The area of the rectangular garden is 15 square feet. Use the formula for the area of a rectangle. $$W + 2 =$$ Substitute in the variables. $$A = L \times W$$ Step 5: Solve the equation. Distribute first. $$15 = \left( {W + 2} \right)W$$ Get zero on one side. $$15 = W^{2} + 2W$$ Factor the trinomial. $$0 = W^{2} + 2W - 15$$ Use the Zero Product Property. $$0 = \left( {W + 5} \right)\left( {W - 3} \right)$$ $$0 = W + 5$$ Solve each equation. $$0 = W - 3$$ $$- 5 = W$$ Since $$3 = W$$ is the width of the garden, it does not make sense for it to be negative. We eliminate that value for $$W$$ . $$W$$ Width is 3 feet. Find the value of the length. $$W = 3$$ length. $$W + 2 =$$ 5 Length is 5 feet. Step 6: Check the answer (Figure 5.51). body_xml:
<example number="5.61" title="Evaluating the Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For the function $$f(x) = 2x^{2} + 3x - 1$$ , evaluate the function.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(3)$$</item>
        <item>$$f\left( {- 2} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$f(a)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To evaluate $$f(3)$$ , substitute 3, for $$x$$ . Simplify. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(x)} & = & {2x^{2} + 3x - 1} \\ {f(\mathbf{3})} & = & {2{(\mathbf{3})}^{2} + 3 \cdot \mathbf{3} - 1} \\ {f(3)} & = & {2 \cdot 9 + 3 \cdot 3 - 1} \\ {f(3)} & = & {18 + 9 - 1} \\ {f(3)} & = & 26 \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>To evaluate $$f( - 2)$$ , substitute $$- 2$$ for $$x$$ . Simplify. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(x)} & = & {2x^{2} + 3x - 1} \\ {f( - \mathbf{2})} & = & {2\left( {- 2} \right)^{2} + 3( - \mathbf{2}) - 1} \\ {f( - 2)} & = & {2 \cdot 4 + ( - 6) - 1} \\ {f( - 2)} & = & {8 + ( - 6) - 1} \\ {f( - 2)} & = & 1 \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>To evaluate $$f(a)$$ , substitute $$a$$ for $$x$$ . Simplify. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(x)} & = & {2x^{2} + 3x - 1} \\ {f\left( \mathbf{a} \right)} & = & {2\left( \mathbf{a} \right)^{2} + 3 \cdot \mathbf{a} - 1} \\ {f(a)} & = & {2a^{2} + 3a - 1} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

The function $$N(t) = 75 + 10t$$ represents the relation between the number of emails, $$N$$ , and the time, $$t$$ , measured in days. Find $$N$$ (5). Explain what this result means.</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Find $$N$$ (5). Explain what this result means.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute in $$t = 5$$ . Simplify.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {N(\mathbf{5})} & = & {75 + 10 \cdot \mathbf{5}} \\ {N(t)} & = & {75 + 10t} \\ {N(5)} & = & {75 + 50} \\ {N(5)} & = & 125 \end{array}$$</paragraph>

    </solution>

title: Determining If a Relation Is a Function with an Equation
snippet: Determining If a Relation Is a Function with an Equation: Determine whether each equation is a function. Assume x is the independent variable. 2x + y = 7 y = x^{2} + 1 x + y^{2} = 3 2x + y = 7 For each value of x , we multiply it by - 2...
body_xml:
<example number="5.65" title="Determining If a Relation Is a Function with an Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether each equation is a function. Assume $$x$$ is the independent variable.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$2x + y = 7$$</item>
        <item>$$y = x^{2} + 1$$</item>
        <item>$$x + y^{2} = 3$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$2x + y = 7$$ For each value of $$x$$ , we multiply it by $$- 2$$ and then add 7 to get the $$y$$ -value. For example, if $$x = 3$$ : $$\begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {- 2x + 7} \\ y & = & {- 2 \cdot 3 + 7} \\ y & = & 1 \end{array}$$ We have that when $$x = 3$$ , then $$y = 1$$ . It would work similarly for any value of $$x$$ . Since each value of $$x$$ , corresponds to only one value of $$y$$ the equation defines a function.</item>
        <item>$$y = x^{2} + 1$$ For each value of $$x$$ , we square it and then add 1 to get the $$y$$ -value. For example, if $$x = 2$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {x^{2} + 1} \\ y & = & {\mathbf{2}^{2} + 1} \\ y & = & 5 \end{array}$$ We have that when $$x = 2$$ , then $$y = 5$$ . It would work similarly for any value of $$x$$ . Since each value of $$x$$ corresponds to only one value of $$y$$ , the equation defines a function.</item>
        <item>$$x + y^{2} = 3$$ $$x + y^{2} = 3$$ Isolate the $$y$$ term. $$y^{2} = - x + 3$$ Let us substitute $$x = 2$$ . $$y^{2} = - \mathbf{2} + 3$$ $$y^{2} = 1$$ This gives us two values for $$y$$ . $$y = 1, y = - 1$$ We have shown that when $$x = 2$$ , then $$y = 1$$ and $$y = - 1$$ . It would work similarly for any value of $$x$$ . Since each value of $$x$$ does not corresponds to only one value of $$y$$ the equation does not define a function.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

Create an interpretation of this graph (i.e., make up a story that goes with it). $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is the $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -intercept and represents Juan at home before his bike ride. The distance from home is 0 miles and 0 minutes have passed. In the first 30 minutes, the slope is $$\frac{1}{5}$$ and indicates Juan is traveling 1 mile for every 5 minutes. Between 30 and 60 minutes, the slope is 0 and indicates that he’s not riding the bike (the distance is not increasing). Then between 60 and 90 minutes, the slope is $$\frac{1}{5}$$ again. Finally, after 90 minutes the slope is $$- \frac{4}{15},$$ meaning Juan is getting 4 miles closer to home every 15 minutes. Answers will vary. Juan left his house for a bike ride. After 30 minutes, he was 6 miles from home and he stopped for ice cream at his local ice-cream truck. He enjoyed his ice cream for 30 minutes. He then jumped back on his bike and rode to his friend’s house. He arrived there 30 minutes later. His friend’s house was 12 miles from his home. His friend was not home so he immediately turned around and quickly rode home in 45 minutes.

title: Converting Temperature
snippet: Converting Temperature: The equation F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32 is used to convert temperatures from degrees Celsius ( C ) to degrees Fahrenheit ( F ). Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 0°. Find the Fahrenheit...
body_xml:
<example number="5.79" title="Converting Temperature">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The equation $$F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$$ is used to convert temperatures from degrees Celsius ( $$C$$ ) to degrees Fahrenheit ( $$F$$ ).</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 0°.</item>
        <item>Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 20°.</item>
        <item>Interpret the slope and $$F$$ -intercept of the equation.</item>
        <item>Graph the equation.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 0°. Find $$F$$ when $$C = 0$$ . $$F = \frac{9}{5}(0) + 32$$ Simplify. $$F = 32$$</item>
        <item>Find the Fahrenheit temperature for a Celsius temperature of 20°. Find $$F$$ when $$C = 20$$ . $$F = \frac{9}{5}(20) + 32$$ Simplify. $$F = 36 + 32$$ Simplify. $$F = 68$$</item>
        <item>Interpret the slope and $$F$$ -intercept of the equation. Even though this equation uses $$F$$ and $$C$$ , it is still in slope-intercept form. $$\begin{array}{l} {y = mx + b} \\ {F = mC + b} \\ {F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32} \end{array}$$ The slope $$\frac{9}{5}$$ means that the temperature Fahrenheit ( $$F$$ ) increases 9 degrees when the temperature Celsius ( $$C$$ ) increases 5 degrees. The $$F$$ -intercept means that when the temperature is 0° on the Celsius scale, it is 32° on the Fahrenheit scale.</item>
        <item>Graph the equation. We will need to use a larger scale than our usual. Start at the $$F$$ -intercept $$\left( {0,32} \right)$$ , and then count out the rise of 9 and the run of 5 to get a second point as shown in Figure 5.80. Figure 5.80</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Driving Costs
snippet: Calculating Driving Costs: Sam drives a delivery van. The equation C = 0.5d + 60 models the relation between his weekly cost, C , in dollars and the number of miles, d , that he drives. Find Sam’s cost for a week when he drives 0 miles....
body_xml:
<example number="5.80" title="Calculating Driving Costs">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Sam drives a delivery van. The equation $$C = 0.5d + 60$$ models the relation between his weekly cost, $$C$$ , in dollars and the number of miles, $$d$$ , that he drives.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find Sam’s cost for a week when he drives 0 miles.</item>
        <item>Find the cost for a week when he drives 250 miles.</item>
        <item>Interpret the slope and $$C$$ -intercept of the equation.</item>
        <item>Graph the equation.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find Sam’s cost for a week when he drives 0 miles. Find $$C$$ when $$d$$ = 0. $$C = 0.5(0) + 60$$ Simplify. $$C = 60$$ Sam’s costs are \$60 when he drives 0 miles.</item>
        <item>Find the cost for a week when he drives 250 miles. Find $$C$$ when $$d = 250$$ . $$C = 0.5(250) + 60$$ Simplify. $$C = 185$$ Sam’s costs are \$185 when he drives 250 miles.</item>
        <item>Interpret the slope and $$C$$ -intercept of the equation. $$\begin{array}{l} {y = mx + b} \\ {C = 0.5d + 60} \end{array}$$ The slope, 0.5, means that the weekly cost, $$C$$ , increases by \$0.50 when the number of miles driven, $$d$$ , increases by 1. The $$C$$ -intercept means that when the number of miles driven is 0, the weekly cost is \$60.</item>
        <item>Graph the equation (Figure 5.81). We’ll need to use a larger scale than usual. Start at the $$C$$ -intercept (0, 60). To count out the slope $$m = 0.5$$ , we rewrite it as an equivalent fraction that will make our graphing easier. $$m = 0.5 = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{50}{100}$$ So to graph the next point go up 50 from the intercept of 60 and then to the right 100. The second point will be (100, 110). Figure 5.81</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to the System: Determine whether the ordered pair is a solution to the system. \left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} {x - y} & = & {- 1} \\ {2x - y} & = & {- 5} \end{array} \right. \left( {- 2, - 1}...
body_xml:
<example number="5.81" title="Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to the System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether the ordered pair is a solution to the system.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} {x - y} & = & {- 1} \\ {2x - y} & = & {- 5} \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left( {- 2, - 1} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {- 4, - 3} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} {x - y} & = & {- 1} \\ {2x - y} & = & {- 5} \end{array} \right.$$ We substitute $$x = - 2$$ and $$y = - 1$$ into both equations. $$\begin{array}{r} {x - y = - 1} \\ {- 2 - ( - 1)\overset{?}{=} - 1} \\ {- 1 = - 1✓} \end{array} \begin{array}{r} {2x - y = - 5} \\ {2( - 2) - ( - 1)\overset{?}{=} - 5} \\ {- 3 \neq - 5} \end{array}$$ $$\left( {- 2, - 1} \right)$$ does not make both equations true. $$\left( {- 2, - 1} \right)$$ is not a solution.</item>
        <item>We substitute $$x = - 4$$ and $$y = - 3$$ into both equations. $$\begin{array}{r} {x - y = - 1} \\ {- 4 - ( - 3)\overset{?}{=} - 1} \\ {- 1 = - 1✓} \end{array} \begin{array}{r} {2x - y = - 5} \\ {2 \bullet ( - 4) - ( - 3)\overset{?}{=} - 5} \\ {- 5 = - 5✓} \end{array}$$ $$\left( {- 4, - 3} \right)$$ makes both equations true. $$\left( {- 4, - 3} \right)$$ is a solution.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="5.82" title="Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to the System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether the ordered pair is a solution to the system</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{3}{2}x + 1} \\ {2x - 3y} & = & 7 \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left( {- 4, - 5} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {- 4,5} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{3}{2}x + 1} \\ {2x - 3y} & = & 7 \end{array} \right.$$ Substitute $$- 4$$ for $$x$$ and $$- 5$$ for $$y$$ into both equations. $$\begin{array}{ll} \begin{array}{l} {- 5\overset{?}{=}\frac{3}{2}( - 4) + 1} \\ {- 5\overset{?}{=}3( - 2) + 1} \\ {- 5\overset{?}{=} - 6 + 1} \\ {- 5 = - 5✓} \end{array} & \begin{array}{r} {2( - 4) - 3( - 5)\overset{?}{=}7} \\ {( - 8) - ( - 15)\overset{?}{=}7} \\ {- 8 + 15\overset{?}{=}7} \\ {7 = 7✓} \end{array} \end{array}$$ $$\left( {- 4, - 5} \right)$$ is a solution.</item>
        <item>$$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{3}{2}x + 1} \\ {2x - 3y} & = & 7 \end{array} \right.$$ Substitute $$- 4$$ for $$x$$ and $$5$$ for $$y$$ into both equations. $$\begin{array}{l} {5\overset{?}{=}\frac{3}{2}( - 4) + 1} \\ {5\overset{?}{=}3( - 2) + 1} \\ {5\overset{?}{=} - 6 + 1} \\ {5 \neq - 5} \end{array} \begin{array}{r} {2( - 4) - 3(5)\overset{?}{=}7} \\ {( - 8) - (15)\overset{?}{=}7} \\ {- 8 - 15\overset{?}{=}7} \\ {- 23 \neq 7} \end{array}$$ $$\left( {- 4,5} \right)$$ is not a solution.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Solving a System of Linear Equations by Graphing
snippet: Solving a System of Linear Equations by Graphing: Solve this system of linear equations by graphing. \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right. Step 1: Graph the first equation. To graph the first line, write...
body_xml: Solve this system of linear equations by graphing. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{r} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right.$$ Step 1: Graph the first equation. To graph the first line, write the equation in slope-intercept form. $$\begin{matrix} { \begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{2\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}} & = & 7 \\ y & = & {- 2x + 7} \end{array}} \\ {m = - 2 b = 7} \end{matrix}$$ $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right.$$ Step 2: Graph the second equation on the same rectangular coordinate system. To graph the second line, use intercepts. $$\begin{matrix} \mathbf{\mathbf{x} - 2\mathbf{y} = 6} \\ {(0, - 3) (6,0)} \end{matrix}$$ Step 3: Determine whether the lines intersect, are parallel, or are the same line. Look at the graph of the lines. The lines intersect. Step 4 and Step 5: Identify the solution to the system. If the lines intersect, identify the point of intersection. Check to make sure it is a solution to both equations. This is the solution to the system. If the lines are parallel, the system has no solution. If the lines are the same, the system has an infinite number of solutions. Since the lines intersect, find the point of intersection. Check the point in both equations. The lines intersect at $$(4, - 1)$$ . $$\begin{matrix} {2x + y} & = & 7 \\ {2(4) + ( - 1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 7 \\ {8 - 1} & \overset{?}{=} & 7 \\ 7 & = & {7✓} \\ & & \\ {x - 2y} & = & 6 \\ {4 - 2( - 1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 6 \\ 6 & = & {6✓} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is $$(4, - 1)$$ .

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
snippet: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution: Solve this system of linear equations by substitution: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right. Step 1: Solve one of the equations for either...
body_xml: Solve this system of linear equations by substitution: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right.$$ Step 1: Solve one of the equations for either variable. We’ll solve the first equation for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right. \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{rcl} {2x + y} & = & 7 \\ y & = & \mathbf{7 - 2\mathbf{x}} \end{array} \end{array}$$ Step 2: Substitute the expression from Step 1 into the other equation. We replace $$y$$ in the second equation with the expression $$7 - 2x$$ . $$\begin{array}{r} {x - 2y = 6} \\ {x - 2(\mathbf{7 - 2\mathbf{x}}) = 6} \end{array}$$ Step 3: Solve the resulting equation. Now we have an equation with just 1 variable. We know how to solve this! $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x - 2(7 - 2x)} & = & 6 \\ {x - 14 + 4x} & = & 6 \\ {5x} & = & 20 \\ x & = & 4 \end{array}$$ Step 4: Substitute the solution from Step 3 into one of the original equations to find the other variable. We’ll use the first equation and replace $$x$$ with 4. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {2x + y} & = & 7 \\ {2(4) + y} & = & 7 \\ {8 + y} & = & 7 \\ y & = & {- 1} \end{array}$$ Step 5: Write the solution as an ordered pair. The ordered pair is ( $$x$$ , $$y$$ ). $$(4, - 1)$$ Step 6: Check that the ordered pair is a solution to both original equations. Substitute $$x = 4$$ , $$y = - 1$$ into both equations and make sure they are both true. $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rcl} {2x + y} & = & 7 \\ {2(4) + ( - 1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 7 \\ 7 & = & {7✓} \end{array} & \begin{array}{rcl} {x - 2y} & = & 6 \\ {4 - 2( - 1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 6 \\ 6 & = & {6✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ Both equations are true. $$(4, - 1)$$ is the solution to the system.

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Elimination
snippet: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Elimination: Solve this system of linear equations by elimination: \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right. Step 1: Write both equations in standard form. If any...
body_xml: Solve this system of linear equations by elimination: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{r} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right.$$ Step 1: Write both equations in standard form. If any coefficients are fractions, clear them. Both equations are in standard form, $$Ax + By = C$$ . There are no fractions. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{r} {2x + y = 7} \\ {x - 2y = 6} \end{array} \right.$$ Step 2: Make the coefficients of one variable opposites. Decide which variable you will eliminate. Multiply one or both equations so that the coefficients of that variable are opposites. We can eliminate the $$y$$ ’s by multiplying the first equation by 2. Multiply both sides of $$2x + y = 7$$ by 2. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{r} {2x + \mathbf{y} = 7} \\ {x - 2\mathbf{y} = 6} \end{array} \right.$$ $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} {2(2x + y)} & = & {2(7)} \\ {x - 2y} & = & 6 \end{array} \right.$$ Step 3: Add the equations resulting from Step 2 to eliminate one variable. We add the $$x$$ ’s, $$y$$ ’s, and constants. $$\begin{array}{r} \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {4x + 2y = 14} \\ \underline{x-2y=6} \end{array} \right. \\ {5x = 20} \end{array}$$ Step 4: Solve for the remaining variable. Solve for $$x$$ . $$x = 4$$ Step 5: Substitute the solution from Step 4 into one of the original equations. Then solve for the other variable. Substitute $$x = 4$$ into the second equation, $$x - 2y = 6$$ . Then solve for $$y$$ . $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x - 2y} & = & 6 \\ {4 - 2y} & = & 6 \\ {- 2y} & = & 2 \\ y & = & {- 1} \end{array}$$ Step 6: Write the solution as an ordered pair. Write it as $$(x,y)$$ . $$(4, - 1)$$ Step 7: Check that the ordered pair is a solution to both original equations. Substitute $$x = 4$$ , $$y = - 1$$ into $$2x + y = 7$$ and $$x - 2y = 6$$ . Do they make both equations true? Yes! $$\begin{matrix} \begin{array}{rcl} {2x + y} & = & 7 \\ {2(4) + ( - 1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 7 \\ 7 & = & {7✓} \end{array} & \begin{array}{rcl} {x - 2y} & = & 6 \\ {4 - 2( - 1)} & \overset{?}{=} & 6 \\ 6 & = & {6✓} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$ The solution is $$(4, - 1)$$ .

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Solving a System of Linear Equations with No Solution
snippet: Solving a System of Linear Equations with No Solution: Solve the system by a method of your choice: \left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{1}{2}x - 3} \\ {x - 2y} & = & 4 \end{array} \right. Let us solve the system of linear equations...
body_xml:
Solve the system by a method of your choice: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{1}{2}x - 3} \\ {x - 2y} & = & 4 \end{array} \right.$$ Let us solve the system of linear equations by graphing. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {\frac{1}{2}x - 3} \\ {x - 2y} & = & 4 \end{array} \right.$$ To graph the first equation, we will use its slope and $$y$$ -intercept. $$\begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{y} & = & \mathbf{\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x} - 3} \\ m & = & \frac{1}{2} \\ b & = & {- 3} \end{array}$$ To graph the second equation, we will use the intercepts. $$\mathbf{\mathbf{x} - 2\mathbf{y} = 4}$$ $$x$$ $$y$$ 0 −2 4 0
Graph the lines (Figure 5.84). Determine the points of intersection. The lines are parallel. Since no point is on both lines, there is no ordered pair that makes both equations true. There is no solution to this system.

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Solving a System of Linear Equations with Infinite Solutions
snippet: Solving a System of Linear Equations with Infinite Solutions: Solve the system by a method of your choice: \left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ {- 6x + 3y} & = & {- 9} \end{array} \right. Let us solve the system of linear...
body_xml:
Solve the system by a method of your choice: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ {- 6x + 3y} & = & {- 9} \end{array} \right.$$ Let us solve the system of linear equations by graphing. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ {- 6x + 3y} & = & {- 9} \end{array} \right.$$ Find the slope and $$y$$ -intercept of the first equation. $$\begin{array}{rcl} y & = & {2x - 3} \\ m & = & 2 \\ b & = & {- 3} \end{array}$$ Find the intercepts of the second equation. $$- 6x + 3y = - 9$$ $$x$$ $$y$$ 0 −3 $$\frac{3}{2}$$ 0
Graph the lines (Figure 5.85). The lines are the same! Since every point on the line makes both equations true, there are infinitely many ordered pairs that make both equations true. There are infinitely many solutions to this system.

unit_title: Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Applying System to a Real-World Application
snippet: Applying System to a Real-World Application: Heather has been offered two options for her salary as a trainer at the gym. Option A would pay her \$25,000 a year plus \$15 for each training session. Option B would pay her \$10,000 a year...
body_xml:
<example number="5.88" title="Applying System to a Real-World Application">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Heather has been offered two options for her salary as a trainer at the gym. Option A would pay her \$25,000 a year plus \$15 for each training session. Option B would pay her \$10,000 a year plus \$40 for each training session. How many training sessions would make the salary options equal?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Read the problem.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Identify what we are looking for.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We are looking for the number of training sessions that would make the pay equal.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Name what we are looking for.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let $$s = \text{Heather’s salary}$$ , and $$n = \text{the number of training sessions}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Translate into a system of equations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Option A would pay her \$25,000 plus \$15 for each training session.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$s = 25,000 + 15n$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Option B would pay her \$10,000 + \$40 for each training session.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$s = 10,000 + 40n$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The system is shown.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {s = 25,000 + 15n} \\ {s = 10,000 + 40n} \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5: Solve the system of equations.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We will use substitution.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute $$25,000 + 15n$$ for $$s$$ in the second equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {s = 25,000 + 15n} \\ {s = 10,000 + 40n} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Solve for $$n$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{25,000 + 15\mathbf{n}} & = & {10,000 + 40n} \\ 25,000 & = & {10,000 + 25n} \\ 15,000 & = & {25n} \\ 600 & = & n \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 6: Check the answer.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Are 600 training sessions a year reasonable?</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Are the two options equal when $$n = 600$$ ?</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute into each equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{l} {s = 25,000 + 15(600) = 34,000} \\ {s = 10,000 + 40(600) = 34,000} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 7: Answer the question.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The salary options would be equal for 600 training sessions.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to a System
snippet: Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to a System: Determine whether the ordered pair is a solution to the system: \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {x + 4y \geq 10} \\ {3x - 2y < 12} \end{array} \right. \left( {- 2,4} \right) \left(...
body_xml:
<example number="5.89" title="Determining Whether an Ordered Pair Is a Solution to a System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether the ordered pair is a solution to the system:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\{ \begin{array}{r} {x + 4y \geq 10} \\ {3x - 2y < 12} \end{array} \right.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left( {- 2,4} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {3,1} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Is the ordered pair $$\left( {- 2,4} \right)$$ a solution? We substitute $$\mathbf{x} = - 2$$ and $$\mathbf{y} = 4$$ into both inequalities. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{x} + 4\mathbf{y}} & \geq & 10 \\ {\mathbf{- 2} + 4(\mathbf{4})} & \overset{?}{\geq} & 10 \\ 14 & \geq & {10 \text{true} } \end{array}\begin{array}{rcc} {3\mathbf{x} - 2\mathbf{y}} & < & 12 \\ {3(\mathbf{- 2}) - 2(\mathbf{4})} & \overset{?}{<} & 12 \\ {- 14} & < & {12 \text{true} } \end{array}$$ The ordered pair $$\left( {- 2,4} \right)$$ made both inequalities true. Therefore $$\left( {- 2,4} \right)$$ is a solution to this system.</item>
        <item>Is the ordered pair $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ a solution? We substitute $$\mathbf{x} = 3$$ and $$\mathbf{y} = 1$$ into both inequalities. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\mathbf{x} + 4\mathbf{y}} & \geq & 10 \\ {3 + 4(1)} & \overset{?}{\geq} & 10 \\ 7 & \geq & {10 \text{false} } \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} {3x - 2y} & < & 12 \\ {3(3) - 2(1)} & \overset{?}{<} & 12 \\ 7 & < & {12 \text{true} } \end{array}$$ The ordered pair $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ made one inequality true, but the other one false. Therefore $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ is not a solution to this system.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

unit_title: Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
title: Solving a System of Linear Inequalities by Graphing
snippet: Solving a System of Linear Inequalities by Graphing: Use Figure 5.88 to solve the system of linear inequalities: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y \geq 2x - 1} \\ {y < x + 1} \end{array} \right. To solve the system of linear inequalities we look...
body_xml: Use Figure 5.88 to solve the system of linear inequalities: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y \geq 2x - 1} \\ {y < x + 1} \end{array} \right.$$ To solve the system of linear inequalities we look at the graph and find the region that satisfies BOTH inequalities. To do this we pick a test point and check. Let's us pick $$\left( {- 1, - 1} \right)$$ . Is $$\left( {\mathbf{- 1},\mathbf{- 1}} \right)$$ a solution to $$y \geq 2x - 1?$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{- 1} & \overset{?}{\geq} & {2\left( \mathbf{- 1} \right) - 1} \\ {- 1} & \geq & {- 3 \text{true} } \end{array}$$ Is $$\left( {\mathbf{- 1},\mathbf{- 1}} \right)$$ a solution to $$y < x + 1?$$ $$\begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{- 1} & \overset{?}{<} & {\mathbf{- 1} + 1} \\ {- 1} & < & {0 \text{true} } \end{array}$$ The region containing $$\left( {- 1, - 1} \right)$$ is the solution to the system of linear inequalities. Notice that the solution is all the points in the area shaded twice, which appears as the darkest shaded region.

body_xml: Solve the system by graphing: $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {x - y > 3} \\ {y < - \frac{1}{5}x + 4} \end{array} \right.$$ Graph $$x - y > 3$$ by graphing $$x - y = 3$$ and testing a point (Figure 5.89). The intercepts are $$x = 3$$ and $$y = - 3$$ and the boundary line will be dashed. Test $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ which makes the inequality false so shade the side that does not contain $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Graph $$y < - \frac{1}{5}x + 4$$ by graphing $$y = - \frac{1}{5}x + 4$$ using the slope $$m = - \frac{1}{5}$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$b = 4$$ (Figure 5.90). The boundary line will be dashed. Test $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ which makes the inequality true, so shade the side that contains $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Choose a test point in the solution and verify that it is a solution to both inequalities. The point of intersection of the two lines is not included as both boundary lines were dashed. The solution is the area shaded twice—which appears as the darkest shaded region.

Test $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , which makes the inequality true, so shade the side that contains $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Graph $$y > - 4$$ by graphing $$y = - 4$$ and recognizing that it is a horizontal line through $$y = - 4$$ (Figure 5.92). The boundary line will be dashed. Test $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , which makes the inequality true so shade the side that contains $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . The point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is in the solution, and we have already found it to be a solution of each inequality. The point of intersection of the two lines is not included as both boundary lines were dashed. The solution is the area shaded twice, which appears as the darkest shaded region.

Graph $$y < - \frac{4}{3}x + 1$$ by graphing $$y = - \frac{4}{3}x + 1$$ using the slope $$m = - \frac{4}{3}$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$b = 1$$ (Figure 5.94). The boundary line will be dashed. Test $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , which makes the inequality true, so shade the side that contains $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Graph $$x - 2y < - 4$$ by graphing $$x - 2y = - 4$$ (Figure 5.96) and testing a point. The intercepts are $$x = - 4$$ and $$y = 2$$ and the boundary line will be dashed. Test $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , which makes the inequality false, so shade the side that does not contain $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . No point on the boundary lines is included in the solution as both lines are dashed. The solution is the region that is shaded twice which is also the solution to $$x - 2y < - 4$$ .

unit_title: Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
title: Applying Linear Inequalities to Calculating Photo Costs
snippet: Applying Linear Inequalities to Calculating Photo Costs: A photographer sells their prints at a booth at a street fair. At the start of the day, they want to have at least 25 photos to display at their booth. Each small photo they display...
body_xml:
<example number="5.95" title="Applying Linear Inequalities to Calculating Photo Costs">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A photographer sells their prints at a booth at a street fair. At the start of the day, they want to have at least 25 photos to display at their booth. Each small photo they display costs \$4 and each large photo costs \$10. They do not want to spend more than \$200 on photos to display.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Write a system of inequalities to model this situation.</item>
        <item>Graph the system.</item>
        <item>Could they display 10 small and 20 large photos?</item>
        <item>Could they display 20 large and 10 small photos?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let $$x =$$ the number of small photos and $$y = \text{the number of large photos}$$ . To find the system of equations translate the information. They want to have at least 25 photos. The number of small plus the number of large should be at least 25. $$x + y \geq 25$$ \$4 for each small and \$10 for each large must be no more than \$200 $$4x + 10y \leq 200$$ The number of small photos must be greater than or equal to 0. $$x \geq 0$$ The number of large photos must be greater than or equal to 0. $$y \geq 0$$ We have our system of equations. $$\left\{ \begin{array}{rcl} {x + y} & \geq & 25 \\ {4x + 10y} & \leq & 200 \\ x & \geq & 0 \\ y & \geq & 0 \end{array} \right.$$</item>
        <item>Since $$x \geq 0$$ and $$y \geq 0$$ (both are greater than or equal to) all solutions will be in the first quadrant. As a result, our graph shows only Quadrant I. To graph $$x + y \geq 25$$ , graph $$x + y = 25$$ as a solid line. Choose $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ as a test point. Since it does not make the inequality true, shade the side that does not include the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . To graph $$4x + 10y \leq 200$$ , graph $$4x + 10y = 200$$ as a solid line. Choose $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ as a test point. Since it does make the inequality true, shade (bottom left) the side that include the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Figure 5.97 The solution of the system is the region of Figure 5.97 that is shaded the darkest. The boundary line sections that border the darkly shaded section are included in the solution as are the points on the $$x$$ -axis from $$\left( {25,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {55,0} \right)$$ .</item>
        <item>To determine if 10 small and 20 large photos would work, we look at the graph to see if the point $$\left( {10,20} \right)$$ is in the solution region. We could also test the point to see if it is a solution of both equations. It is not, so the photographer would not display 10 small and 20 large photos.</item>
        <item>To determine if 20 small and 10 large photos would work, we look at the graph to see if the point $$\left( {20,10} \right)$$ is in the solution region. We could also test the point to see if it is a solution of both equations. It is, so the photographer could choose to display 20 small and 10 large photos. Notice that we could also test the possible solutions by substituting the values into each inequality.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="5.96" title="Composing an Objective Function for Selling Two Products">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Miriam starts her own business, where she knits and sells scarves and sweaters out of high-quality wool. She can make a profit of \$8 per scarf and \$10 per sweater. Write an objective function that describes her profit.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$x$$ represent the number of scarves sold, and let $$y$$ represent the number of sweaters sold. Let $$P$$ represent profit. Since each scarf has a profit of \$8 and each sweater has a profit of \$10, the objective function is $$P = 8x + 10y$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="5.97" title="Composing an Objective Function for Production">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>William’s factory produces two products, widgets and wadgets. It takes 24 minutes for his factory to make 1 widget, and 32 minutes for his factory to make 1 wadget. Write an objective function that describes the time it takes to make the products.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$x$$ equal the number of widgets made; let $$y$$ equal the number of wadgets made; let $$T$$ represent total time. The objective function is $$T = 24x + 32y$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Representing the Constraints for Selling Two Products
snippet: Representing the Constraints for Selling Two Products: Two friends start their own business, where they knit and sell scarves and sweaters out of high-quality wool. They can make a profit of \$8 per scarf and \$10 per sweater. To make a...
body_xml:
<example number="5.98" title="Representing the Constraints for Selling Two Products">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Two friends start their own business, where they knit and sell scarves and sweaters out of high-quality wool. They can make a profit of \$8 per scarf and \$10 per sweater. To make a scarf, 3 bags of knitting wool are needed; to make a sweater, 4 bags of knitting wool are needed. The friends can only make 8 items per day, and can use not more than 27 bags of knitting wool per day. Write the inequalities that represent the constraints. Then summarize what has been described thus far by writing the objective function for profit and the two constraints.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$x$$ represent the number of scarves sold, and let $$y$$ represent the number of sweaters sold. There are two constraints: the number of items the business can make in a day (a maximum of 8) and the number of bags of knitting wool they can use per day (a maximum of 27). The first constraint (total number of items in a day) is written as:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x + y \leq 8$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since each scarf takes 3 bags of knitting wool and each sweater takes 4 bags of knitting wool, the second constraint, total bags of knitting wool per day, is written as:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$3x + 4y \leq 27$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In summary, here are the equations that represent the new business:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$P = 8x + 10y$$ ; This is the profit equation: The business makes \$8 per scarf and \$10 per sweater.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {x + y} & \leq & 8 \\ {3x + 4y} & \leq & 27 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Representing Constraints for Production
snippet: Representing Constraints for Production: A factory produces two products, widgets and wadgets. It takes 24 minutes for the factory to make 1 widget, and 32 minutes for the factory to make 1 wadget. Research indicates that long-term demand...
body_xml:
<example number="5.99" title="Representing Constraints for Production">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A factory produces two products, widgets and wadgets. It takes 24 minutes for the factory to make 1 widget, and 32 minutes for the factory to make 1 wadget. Research indicates that long-term demand for products from the factory will result in average sales of 12 widgets per day and 10 wadgets per day. Because of limitations on storage at the factory, no more than 20 widgets or 17 wadgets can be made each day. Write the inequalities that represent the constraints. Then summarize what has been described thus far by writing the objective function for time and the two constraints.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$x$$ equal the number of widgets made; let $$y$$ equal the number of wadgets made. Based on the long-term demand, we know the factory must produce a minimum of 12 widgets and 10 wadgets per day. We also know because of storage limitations, the factory cannot produce more than 20 widgets per day or 17 wadgets per day. Writing those as inequalities, we have:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x \geq 12$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$y \geq 10$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$x \leq 20$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$y \leq 17$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The number of widgets made per day must be between 12 and 20, and the number of wadgets made per day must be between 10 and 17. Therefore, we have:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$12 \leq x \leq 20$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$10 \leq y \leq 17$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The system is:</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$T = 24x + 32y$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$12 \leq x \leq 20$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$10 \leq y \leq 17$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$T$$ is the variable for time; it takes 24 minutes to make a widget and 32 minutes to make a wadget.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Linear Programming Problem for Two Products
snippet: Solving a Linear Programming Problem for Two Products: Three friends start their own business, where they knit and sell scarves and sweaters out of high-quality wool. They can make a profit of \$8 per scarf and \$10 per sweater. To make a...
body_xml:
Three friends start their own business, where they knit and sell scarves and sweaters out of high-quality wool. They can make a profit of \$8 per scarf and \$10 per sweater. To make a scarf, 3 bags of knitting wool are needed; to make a sweater, 4 bags of knitting wool are needed. The friends can only make 8 items per day, and can use not more than 27 bags of knitting wool per day. Determine the number of scarves and sweaters they should make each day to maximize their profit. Step 1: Compose an objective function to be minimized or maximized. From Example 5.98, the objective function is $$P = 8x + 10y$$ . Step 2: Compose inequalities representing the constraints of the system. From Example 5.98, the constraints are $$x + y \leq 8$$ and $$3x + 4y \leq 27$$ . Step 3: Graph the system of inequalities representing the constraints. Using methods discussed in Graphing Linear Equations and Inequalities, the graphs of the constraints are shown below. Because the number of scarves ( $$x$$ ) and the number of sweaters ( $$y$$ ) both must be non-negative numbers (i.e., $$x \geq 0$$ and $$y \geq 0$$ ), we need to graph the system of inequalities in Quadrant I only. Figure 5.99 shows each constraint graphed on its own axes, while Figure 5.100 shows the graph of the system of inequalities (the two constraints graphed together). In Figure 5.100, the large shaded region represents the area where the two constraints intersect. If you are unsure how to graph these regions, refer back to Graphing Linear Equations and Inequalities. Step 4: Find the value of the objective function at each corner point of the graphed region. The “graphed region” is the area where both of the regions intersect; in Figure 5.101, it is the large shaded area. The “corner points” refer to each vertex of the shaded area. Why the corner points? Because the maximum and minimum of every objective function will occur at one (or more) of the corner points. Figure 5.101 shows the location and coordinates of each corner point. Three of the four points are readily found, as we used them to graph the regions; the fourth point, the intersection point of the two constraint lines, will have to be found using methods discussed in Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables, either using substitution or elimination. As a reminder, set up the two equations of the constraint lines: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {3x + 4y} & = & 27 \\ {x + y} & = & 8 \end{array}$$ For this example, substitution will be used. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x + y} & = & 8 \\ y & = & {8 - x.} \end{array}$$ Substituting $$8 - x$$ into the first equation for $$y$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{rcl} {3x + 4\left( {8 - x} \right)} & = & 27 \\ {3x + 32 - 4x} & = & 27 \\ {- x} & = & {- 5} \\ x & = & 5 \end{array}$$ Now, substituting the 5 in for $$x$$ in either equation to solve for $$y$$ . Choosing the second equation, we have: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {5 + y} & = & 8 \\ y & = & 3 \end{array}$$ Therefore, $$x = 5$$ , and $$y = 3$$ . To find the value of the objective function, $$P = 8x + 10y$$ , put the coordinates for each corner point into the equation and solve. The largest solution found when doing this will be the maximum value, and thus will be the answer to the question originally posed: determining the number of scarves and sweaters the new business should make each day to maximize their profit. Corner ( $$x$$ , $$y$$ ) Objective Function $$P = 8x + 10y$$ $$(0,0)$$ $$P = 8(0) + 10(0) = 0$$ $$(0,6.75)$$ $$P = 8(0) + 10(6.75) = 67.5$$ $$(5,3)$$ $$P = 8(5) + 10(3) = 40 + 30 = 70$$ $$(8,0)$$ $$P = 8(8) + 10(0) = 64$$
The maximum value for the profit $$P$$ occurs when $$x = 5$$ and $$y = 3$$ . This means that to maximize their profit, the new business should make 5 scarves and 3 sweaters every day.

title: Finding the Percent of a Total
snippet: Finding the Percent of a Total: Determine 70% of 3,500 Determine 156% of 720 The total is x = 3,500, and the percent is n = 70. The decimal form of 70% is 0.70. To find the part, or percent of the total, substitute those values into the...
body_xml:
<example number="6.4" title="Finding the Percent of a Total">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Determine 70% of 3,500</item>
        <item>Determine 156% of 720</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The total is $$x$$ = 3,500, and the percent is $$n$$ = 70. The decimal form of 70% is 0.70. To find the part, or percent of the total, substitute those values into the formula and calculate. $$\begin{array}{rcl} \text{part} & = & {{percent} \times {total}} \\ & = & {0.70 \times 3500} \\ & = & 2450 \end{array}$$ From this, we say that 70% of 3,500 is 2,450.</item>
        <item>The total is $$x$$ = 720, and the percent is $$n$$ = 156. The decimal form of 156% is 1.56. To find the part, or percent of the total, substitute those values into the formula and calculate. $$\begin{array}{rcl} \text{part} & = & { \text{percent} \times \text{total} } \\ & = & {1.56 \times 720} \\ & = & 1,123.2 \end{array}$$ From this, we say that 156% of 720 is 1,123.2.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Total from the Percent and the Part
snippet: Finding the Total from the Percent and the Part: What is the total if 35% of the total is 70? What is the total if 10% of the total is 4,000? Step 1: The percent is 35, which in decimal form is 0.35. We were given that 35% of the total is...
body_xml:
<example number="6.5" title="Finding the Total from the Percent and the Part">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>What is the total if 35% of the total is 70?</item>
        <item>What is the total if 10% of the total is 4,000?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Step 1: The percent is 35, which in decimal form is 0.35. We were given that 35% of the total is 70, so the part is 70. We are to find the total. Substituting into the formula, we have $$\begin{array}{rcl} \text{part} & = & { \text{percent} \times \text{total} } \\ 70 & = & {0.35 \times \text{total} } \end{array}$$ Step 2: To find the total, we solve the equation for the total. $$\begin{array}{rcl} 70 & = & {0.35 \times \text{total} } \\ \frac{70}{0.35} & = & \frac{0.35 \times \text{total} }{0.35} \\ 200 & = & \frac{0.35 \times \text{total} }{0.35} \\ 200 & = & \text{total} \end{array}$$ From this we see that 200 is the total, or, that 35% of 200 is 70.</item>
        <item>Step 1: The percent is 10, which in decimal form is 0.1. We were given that 10% of the total is 4,000, so the part is 4,000. Substituting into the formula, we have $$\begin{array}{rcl} \text{part} & = & { \text{percent} \times \text{total} } \\ 4,000 & = & {0.1 \times \text{total} } \end{array}$$ Step 2: To find the total, we solve the equation for the total. $$\begin{array}{rcl} 4,000 & = & {0.1 \times \text{total} } \\ \frac{4,000}{0.1} & = & \frac{0.1 \times \text{total} }{0.1} \\ 40,000 & = & \frac{0.1 \times \text{total} }{0.1} \\ 40,000 & = & \text{total} \end{array}$$ From this we see that 40,000 is the total, or that 10% of 40,000 is 4,000.</item>

Converting from the decimal form yields 35%. We say that 175 is 35% of 500.</item>

<example number="6.7" title="Retention Rate at College">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Justine applies to a medium size university outside her hometown and finds out that the retention rate (percent of students who return for their sophomore year) for the 2021 academic year at the university was 84%. During a visit to the registrar’s office, she finds out that 1,350 people had enrolled in academic year 2021. How many students from the academic year 2021 are returning for the 2022 academic year?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The percent of students who will return for the 2022 academic year (the retention rate) is 84%. The total number of students who enrolled in the 2021 academic year was 1,350. This means the percent is known and the total is known. From this, we can determine the number of students who will return (percent of the total) for the 2022 academic year using the formula $$\text{part} = \text{percent} \times \text{total}$$ . Substituting into the formula and calculating, we find that the number of students that are returning is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \text{part} & = & { \text{percent} \times \text{total} } \\ & = & {0.84 \times 1,350} \\ & = & 1,134 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So 1,134 students will return for the 2022 academic year.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph>In this problem, Mariel’s total sales is to be determined. We know the percent she earns is 20%. We also know that her sales commission was \$153.00, which is the percent of the total. Using this information and the formula $$\text{part} = \text{percent} \times \text{total}$$ we can find Mariel’s total sales. The decimal form of 20% is 0.2. The part, or percent of the total, is 153. Substituting and solving, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \text{part} & = & { \text{percent} \times \text{total} } \\ 153 & = & {0.2 \times \text{total} } \\ \frac{153}{0.2} & = & \frac{0.2 \times \text{total} }{0.2} \\ 765 & = & \frac{0.2 \times \text{total} }{0.2} \\ 765 & = & \text{total} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Mariel’s total sales were \$765.00.</paragraph>

<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>The formula for a discount based on a percentage is $${discount} = {percent discount} \times {original price}$$ , with the percent discount expressed as a decimal. The price of the item after the discount is $${sale price} = {original price} - {discount}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>These are often combined into the following formula</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${sale price} = {original price} - {percent discount} \times {original price} = {original price} \times (1 - {percent discount})$$</paragraph>
  </note>

The discount is \$50.67. The sale price of the item is then $${sale price} = {original price} - {discount} = 168.90 - 50.67 = 118.23$$ , or \$118.23.</item>

<example number="6.11" title="Calculating the Percent Discount from the Original and Sale Prices">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine the percent discount based on the given original and sale prices.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Original price = \$1,200.00; sale price = \$900.00</item>
        <item>Original price = \$36.70; sale price = \$29.52</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Step 1. Find the discount. Using the original price and the sale price, we can find the discount with the formula $${sale price} = {original price} - {discount}$$ . Substituting and calculating, we find the discount to be $$900.00 = 1,200.00 - {discount}$$ . Solving for the discount gives \$300.00. Step 2. Find the percent discount. Substituting the discount of \$300.00 and the original price of \$1,200.00, into the formula $${discount} = {percent discount} \times {original price}$$ , we can find the percent discount. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {{300}{.00}} & = & {{percent discount} \times {1,200}{.00}} \\ \frac{{300}{.00}}{1,200.00} & = & {percent discount} \\ 0.25 & = & {percent discount} \end{array}$$ Converting to percent form, the percent discount is 25%.</item>
        <item>Step 1. Find the discount. Using the original price and the sale price, we can find the discount with the formula $${sale price} = {original price} - {discount}$$ . Substituting and calculating, we find the discount to be $$29.52 = 36.70 - {discount}$$ . Solving for the discount gives \$7.38. Step 2. Find the percent discount. Substituting the discount of \$7.38 and the original price of \$36.70, into the formula $${discount} = {percent discount} \times {original price}$$ , we can find the percent discount. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {{29}{.52}} & = & {{percent discount} \times {36}{.70}} \\ \frac{{29}{.52}}{36.70} & = & {percent discount} \\ 0.2 & = & {percent discount} \end{array}$$ Converting to percent form, the percent discount is 20%.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph>We know the original price of the item, \$240. We also know the sale price of the item, \$168. From this we know the discount is $$\$240 - \$168 = \$72$$ . Substituting these values into the formula $${discount} = {percent discount} \times {original price}$$ , we can find the percent discount.</paragraph>

      <paragraph>The student percent discount on the bus pass is 30%.</paragraph>
    </solution>

      <paragraph>Bob decided to order a t-shirt for his gaming friend online for \$29.50. He knows the markup on such t-shirts is 18%. What was the t-shirt’s cost before the markup?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using the percent markup and the retail price, \$29.50, we can find the cost with the formula $${retail price} = {original price} \times {(1} + {percent markup)}$$ . Substituting and solving for cost we find</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {retail price} & = & {{cost} \times {(1} + {percent markup)}} \\ {{29}{.50}} & = & {{cost} \times {(1+0}{.18)}} \\ {{29}{.50}} & = & {{cost} \times {(1}{.18)}} \\ {{25}{.00}} & = & {cost} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The cost of the t-shirt was \$25.00.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>To calculate the amount of sales tax paid on the purchase price in a locality with sales tax given in decimal form, calculate $${sales tax} = {purchase price} \times {tax rate}$$ The total price is then $${Total price} = {purchase price} + {purchase price} \times {tax rate} = {purchase price} \times \left( 1 + {tax rate)} \right.$$</paragraph>

Since the third decimal place (fraction of a penny) is 1, we round down and the sales tax is \$35.39. The total price is the sales tax plus the purchase price, so is $$\$428.99 + \$35.88 = \$464.87$$ .</item>
        <item>The sales tax on the item is found using $${sales tax} = {purchase price} \times {tax rate}$$ . The purchase price is \$34.88 and the tax rate is 8.25%. Substituting and calculating, the sales tax is $${sales tax} = \$34.88 \times 0.0825 = \$2.8776$$ . The sales tax needs to be rounded off. Since the third decimal place (fraction of a penny) is 7, we round up and the sales tax is \$2.88. The total price of the item is the sales tax plus the purchase price, so is $$\$34.88 + \$2.88 = \$37.76$$ .</item>
