<example number="6.25" title="Compute Sales Tax for Denver, Colorado">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The sales tax rate in Denver Colorado is 8.81%. Keven buys a TV in Denver, and the purchase price (before taxes) is \$499.00. How much will Keven pay in sales tax and what will be the total amount he spends when he buys the TV?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The sales tax rate in Denver is 8.81%. To find the sales tax Keven will pay, find 8.81% of the purchase price. In decimal form, that sales tax rate is 0.0881. Using the formula and substituting 499.00 for purchase price, we find that Keven will pay $${purchase price} \times {tax rate} = {\$ 499} \times 0.0881 = \$43.96$$ in sales tax for the TV.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The total price that Keven will pay is the purchase price plus the sales tax, or $$\$499.00 + \$43.96 = \$542.96$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Compute Sales Tax for Austin, Texas
snippet: Compute Sales Tax for Austin, Texas: Jillian visits Austin, Texas, and purchases a new set of weights for her home. She spends, including sales tax, \$467.64. The sales tax rate in Austin Texas is 8.25%. How much of the total price is...
body_xml:
<example number="6.26" title="Compute Sales Tax for Austin, Texas">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Jillian visits Austin, Texas, and purchases a new set of weights for her home. She spends, including sales tax, \$467.64. The sales tax rate in Austin Texas is 8.25%. How much of the total price is sales tax?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The sales tax paid for this purchase is the difference in the total price and the purchase price. We know the total price is \$467.64. We also know the sales tax rate, which is 8.25%. In decimal form, this is 0.0825. Using these values and the formula $${total price} = {purchase price} \times {(1} + {tax rate)}$$ to find the purchase price.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {total price} & = & {{purchase price} \times {(1} + {tax rate)}} \\ {\$467.64} & = & {{purchase price} \times (1 + 0.0825)} \\ {\$467.64} & = & {{purchase price} \times (1.0825)} \\ {\$432} & = & {purchase price} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Knowing both the total price and the now the purchase price, we can find the difference, which is the sales tax.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The total price was \$467.64. The purchase price was \$432. The difference of the total price and the purchase price, or the sales tax, is then \$467.64 − \$432.00, which is \$35.64. Jillian pays \$35.64 in sales tax.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: FORMULA
snippet: FORMULA: The simple interest, I , to be paid on a loan with annual interest rate r for a number of years (term of the loan) t , with principal P , is found using I = P \times r \times t , where the decimal form of the interest rate, r , is...
body_xml:
<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>The simple interest, $$I$$ , to be paid on a loan with annual interest rate $$r$$ for a number of years (term of the loan) $$t$$ , with principal $$P$$ , is found using $$I = P \times r \times t$$ , where the decimal form of the interest rate, $$r$$ , is used. The total repaid, then is $$T = P + I$$ or, more directly, $$T = P + P \times r \times t$$ . This total is often referred to as the loan payoff amount, or more simply just the payoff.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Simple Interest on Loans with Integer Year Terms
snippet: Simple Interest on Loans with Integer Year Terms: Calculate the simple interest to be paid on a loan with the given principal, annual percentage rate, and number of years. Then, calculate the loan payoff amount. Principal P = \$4,000,...
body_xml:
<example number="6.27" title="Simple Interest on Loans with Integer Year Terms">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate the simple interest to be paid on a loan with the given principal, annual percentage rate, and number of years. Then, calculate the loan payoff amount.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Principal $$P$$ = \$4,000, annual interest rate $$r$$ = 5.5%, and number of years $$t$$ = 4</item>
        <item>Principal $$P$$ = \$14,800, annual interest rate $$r$$ = 7.9%, and number of years $$t$$ = 7</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Substitute the principal $$P$$ = \$4,000, the decimal form of the annual interest rate $$r$$ = 0.055, and number of years $$t$$ = 4 into the formula for simple interest, and calculate. $$I = P \times r \times t = 4,000 \times 0.055 \times 4 = 880$$ . The simple interest, or cost of the loan, to be paid on the loan is \$880. The loan payoff amount, or the total to be repaid, is $$T = P + I = 4,000 + 880 = 4,880$$ , or \$4,880.00.</item>
        <item>Substitute the principal $$P$$ = \$14,800, the decimal form of the annual interest rate $$r$$ = 0.079, and number of years $$t$$ = 7 into the formula for simple interest, and calculate. $$I = P \times r \times t = 14,800 \times 0.079 \times 7 = 8,184.4$$ . The simple interest, or cost to borrow, to be paid on the loan is \$8,184.40. The loan payoff amount, or the total to be repaid, is $$T = P + I = 14,800 + 8,184.4 = 22,984.4$$ , or \$22,984.40.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Simple Interest Equipment Loan
snippet: Simple Interest Equipment Loan: Riley runs an auto repair shop, and needs to purchase a new brake lathe, which costs \$11,995. She takes out a two-year, simple interest loan at an annual interest rate of 14.9%. How much interest will she...
body_xml:
<example number="6.28" title="Simple Interest Equipment Loan">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Riley runs an auto repair shop, and needs to purchase a new brake lathe, which costs \$11,995. She takes out a two-year, simple interest loan at an annual interest rate of 14.9%. How much interest will she pay and how much total will she repay on the loan?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1. Determine the variables, or parts of the formula. The principal $$P$$ is the cost of the brake lathe, so $$P$$ = \$11,995. The interest rate Riley pays is 14.9%, or $$r$$ = 0.149 in decimal form. The length of the loan is two years, so $$t$$ = 2. We are first asked to find $$I$$ , the interest Riley will pay.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. Substitute the known variables into the formula for simple interest $$I = P \times r \times t$$ and solve for $$I$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>From Step 1 we have $$I = P \times r \times t = 11995 \times 0.149 \times 2 = 3,574.51$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This tells us that the simple interest, or cost to borrow, to be paid on the loan is \$3,574.51.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3. Use the formula $$T = P + I$$ to determine the total amount Riley will repay, $$T$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The total to be repaid is $$T = P + I = 11,995 + 3,574.51 = 15,569.51$$ , or \$15,569.51.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Loan to Purchase Equipment
snippet: Loan to Purchase Equipment: Abeje needs a loan to purchase equipment for the gym she is going to open. She visits the bank and secures a 4-month loan of \$20,000. Her annual percentage rate is 6.75%. How much interest will Abeje pay and...

<example number="6.29" title="Loan to Purchase Equipment">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Abeje needs a loan to purchase equipment for the gym she is going to open. She visits the bank and secures a 4-month loan of \$20,000. Her annual percentage rate is 6.75%. How much interest will Abeje pay and what is her loan payoff amount?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Abeje’s loan is for \$20,000, so her principal is $$P$$ = 20,000. The interest rate Abeje will pay is 6.75%, or $$r$$ = 0.0675 in decimal form. The length of the loan is 4 months, so $$t = \frac{4}{12}$$ . Substituting these in the formula for simple interest, we find her interest to be $$I = P \times r \times t = 20,000 \times 0.0675 \times 4/12 = 450$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The simple interest, or cost to borrow, to be paid on the loan is \$450.00.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The payoff is $$T = P + I = 20,000 + 450 = 20,450$$ , or \$20,450.00.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: FORMULA
snippet: FORMULA: To determine the interest, I , on a loan with term t expressed in days, with principal of P , and interest rate in decimal form of r , calculate I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t . Here, \frac{r}{365} represents the daily...
body_xml:
<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>To determine the interest, $$I$$ , on a loan with term $$t$$ expressed in days, with principal of $$P$$ , and interest rate in decimal form of $$r$$ , calculate $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t$$ . Here, $$\frac{r}{365}$$ represents the daily interest rate.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Alternately, the above formula is equivalent to $$I = P \times r \times \frac{t}{365}$$ , where the interest rate remains an annual rate, but the time is expressed as a fraction of the year.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Loan for Moving Costs
snippet: Loan for Moving Costs: David plans to move his family from Raleigh, North Carolina to Tempe, Arizona. His company will reimburse (pay after the move) David for the move. David does research and determines that movers will cost \$5,600 to...
body_xml:
<example number="6.30" title="Loan for Moving Costs">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>David plans to move his family from Raleigh, North Carolina to Tempe, Arizona. His company will reimburse (pay after the move) David for the move. David does research and determines that movers will cost \$5,600 to move his family’s belongings to Tempe. He takes out a simple interest, 45-day loan at 11.75% interest to pay this cost. How much interest will be paid on this 45-day loan, and what is David’s loan payoff amount?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This loan is in terms of days, so we will use the formula $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t$$ , where t is the number of days and $$r$$ is the annual interest rate.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The principal for the loan is the moving cost, or $$P$$ = 5,600. The annual interest rate that David will pay is 11.75%, which in decimal is 0.1175. The length of time for the loan is 45 days, so $$t$$ = 45.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substituting these values into the formula and calculating, we find that the interest to be paid is $$I = 5,600 \times \frac{0.1175}{365} \times 45 = 81.13$$ , or \$81.13 (remember, interest is almost always rounded up to the next cent).</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The payoff for the loan is \$5,681.13.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: FORMULA
snippet: FORMULA: The future value, \mathit{FV} , of an investment that yields simple interest is FV = P + I = P + P \times r \times t , where P is the principal (amount invested at the start), r is the annual interest rate in decimal form, and t...
body_xml:
<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>The future value, $$\mathit{FV}$$ , of an investment that yields simple interest is $$FV = P + I = P + P \times r \times t$$ , where $$P$$ is the principal (amount invested at the start), $$r$$ is the annual interest rate in decimal form, and $$t$$ is the length of time the money is invested. The time $$t$$ will be an integer if the term of the deposit is an integer number of years, will be number of months/12 if the term is in months, will be actual/365 if the deposit is for a number of days.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Simple Interest on a Deposit
snippet: Simple Interest on a Deposit: In the following, determine how much interest was earned on the investment and the future value of the investment, if the investment yields simple interest. Principal is \$1,000, annual interest rate is 2.01%,...
body_xml:
<example number="6.31" title="Simple Interest on a Deposit">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In the following, determine how much interest was earned on the investment and the future value of the investment, if the investment yields simple interest.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Principal is \$1,000, annual interest rate is 2.01%, and time is 5 years</item>
        <item>Principal is \$5,000, annual interest rate is 1.85%, and time is 30 years</item>
        <item>Principal is \$10,000, annual interest rate is 1.25%, and time is 18 months</item>
        <item>Principal is \$7,000, annual interest rate is 3.26%, and time is 100 days</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The principal is $$P$$ = \$1,000, the annual interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.0201, and the term is 5 years, or $$t$$ = 5. Since the term is an integer number of years, the interest earned on the investment is $$I = P \times r \times t = 1,000 \times 0.0201 \times 5 = 100.5$$ , or the interest earned was \$100.50. To find the future value, we use the formula $$FV = P + I$$ . Substituting the values and calculating, we find the future value of the investment to be $$FV = P + I = 1,000 + 100.5 = 1100.5$$ . The future value of the investment at the end of 5 years is \$1,100.50. Notice that the future value could have been calculated directly with $$FV = P + P \times r \times t$$</item>
        <item>The principal is $$P$$ = \$5,000, the annual interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.0185, and the term is 30 years, or $$t$$ = 30. Since the term is an integer number of years, the interest earned on the investment is $$I = P \times r \times t = 5,000 \times 0.0185 \times 30 = 2,775$$ , or the interest earned was \$2,775.00. To find the future value, we use the formula $$FV = P + I$$ . Substituting the values and calculating, we find the future value of the investment to be $$FV = P + I = 5,000 + 2,775 = 7,775$$ . The future value of the investment at the end of 30 years is \$7,775.00.</item>
        <item>The principal is $$P$$ = \$10,000, the annual interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.0125, and the term is 18 months. Since the term is in months, we have to write the months in terms of years. For 18 months, we use 18/12 as $$t$$ . The interest earned on the investment is $$I = P \times r \times t = 10,000 \times 0.0125 \times \frac{18}{12} = 187.5$$ , or the interest earned was \$187.50. To find the future value, we use the formula $$FV = P + I$$ . Substituting the values and calculating, we find the future value of the investment to be $$FV = P + I = 10,000 + 187.5 = 10,187.5$$ . The future value of the investment at the end of 18 months is \$10,187.50.</item>
        <item>Principal is \$7,000, annual interest rate is 3.26%, and time is 100 days. The principal is $$P$$ = \$7,000, the annual interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.0326, and the term is 100 days. Since the term is in days, we have to write the time using actual/365, or $$t$$ = 100/365. The interest earned on the investment is $$I = P \times r \times t = 7,000 \times 0.0326 \times \frac{100}{365} = 62.52$$ , or the interest earned was \$62.52. To find the future value, we use the formula $$FV = P + I$$ . Substituting the values and calculating, we find the future value of the investment to be $$FV = P + I = 7,000 + 62.52 = 7,062.52$$ . The future value of the investment at the end of 100 days is \$7,062.52.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.32" title="Certificate of Deposit">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Jonas deposits \$2,500 in a CD bearing 3.25% simple interest for a term of 3 years. When he redeems his CD at the end of the 3 years, how much will he receive?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This is a future value example. We know that $$P$$ = \$2,500 is the amount deposited. The annual simple interest rate in decimal form is $$r$$ = 0.0325. The term of the investment is $$t$$ = 3 years.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substituting those values into the future value formula, we have $$FV = P + P \times r \times t = 2,500 + 2,500 \times 0.0325 \times 3 = 2,500 + 243.75 = 2,743.75$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>When the CD is redeemed, Jonas will receive \$2,743.75.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.33" title="Interest Paid in a Partial Payment on a Loan">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>A simple interest loan for \$6,500 is taken out at 12.6% annual percentage rate. A partial payment is made 45 days into the loan period. How much of the partial payment will be for interest?</item>
        <item>A simple interest loan for \$13,700 is taken out at 6.55% annual interest rate. A partial payment is to be made after 60 days. How much of the partial payment will be for interest?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To find the interest paid in this partial payment, we calculate the interest on the principal for the time between the origination of the loan and the payment day, or 45 days. The principal is \$6,500. The annual interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.126. The interest paid for 45 days is found by substituting the values for principal $$P$$ , rate $$r$$ , and time $$t$$ into the formula $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t$$ . Calculating, we have $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t = 6,500 \times \frac{0.126}{365} \times 45 = 100.9726$$ . Rounding up, the portion of the partial payment that will be paid for interest is \$100.98.</item>
        <item>To find the interest paid in this partial payment, we calculate the interest on the principal for the time between the origination of the loan and the payment day, or 60 days. The principal is \$13,700. The annual interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.0655. The interest paid for those 60 days is found by substituting those values into the formula $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t$$ . Calculating, we have $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t = 13,700 \times \frac{0.0655}{365} \times 60 = 147.5096$$ . Rounding up, the portion of the partial payment that will be paid for interest is \$147.51.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>A simple interest loan for \$45,500 is taken out at 11.8% annual percentage rate. A partial payment of \$20,000 is made 50 days into the loan period. After this payment, what will the remaining balance of the loan be?</item>
        <item>A simple interest loan for \$150,000 is taken out at 5.85% annual percentage rate. A partial payment of \$50,000 is made 70 days into the loan period. After this payment, what will the remaining balance of the loan be?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The principal is \$45,500, which will be treated as the balance, $$B$$ , of the loan. The annual simple interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.118. The time is $$t$$ = 50 days. Step 1: Determine the amount of the partial payment that is applied to interest. To find this, substitute the values above into the formula $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t$$ and calculate. Calculating, the amount of the payment that is applied to interest is $$I = 45,500 \times \frac{0.118}{365} \times 50 = 735.4795$$ . Rounding up, we have $$I$$ = \$735.48. Step 2: The amount of the payment that is to be applied to the balance of the loan is partial payment minus the amount of the partial payment that is applied to the interest. The payment is \$2,000. The amount that is applied to the balance is $$P - I = \$20,000 - \$735.48 = \$19,264.52$$ . Step 3: The remaining balance is found by subtracting the amount applied to the balance from the previous balance, or $$B - \left( {P - I} \right) = \$45,500 - \$19,264.52 = \$26,235.48$$ . The remining balance after the partial payment is \$26,235.48.</item>
        <item>The principal is \$150,000, which will be treated as the balance, $$B$$ , of the loan. The annual simple interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.0585. The time is $$t$$ = 70 days. Step 1: Determine the amount of the partial payment that is applied to interest. To find this, substitute the values above into the formula $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t$$ and calculate. Calculating, the amount of the payment that is applied to interest is $$I = 150,000 \times \frac{0.0585}{365} \times 70 = 1,682.8767$$ . Rounding up, we have $$I$$ = \$1,682.88. Step 2: The amount of the payment that is to be applied to the balance of the loan is partial payment minus the amount of the partial payment that is applied to the interest. The payment is \$50,000. The amount that is applied to the balance is $$P - I = \$50,000 - \$1,682.88 = \$48,317.12$$ . Step 3: The remaining balance is found by subtracting the amount applied to the balance from the previous balance, or $$B - \left( {P - I} \right) = \$150,000 - \$48,317.12 = \$101,682.88$$ . The remining balance after the partial payment is \$101,682.88.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding Loan Pay Off After a Partial Payment
snippet: Finding Loan Pay Off After a Partial Payment: Laura takes out an \$18,400 loan for 120 days at 17.9% simple interest. She makes a partial payment of \$7,500 after 45 days. What is her payoff amount at the end of the loan? The initial...
body_xml:
<example number="6.35" title="Finding Loan Pay Off After a Partial Payment">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Laura takes out an \$18,400 loan for 120 days at 17.9% simple interest. She makes a partial payment of \$7,500 after 45 days. What is her payoff amount at the end of the loan?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The initial balance, or principal, of her loan is \$18,400. The interest rate in decimal form is 0.179. Her partial payment of \$7,500 is made after 45 days. Using these values, we can determine how much of the partial payment is applied to the balance. From there, we can determine her final loan payoff after 120 days.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Determine the remaining balance after the partial payment. Using the partial payment process outlined in the previous example, we first find that the amount of the partial payment that is applied to the balance. Their interest paid in the partial payment is $$I = P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t = 18,400 \times \frac{0.179}{365} \times 45 = 406.0603$$ , or \$406.07 (remember to round up!). Using this and that the loan amount was for \$18,400, the remaining balance on the loan after the partial payment is $$B - (P - I) = \$18,400 - (\$7,500 - \$406.07) = \$11,306.07$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: The number of days between the partial payment and the date that the loan is to be paid off is 120 – 45 = 75. This means that the time between the partial payment and the final payment is 75 days.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: To calculate the payoff amount, use $$\text{payoff} = P + P \times \frac{r}{365} \times t$$ , with $$P$$ = \$11,306.07 (the remaining balance), $$t$$ = 75 (from Step 2) and $$r$$ = 0.179. The payoff amount, then, is $$\text{payoff} = 11,306.07 + 11,306.07 \times \frac{0.179}{365} \times 75 = 11,721.9165$$ . Rounding up, the payoff amount is \$11,721.92.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

The monthly interest rate is the annual rate divided by 12. The number of months is the number of years times 12.</paragraph>

title: Calculating Car Payments
snippet: Calculating Car Payments: Desiree buys a new car, by taking a loan out from her credit union. The balance of her loan is \$27,845.00. The annual interest rate that Desiree will pay is 7.3%. She plans to pay this off over 4 years. How much...
body_xml:
<example number="6.36" title="Calculating Car Payments">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Desiree buys a new car, by taking a loan out from her credit union. The balance of her loan is \$27,845.00. The annual interest rate that Desiree will pay is 7.3%. She plans to pay this off over 4 years. How much will Desiree’s monthly payment be?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To use the formula for monthly payments, we need the principal, the interest rate, and the number of years. The principal is \$27,845. The annual rate, in decimal form, is 0.073. Dividing 0.073 by 12 gives the monthly interest rate $$0.073/12 = 0.00608\overline{3}$$ . She takes the loan out for 4 years, which is $$t = 12 \times 4 = 48$$ months. Substituting these values into the formula, $$A = P \times \frac{r \times {(1 + r)}^{t}}{{(1 + r)}^{t} - 1}$$ , we calculate:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {27,845 \times \frac{0.00608\overline{3} \times {(1 + 0.00608\overline{3})}^{48}}{{(1 + 0.00608\overline{3})}^{48} - 1}} \\ & = & {27,845 \times \frac{0.00608\overline{3} \times {(1.00608\overline{3})}^{48}}{{(1.00608\overline{3})}^{48} - 1}} \\ & = & {27,845 \times \frac{0.00608\overline{3} \times 1.337918996}{1.337918996 - 1}} \\ & = & {27,845 \times \frac{0.008139007}{0.337918996}} \\ & = & {27,845 \times 0.024085675} \\ & = & 670.6656 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using the formula and rounding up to the next cent, we see that Desiree’s monthly payment will be \$670.67.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: FORMULA
snippet: FORMULA: The present value, PV , of money deposited at an annual, simple interest rate of r (in decimal form) for time t (in years) with a specified future value of FV , is calculated with the formula PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + rt)} . Note:...
body_xml:
<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>The present value, $$PV$$ , of money deposited at an annual, simple interest rate of $$r$$ (in decimal form) for time $$t$$ (in years) with a specified future value of $$FV$$ , is calculated with the formula $$PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + rt)}$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note: Present value, in this calculation, is always rounded up. Otherwise, future value may fall short of the target future value.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 6.37
snippet: Example 6.37: Compute the present value of the investment described. Interpret the result. FV = \$10,000, t = 15 years, annual simple interest rate of 5.5% FV = \$150,000, t = 20 years, annual simple interest rate of 6.25% FV = \$250,000,...
body_xml:
<example number="6.37">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Compute the present value of the investment described. Interpret the result.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$FV$$ = \$10,000, $$t$$ = 15 years, annual simple interest rate of 5.5%</item>
        <item>$$FV$$ = \$150,000, $$t$$ = 20 years, annual simple interest rate of 6.25%</item>
        <item>$$FV$$ = \$250,000, $$t$$ = 486 months, annual simple interest rate of 4.75%</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The future value is $$FV$$ = \$10,000. The time of the investment is in years, so $$t$$ = 15. The annual, simple interest rate is 5.5%, which in decimal form is 0.055. We substitute those values into the formula and calculate. $$PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + rt)} = \frac{10,000}{(1 + (0.055) \times (15))} = \frac{10,000}{(1 + 0.825)} = \frac{10,000}{(1.825)} = 5,479.452$$ . Rounding up, we see that the present value of \$10,000 invested at a simple annual interest rate of 5.5% for 15 years is \$5,479.46. This means that \$5,479.46 needs to be invested so that, after 15 years at 5.5% interest, the investment will be worth \$10,000.</item>
        <item>The future value is $$FV$$ = \$150,000. The time of the investment is in years, so $$t$$ = 20. The annual, simple interest rate is 6.25%, which in decimal form is 0.0625. We substitute those values into the formula and calculate. $$PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + rt)} = \frac{150,000}{(1 + (0.0625) \times (20))} = \frac{150,000}{(1 + 1.25)} = \frac{150,000}{(2.25)} = 66,666.\overline{6}$$ . Rounding up, we see that the present value of \$150,000 invested at a simple annual interest rate of 6.25% for 20 years is \$66,666.67. This means that \$66,666.67 needs to be invested so that, after 20 years at 6.25% interest, the investment will be worth \$150,000.</item>
        <item>The future value is $$\mathit{FV}$$ = \$250,000. The time of the investment is 486 months. This needs to be converted to years. To do so, divide the number of months by 12, giving $$years = \frac{486}{12} = 40.5$$ , so $$t$$ = 40.5 years. The annual, simple interest rate is 4.75%, which in decimal form is 0.0475. We substitute those values into the formula and calculate. $$PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + rt)} = \frac{250,000}{(1 + (0.0475) \times (40.5))} = \frac{150,000}{(1 + 1.92375)} = \frac{150,000}{(2.92375)} = 129,954.5159$$ . Rounding up, we see that the present value of \$250,000 invested at a simple annual interest rate of 4.75% for 486 months is \$129,954.52. This means that \$129,954.52 needs to be invested so that, after 486 months at 4.75% interest, the investment will be worth \$150,000.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Present Value of a CD
snippet: Present Value of a CD: Beatriz will invest some money in a CD that yields 3.99% simple interest when invested for 30 years. How much must Beatriz invest so that after those 30 years, her CD is worth \$300,000? Beatriz needs to know how...

<example number="6.38" title="Present Value of a CD">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Beatriz will invest some money in a CD that yields 3.99% simple interest when invested for 30 years. How much must Beatriz invest so that after those 30 years, her CD is worth \$300,000?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Beatriz needs to know how much to deposit now so that her CD is worth \$300,000 after 30 years. This means she needs to know the present value of that \$300,000. The time is 30 years and the annual simple interest rate, in decimal form, is 0.0399. Using that information and the formula for present value, we calculate the present value of that \$300,000. $$PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + rt)} = \frac{300,000}{(1 + (0.0399) \times (30))} = \frac{300,000}{(1 + 1.197)} = \frac{300,000}{(2.197)} = 136,549.8407$$ . Rounding up, Beatriz needs to invest \$136,549.85 so that she has \$300,000 in 30 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Interest Compounded Annually
snippet: Interest Compounded Annually: Abena invests \$1,000 in a CD (certificate of deposit) earning 4% compounded annually. How much will Abena’s CD be worth after 3 years? Since the interest is compounded annually, the interest will be computed...
body_xml:
<example number="6.39" title="Interest Compounded Annually">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Abena invests \$1,000 in a CD (certificate of deposit) earning 4% compounded annually. How much will Abena’s CD be worth after 3 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the interest is compounded annually, the interest will be computed at the end of each year and added to the CD’s value. The interest at the end of the following year will be based on the value found form the previous year.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: After the first year, the interest in Abena’s CD is computed using the interest formula $$I = P \times r \times t$$ . The principal is $$P$$ = 1,000, the rate, as a decimal, is 0.04, and the time is one year, so $$t$$ = 1. Using that, the interest earned in the first year is $$I = P \times r \times t = 1,000 \times 0.04 \times 1 = 40$$ , so the interest earned in the first year was \$40.00. This is added to the value of the CD, making the CD worth $$\$1,000 + \$40 = \$1,040$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: At the end of the second year, interest is again computed, but is computed based on the CD’s new value, \$1,040. Using this new value and the interest formula ( $$r$$ and $$t$$ are still 0.04 and 1, respectively), we see that the CD earned $$I = P \times r \times t = 1,040 \times 0.04 \times 1 = 41.6$$ , or \$41.60. This is added to the value of the CD, making the CD now worth $$\$1,040.00 + \$41.60 = \$1,081.60$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: At the end of the third year, interest is again computed, but is computed based on Abena’s CD’s new value, \$1,081.60. Using this value and the interest formula ( $$r$$ and $$t$$ are still 0.04 and 1, respectively), we see that the CD earned $$I = P \times r \times t = 1,081.60 \times 0.04 \times 1 = 43.264$$ , or \$43.26 (remember to round down). This is added to the value of the CD, making the CD now worth $$\$1,081.60 + \$43.26 = \$1,124.86$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>After 3 years, Abena’s CD is worth \$1,124.86.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Comparing Simple to Compound Interest on a 3-Year CD
snippet: Comparing Simple to Compound Interest on a 3-Year CD: Abena invested \$1,000 in a CD that earned 4% compounded annually, and the CD was worth \$1,124.86 after 3 years. Had Abena invested in a CD with simple interest, how much would the CD...
body_xml:
<example number="6.40" title="Comparing Simple to Compound Interest on a 3-Year CD">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Abena invested \$1,000 in a CD that earned 4% compounded annually, and the CD was worth \$1,124.86 after 3 years. Had Abena invested in a CD with simple interest, how much would the CD have been worth after 3 years? How much more did Abena earn using compound interest?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Had Abena invested \$1,000 in a 4% simple interest CD for 3 years, her CD would have been worth $$P + P \times r \times t = 1,000 + 1,000 \times 0.04 \times 3 = 1,120$$ , or \$1,120.00. With interest compounded annually, Abena’s CD was worth \$1,124.86. The difference between compound and simple interest is $$\$1,124.86 - \$1,120.00 = \$4.86$$ . So compound interest earned Abena \$4.86 more than the simple interest did.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

This is also referred to as the future value of the investment.</paragraph>

title: Computing Future Value for Compound Interest
snippet: Computing Future Value for Compound Interest: In the following, compute the future value of the investment with the given conditions. Principal is \$5,000, annual interest rate is 3.8%, compounded monthly, for 5 years. Principal is...

<example number="6.41" title="Computing Future Value for Compound Interest">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In the following, compute the future value of the investment with the given conditions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Principal is \$5,000, annual interest rate is 3.8%, compounded monthly, for 5 years.</item>
        <item>Principal is \$18,500, annual interest rate is 6.25%, compounded quarterly, for 17 years.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The principal is $$P$$ = \$5,000, interest rate, in decimal form, $$r$$ = 0.038, compounded monthly so $$n$$ = 12, and for $$t$$ = 5 years. Substituting these values into the formula, we find $$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt} = 5,000\left( {1 + \frac{0.038}{12}} \right)^{12 \times 5}} \\ & = & {5,000\left( {1 + 0.0031\overline{6}} \right)^{60}} \\ & = & {5,000\left( {1.0031\overline{6}} \right)^{40}} \\ & = & {5,000 \times 1.20888663572} \\ & = & {6,044.4332} \end{array}$$ The future value of the investment is \$6,044.43.</item>
      </list>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The principal is $$P$$ = \$18,500, interest rate, in decimal form, $$r$$ = 0.0625, compounded quarterly so $$n$$ = 4, and for $$t$$ = 17 years. Substituting these values into the formula, we $$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt} = 18,500\left( {1 + \frac{0.0625}{4}} \right)^{4 \times 17}} \\ & = & {18,500\left( {1 + 0.015625} \right)^{68}} \\ & = & {18,500(1.015625)^{68}} \\ & = & {18,500 \times 2.86992151999} \\ & = & {53,093.5481} \end{array}$$ The future value of the investment is \$53,093.54.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.42" title="Interest Compounded Quarterly">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Cody invests \$7,500 in an account that earns 4.5% interest compounded quarterly (4 times per year). Determine the value of Cody’s investment after 10 years.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Cody’s initial investment is \$7,500, so $$P$$ = \$7,500. The annual interest rate is 4.5%, which is 0.045 in decimal form. Compounding quarterly means there are four periods in a year, so $$n$$ = 4. He invests the money for 10 years. Substituting those values into the formula, we calculate</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcc} A & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt} = 7,500\left( {1 + \frac{0.045}{4}} \right)^{4 \times 10}} \\ & = & {7,500\left( {1 + 0.01125} \right)^{40}} \\ & = & {7,500(1.01125)^{40}} \\ & = & {7,500 \times 1.564376865391} \\ & = & {11,732.8265} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>After 10 years, Cody’s initial investment of \$7,500 is worth \$11,732.82.</paragraph>

<example number="6.43" title="Interest Compounded Daily">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Kathy invests \$10,000 in an account that yields 5.6% compounded daily. How much money will be in her account after 20 years?</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Kathy’s initial investment is \$10,000, so $$P$$ = \$10,000. The annual interest rate is 5.6%, which is 0.056 in decimal form. Compounding daily means there are 364 periods in a year, so $$n$$ = 365. She invests the money for 20 years, so $$t$$ = 20. Substituting those values into the formula, we calculate</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt} = 10,000\left( {1 + \frac{0.056}{365}} \right)^{365 \times 20}} \\ & = & {10,000\left( {1 + 0.000153424657534} \right)^{7300}} \\ & = & {10,000(1.000153424657534)^{7300}} \\ & = & {10,000 \times 3.06459091598} \\ & = & 30,645.909 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>After 20 years, Kathy’s initial investment of \$10,000 is worth \$30,645.90.</paragraph>

title: FORMULA
snippet: FORMULA: The money invested in an account bearing an annual interest rate of r (in decimal form), compounded n times per year for t years, is called the present value, PV , of the account (or of the money) and found using the formula PV =...

Always round this value up to the nearest penny.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Computing Present Value
snippet: Computing Present Value: Find the present value of the accounts under the following conditions. A = \$250,000, invested at 6.75 interest, compounded monthly, for 30 years. A = \$500,000, invested at 7.1% interest, compounded quarterly, for...

<example number="6.44" title="Computing Present Value">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the present value of the accounts under the following conditions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$A$$ = \$250,000, invested at 6.75 interest, compounded monthly, for 30 years.</item>
        <item>$$A$$ = \$500,000, invested at 7.1% interest, compounded quarterly, for 40 years.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To reach a final account value of $$A$$ = \$250,000, invested at 6.75% interest, in decimal form $$r$$ = 0.0675 (decimal form!), compounded monthly, so $$n$$ = 12, for 30 years, substitute those values into the formula for present value. Calculating, we find the present value of the \$250,000. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {PV} & = & {\frac{A}{\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{n \times t}} = \frac{250,000}{\left( {1 + \frac{0.0675}{12}} \right)^{12 \times 30}}} \\ & = & \frac{250,000}{\left( {1 + 0.005625} \right)^{360}} \\ & = & \frac{250,000}{(1.005625)^{360}} \\ & = & \frac{250,000}{7.5332454772} \\ & = & 33,186.2277 \end{array}$$ In order for this account to reach \$250,000 after 30 years, \$33,186.23 needs to be invested.</item>
      </list>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To reach a final account value of $$A$$ = \$500,000, invested at 7.1% interest, in decimal form $$r$$ = 0.071, compounded quarterly, so $$n$$ = 4, for 40 years, substitute those values into the formula for present value. Calculating, we find the present value of the \$500,000. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {PV} & = & {\frac{A}{\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{n \times t}} = \frac{500,000}{\left( {1 + \frac{0.071}{4}} \right)^{4 \times 40}}} \\ & = & \frac{500,000}{\left( {1 + 0.01775} \right)^{160}} \\ & = & \frac{500,000}{(1.01775)^{160}} \\ & = & \frac{500,000}{16.6946672846} \\ & = & {29,949.6834} \end{array}$$ In order for this account to reach \$500,000 after 40 years, \$29,949.69 needs to be invested.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.45" title="Investment Goal with Compound Interest">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Pilar plans early for retirement, believing she will need \$1,500,000 to live comfortably after the age of 67. How much will she need to deposit at age 23 in an account bearing 6.35% annual interest compounded monthly?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Knowing how much to deposit at age 23 to reach a certain value later is a present value question. The target value for Pilar is \$1,500,000. The interest rate is 6.35%, which in decimal form is 0.0635. Compounded monthly means $$n$$ = 12. She’s 23 and will leave the money in the account until the age of 67, which is 44 years, making $$t$$ = 44. Using this information and substituting in the formula for present value, we calculate</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {PV} & = & {\frac{A}{\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{n \times t}} = \frac{1,500,000}{\left( {1 + \frac{0.0635}{12}} \right)^{12 \times 44}}} \\ & = & \frac{1,500,000}{\left( {1 + 0.005291\overline{6}} \right)^{528}} \\ & = & \frac{1,500,000}{\left( {1.005291\overline{6}} \right)^{528}} \\ & = & \frac{1,500,000}{16.226302189} \\ & = & 92,442.5037 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Pilar will need to invest \$92,442,51 in this account to have \$1,500,000 at age 67.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determine and Interpret Effective Annual Yield for 6% Compounded Quarterly
snippet: Determine and Interpret Effective Annual Yield for 6% Compounded Quarterly: Suppose you have an investment paying a rate of 6% compounded quarterly. Determine and interpret that effective annual yield of the investment. Here, n = 4...
body_xml:
<example number="6.46" title="Determine and Interpret Effective Annual Yield for 6% Compounded Quarterly">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose you have an investment paying a rate of 6% compounded quarterly. Determine and interpret that effective annual yield of the investment.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Here, $$n$$ = 4 (quarterly) and $$r$$ = 0.06 (decimal form). Substituting into the formula we find that the effective annual yield is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} Y & = & {\left( {1 + \frac{0.06}{4}} \right)^{4} - 1} \\ & = & {(1.015)^{4} - 1} \\ & = & {1.06136 - 1} \\ & = & 0.0614 \\ & = & {6.14\%} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, a rate of 6% compounded quarterly is equivalent to a simple interest rate of 6.14%.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determine and Interpret Effective Annual Yield for 5% Compounded Daily
snippet: Determine and Interpret Effective Annual Yield for 5% Compounded Daily: Calculate and interpret the effective annual yield on a deposit earning interest at a rate of 5% compounded daily. In this case, the rate is r = 0.05 and n = 365...
body_xml:
<example number="6.47" title="Determine and Interpret Effective Annual Yield for 5% Compounded Daily">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate and interpret the effective annual yield on a deposit earning interest at a rate of 5% compounded daily.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>In this case, the rate is $$r$$ = 0.05 and $$n$$ = 365 (daily). Using the formula $$Y = \left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{n} - 1$$ , we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} Y & = & {\left( {1 + \frac{0.05}{365}} \right)^{365} - 1} \\ & = & {(1.0001369863)^{365} - 1} \\ & = & {1.051267 - 1} \\ & = & 0.0513 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This tells us that an account earning 5% compounded daily is equivalent to earning 5.13% as simple interest.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Choosing a Bank
snippet: Choosing a Bank: Minh has a choice of banks in which he will open a savings account. He will deposit \$3,200 and he wants to get the best interest he can. The banks advertise as follows: Bank Interest Rate ABC Bank 2.08% compounded monthly...
body_xml:
Minh has a choice of banks in which he will open a savings account. He will deposit \$3,200 and he wants to get the best interest he can. The banks advertise as follows: Bank Interest Rate ABC Bank 2.08% compounded monthly 123 Bank 2.09% compounded annually XYZ Bank 2.05% compounded daily
Which bank offers the best interest? To compare these directly, Minh could change each interest rate to its effective annual yield, which would allow direct comparison between the rates. Computing the effective annual yield for all three choices gives: ABC Bank: $$Y = \left( {1 + \frac{0.0208}{12}} \right)^{12} - 1 = 0.0210 = 2.10\%$$ 123 Bank: $$Y = \left( {1 + \frac{0.0209}{1}} \right)^{1} - 1 = 0.0209 = 2.09\%$$ XYZ Bank: $$Y = \left( {1 + \frac{0.0205}{365}} \right)^{365} - 1 = 0.0207 = 2.07\%$$ ABC Bank has the highest effective annual yield, so Minh should choose ABC bank.

title: Creating a Budget
snippet: Creating a Budget: Heather has graduated college and currently works as a nurse for a rural medical group. Her net monthly income from that job is \$3,765.40. She also works part-time on the weekends, earning another \$672.00 per month....
body_xml:
Heather has graduated college and currently works as a nurse for a rural medical group. Her net monthly income from that job is \$3,765.40. She also works part-time on the weekends, earning another \$672.00 per month. Her monthly expenses are rent at \$1,050, car payments at \$489, student loan payments at \$728, car insurance at \$139, utilities at \$130, clothing at \$150, entertainment (going out with friends, Netflix, Amazon Prime, movies) at \$300, credit card debt at \$200, food at \$360, and gasoline at \$275. Create her budget in a table, compare the total income to total expenses, and determine how much excess income per month she has or how much she falls short by each month. Step 1: To begin, we create the table with appropriate headings. Income Source Amount Expense Amount
Step 2: Her income categories are her nursing job, with \$3,765.40 per month, and her part-time job, with \$672.00 per month. Entering these into the table, we have the following. Income Source Amount Expense Amount Nursing \$3,765.40 Part-time \$672.00
Step 3: Her monthly expenses are listed above. Entering the categories and the amount for each of those expenses, the table is now Income Source Amount Expense Amount Nursing \$3,765.40 Rent \$1,050 Part-time \$672.00 Car Payment \$489 Student Loan \$728 Car Insurance \$139 Utilities \$130 Clothing \$150 Entertainment \$300 Credit Card \$200 Food \$400 Gasoline \$250
Step 4: Totaling the income and expenses, we see that her total income is \$4,437.40 per month, and her total expenses are \$3,836 per month. Comparing these, we see that Heather has \$601.40 in excess income per month. This provides a cushion in her budget.

Step 1: To begin, we create the table with appropriate headings. Income Source Amount Expense Amount

Step 3: Her monthly expenses are listed above. Entering the categories and the amount for each of those expenses, the table is now Income Source Amount Expense Amount Job \$2,816.00 Rent \$700 Child support \$320.00 Car Payment \$229 Student Loan \$250 Car Insurance \$119 Utilities \$80 Health insurance \$225 Clothing \$75 Entertainment \$200 Food \$275 Gasoline \$275
Step 4: Totaling the income and expenses, we see that her total income is \$3,136.00 per month, and her total expenses are \$2,428.00 per month. Comparing these, we see that Carol has \$708.00 in excess income per month. This is the cushion in her budget.

title: Evaluate a Budget Using 50-30-20 model
snippet: Evaluate a Budget Using 50-30-20 model: In the example above, after Carol added before school care for her daughter to the budget, her budget was as shown below. Evaluate Carol’s budget using the 50-30-20 budget philosophy. Income Source...

In the example above, after Carol added before school care for her daughter to the budget, her budget was as shown below. Evaluate Carol’s budget using the 50-30-20 budget philosophy. Income Source Amount Expense Amount Job \$2,816.00 Rent \$700 Child support \$320.00 Car Payment \$229 Student Loan \$250 Car Insurance \$119 Utilities \$80 Health insurance \$225 Clothing \$75 Entertainment \$200 Food \$275 Gasoline \$275 Before-school care \$252
Carol’s total income is \$3,136.00. Applying the 50-30-20 budget philosophy to this income requires the calculation of each of those percentages. For the necessities, Carol should budget 50% of her income, or $$0.5 \times \$3,136.00 = \$1,568.00$$ . For her wants, she should budget 30% of her income, or $$0.3 \times \$3,136.00 = \$940.80$$ . For savings and extra debt service, she should budget 20% of her income, or $$0.2 \times \$3,136.00 = \$627.20$$ . In her budget, her necessities include all expenses except for entertainment. These expenses total \$2,480, which exceeds the suggested budget amount of \$1568.00. To follow the guidelines, Carol would have to cut back on these necessities. For her wants, she spends \$200.00 on entertainment, which is well below the suggested budget amount of \$940.80. If she modifies how much she spends on needs, she may be able to increase the spending on her wants. Her excess income is \$456.00, which is below what she should be saving and using to pay down extra debt. If she does adjust how much she spends on needs, she could increase the amount for savings.

title: Creating a Budget Based on the 50-30-20 Budget Philosophy
snippet: Creating a Budget Based on the 50-30-20 Budget Philosophy: Carmen is about to graduate and has been offered a job at a bank as a data scientist. She estimates her monthly take home pay to be \$5,662.50. Apply the 50-30-20 philosophy to...
body_xml:
<example number="6.53" title="Creating a Budget Based on the 50-30-20 Budget Philosophy">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Carmen is about to graduate and has been offered a job at a bank as a data scientist. She estimates her monthly take home pay to be \$5,662.50. Apply the 50-30-20 philosophy to that monthly income. How should Carmen use this information?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1. To apply the 50-30-20 budget philosophy to Carmen’s income, she needs to calculate 50%, 30%, and 20% of her income. Fifty percent of her income is $$0.5 \times \$5,662.50 = \$2,831.25$$ . Thirty percent of her income is $$0.3 \times \$5,662.50 = \$1,698.75$$ . Twenty percent of her income is $$0.2 \times \$5,662.50 = \$1,132.50$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. She would then budget \$2,831.25 for her needs, \$1,698.75 for her wants, and \$1,132.50 for savings and debt service.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3. When choosing where to live, what to eat, and what to drive, she should make choices that keep those costs, combined with her debt service costs, gasoline, and utilities, below \$2,831.25. This means she will have to make decisions about what her priorities are.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4. She should then figure out what she wants to do with her money, and stay within the limits, that is, keep those costs below \$1,698.75.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5. Finally, she can begin building her savings with the remaining \$1,132.50.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the 50-30-20 Budget Philosophy to Analyze Affordability
snippet: Using the 50-30-20 Budget Philosophy to Analyze Affordability: Steve is thinking of moving out of his family’s home. He currently works at a full-time job making \$18 per hour, which will give him, approximately, a net annual income of...
body_xml:
<example number="6.54" title="Using the 50-30-20 Budget Philosophy to Analyze Affordability">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Steve is thinking of moving out of his family’s home. He currently works at a full-time job making \$18 per hour, which will give him, approximately, a net annual income of \$29,180 (working 40 hours per week for 52 weeks per year). He has student debt that he pays off at \$218.00 per month, and already owns a car that he pays \$162.00 per month for.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Apply the 50-30-20 budget philosophy to Steve’s income.</item>
        <item>If he follows the budget, how much does he have, after paying his car payment and student loan, to spend on necessities.</item>
        <item>If he follows the budget, how much will he set aside for wants? For savings?</item>
        <item>Discuss the affordability of moving out, based on Steve’s budget.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Before the 50-30-20 philosophy can be applied, Steve’s monthly income needs to be determined. This is found by dividing his annual income by 12. This gives $$\$29,180/12 = \$2,431.67$$ . This will be used for his monthly budget.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To apply the 50-30-20 philosophy to Steve’s income, find 50%, 30%, and 20% of his monthly income. Needs (50%): 50% of his income is $$0.50 \times \$2,431.67 = \$1,215.83$$ . Wants (30%): $$0.30 \times \$2,431.67 = \$729.50$$ Savings (20%): $$0.20 \times \$2,431.67 = \$486.33$$</item>
        <item>The total for Steve’s needs is \$1,215.83. From this, he already pays \$218.00 for his student loans, and \$162.00 for his car payment. Together that is \$380.00. Subtracting from the amount he should budget for his needs, he can spend \$835.83 on other needs.</item>
        <item>Steve budgeted \$729.50 for wants, and \$486.33 for savings and other debt servicing.</item>
        <item>Steve will have other needs to pay for, including rent, utilities, food, heath care, gasoline, and car insurance. It is difficult to imagine Steve being able to afford to move out, unless he reallocates money that he would want to save, or use for entertainment and other wants, or takes on another job. Even if Steve uses all the money that the 50-30-20 budget sets aside for savings, he still only has \$1,322.16 to spend on those necessities. It does not appear he can afford to move out.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Single Deposit in a Savings Account
snippet: Single Deposit in a Savings Account: Violet deposits \$4,520.00 in a savings account bearing 1.45% interest compounded annually. If she does not add to or withdraw any of that money, how much will be in the account after 3 years? To find...
body_xml:
<example number="6.55" title="Single Deposit in a Savings Account">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Violet deposits \$4,520.00 in a savings account bearing 1.45% interest compounded annually. If she does not add to or withdraw any of that money, how much will be in the account after 3 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find the compound interest, use the formula from Compound Interest, $$A = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}$$ , where $$A$$ represents the amount in the account after $$t$$ years, with initial deposit (or principal) of $$P$$ , at an annual interest rate, in decimal form, of $$r$$ , compounded $$n$$ times per year. Violet has a principal of \$4,520.00, which will earn an interest of $$r$$ = 0.0145, compounded yearly (so $$n$$ = 1), for $$t$$ = 3 years. Substituting and calculating, we find that Violet’s account will be worth</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}} \\ & = & {\$4,520.00\left( {1 + \frac{0.0145}{1}} \right)^{1 \times 3}} \\ & = & {\$4,520.00{(1.0145)}^{3}} \\ & = & {\$4,719.48} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Or, Violet will have \$4,719.48 after 3 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: 5-Year CD
snippet: 5-Year CD: Silvio deposits \$10,000 in a CD that yields 2.17% compounded semiannually for 5 years. How much is the CD worth after 5 years? This also uses the compound interest formula from Compound Interest, A = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}}...
body_xml:
<example number="6.56" title="5-Year CD">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Silvio deposits \$10,000 in a CD that yields 2.17% compounded semiannually for 5 years. How much is the CD worth after 5 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This also uses the compound interest formula from Compound Interest, $$A = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{\mathit{nt}}$$ , Substituting the values $$P$$ = \$10,000, $$r$$ = 0.0217, $$n$$ = 2 (semiannually means twice per year), and $$t$$ = 5, we find the account will be worth</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{\mathit{nt}}} \\ & = & {\$10,000.00\left( {1 + \frac{0.0217}{2}} \right)^{2 \times 5}} \\ & = & {\$10,000.00{(1.01085)}^{10}} \\ & = & {\$11,239.53} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The CD will be worth \$11,219.53 after 5 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Single Deposit to a Money Market Account
snippet: Single Deposit to a Money Market Account: Marietta opens a money market account, and deposits \$2,500.00 in the account. It bears 1.76% interest compounded monthly. If she makes no other transactions on the account, how much will be in the...
body_xml:
<example number="6.57" title="Single Deposit to a Money Market Account">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Marietta opens a money market account, and deposits \$2,500.00 in the account. It bears 1.76% interest compounded monthly. If she makes no other transactions on the account, how much will be in the account after 4 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This, once again, uses the compound interest formula from Compound Interest: $$A = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{\mathit{nt}}$$ , Substituting the values $$P$$ = \$25,000, $$r$$ = 0.0176, $$n$$ = 12, and $$t$$ = 4, we find the account will be worth</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{\mathit{nt}}} \\ & = & {\$2,500.00\left( {1 + \frac{0.0176}{12}} \right)^{12 \times 4}} \\ & = & {\$2,500.00{(1.0014\overline{6})}^{48}} \\ & = & {\$2,682.20} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The money market account will be worth \$2,682.20 after 4 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: FORMULA
snippet: FORMULA: The return on investment, often denoted ROI, is the percent difference between the initial investment, P , and the final value of the investment, FV , or {ROI} = \frac{FV - P}{P} , expressed as a percentage.
body_xml:
<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>The return on investment, often denoted ROI, is the percent difference between the initial investment, $$P$$ , and the final value of the investment, $$FV$$ , or $${ROI} = \frac{FV - P}{P}$$ , expressed as a percentage.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Calculating Return on Investment
snippet: Calculating Return on Investment: Determine the return on investment for the 5-year CD from Example 6.56. Round the percentage to two decimal places. Determine the return on investment for the money market account from Example 6.57. Round...
body_xml:
<example number="6.58" title="Calculating Return on Investment">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Determine the return on investment for the 5-year CD from Example 6.56. Round the percentage to two decimal places.</item>
        <item>Determine the return on investment for the money market account from Example 6.57. Round the percentage to two decimal places.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The initial deposit in the CD was \$10,000, so $$P$$ = \$10,000. The value at the end of 5 years was \$11,239.53. so $$FV$$ = \$11,239.53. Substituting and computing we find the return on investment. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {ROI} & = & \frac{FV - P}{P} \\ & = & \frac{\$11,239.53 - \$10,000}{\$10,000} \\ & = & \frac{\$1,239.53}{\$10,000} \\ & = & 0.123953 \end{array}$$ The ROI is 12.40%.</item>
      </list>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The initial deposit in the money market was \$2,500, so $$P$$ = \$2,500. The value at the end of 4 years was \$2,682.20. so $$FV$$ = \$2,682.20. Substituting and computing we find the return on investment. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {ROI} & = & \frac{FV - P}{P} \\ & = & \frac{\$2,682.20 - \$2,500}{\$2,500} \\ & = & \frac{\$182.20}{\$2,500} \\ & = & 0.07288 \end{array}$$ The ROI is 7.29%.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Future Value of an Ordinary Annuity
snippet: Future Value of an Ordinary Annuity: Jill has an account that bears 3.75% interest compounded monthly. She decides to deposit \$250.00 each month, at the end of the compounding period, into this account. What is the future value of this...
body_xml:
<example number="6.59" title="Future Value of an Ordinary Annuity">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Jill has an account that bears 3.75% interest compounded monthly. She decides to deposit \$250.00 each month, at the end of the compounding period, into this account. What is the future value of this account, after 8 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>These are regular payments into an account bearing compound interest. She is depositing them at the end of each compounding period. This makes this an ordinary annuity. Substituting the values $$\mathit{pmt}$$ = 250, $$r$$ = 0.0375, $$n$$ = 12, and $$t$$ = 8 into the formula, we find the future value of the account.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {FV} & = & {\mathit{pmt} \times \frac{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}{r/n}} \\ & = & {250 \times \frac{{(1 + 0.0375/12)}^{12 \times 8} - 1}{0.0375/12}} \\ & = & {250 \times \frac{{(1.003125)}^{96} - 1}{0.003125}} \\ & = & {250 \times \frac{1.34922752406 - 1}{0.003125}} \\ & = & {250 \times \frac{0.34922752406}{0.003125}} \\ & = & {250 \times 111.752807699} \\ & = & {27,938.202} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The account, after 8 years, will contain \$27,938.20.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Saving for College
snippet: Saving for College: When Yusef was born, Rita and George began to save for Yusef’s college years by investing \$2,500 each year in a savings account bearing 3.4% interest compounded annually. How much will they have saved after 18 years?...
body_xml:
<example number="6.60" title="Saving for College">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>When Yusef was born, Rita and George began to save for Yusef’s college years by investing \$2,500 each year in a savings account bearing 3.4% interest compounded annually. How much will they have saved after 18 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find the future value of the account, we use the ordinary annuity formula $$FV = \mathit{pmt} \times \frac{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}{r/n}$$ . The payment is \$2,500, rate is 0.034, the number of compounding periods is 1, and the number of years is 18. Substituting these values and computing, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {FV} & = & {\mathit{pmt} \times \frac{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}{r/n}} \\ & = & {\$2,500 \times \frac{{(1 + 0.034/1)}^{1 \times 18} - 1}{0.034/1}} \\ & = & {\$2,500 \times \frac{{(1.034)}^{18} - 1}{0.034}} \\ & = & {\$2,500 \times \frac{1.82544897331 - 1}{0.034}} \\ & = & {\$2,500 \times 24.2779109798} \\ & = & {\$60,694.77} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>After saving for 18 years, Rita and George will have \$60,694.77 for Yusef’s college.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: FORMULA
snippet: FORMULA: The formula for the amount that needs to be deposited per period, \mathit{pmt} , of an ordinary annuity to reach a specified goal, \mathit{FV} , is \mathit{pmt} = \frac{FV \times (r/n)}{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1} , where r is...
body_xml:
<note type="key_concept" source_type="FORMULA" title="FORMULA">
    <paragraph>The formula for the amount that needs to be deposited per period, $$\mathit{pmt}$$ , of an ordinary annuity to reach a specified goal, $$\mathit{FV}$$ , is $$\mathit{pmt} = \frac{FV \times (r/n)}{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}$$ , where $$r$$ is the annual interest rate (in decimal form), $$n$$ is the number of periods per year, and $$t$$ is the number of years.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Saving for a Car
snippet: Saving for a Car: Yaroslava wants to save in order to buy a car, in 3 years, without taking out a loan. She determines that she’ll need \$35,500 for the purchase. If she deposits money into an ordinary annuity that yields 4.25% interest...
body_xml:
<example number="6.61" title="Saving for a Car">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Yaroslava wants to save in order to buy a car, in 3 years, without taking out a loan. She determines that she’ll need \$35,500 for the purchase. If she deposits money into an ordinary annuity that yields 4.25% interest compounded monthly, how much will she need to deposit each month?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Yaroslava has a goal and needs to know the payments to make to reach the goal. Her goal is $$\mathit{FV}$$ = \$35,500, with an interest rate $$r$$ = 0.0425, compounded per month so $$n$$ = 12, and for 3 years, making $$t$$ = 3. Substituting into the formula, Yaroslava finds the necessary payment.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \mathit{pmt} & = & \frac{FV \times (r/n)}{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{35,500 \times (0.0425/12)}{{(1 + 0.0425/12)}^{12 \times 3} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{35,500 \times (0.003541\overline{6})}{{(1.003541\overline{6})}^{36} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{125.7291\overline{6}}{0.13572901696} \\ & = & 926.325 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To reach her goal, Yaroslava would need to deposit \$926.33 in her account each month.</paragraph>
    </solution>

    <problem>
      <paragraph>Haniah buys stock in the ABC company, investing a total of \$13,000. She expects the stock to grow, through stock price increase and reinvestment of dividends, by 12.3% per year and compounded annually. If she leaves that money invested, how much will the stocks be worth in 20 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Calculating this is a compound interest calculation, if Haniah’s assumption about the stock’s performance is correct. If so, then the principal is \$13,000, the rate is 0.123, the number of compounding periods per year is 1, and the time is 20 years. Substituting into the compound interest formula from Methods of Savings, and computing, we have $$A = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt} = \$13,000\left( {1 + \frac{0.123}{1}} \right)^{1 \times 20} = \$13,000 \times 10.1764223996 = \$132,293.49$$ . After 20 years, her stock is now worth \$132,293.49.</paragraph>

<example number="6.64" title="Computing Percent Yield">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find the percent yield for a stock with a price of \$30.69 and an annual dividend of \$1.48.</item>
        <item>Find the percent yield for a stock with a price of \$62.25 and an annual dividend of \$1.76.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Substituting the values for price, \$30.69, and annual dividend, \$1.48, we find the percent yield for the stock to be $$\text{Y} \text{l} \text{d} \% = \frac{ \text{Annual Dividend} }{ \text{Share Price} } \times 100\% = \frac{\$1.48}{\$30.69} \times 100\% = 4.82\%$$</item>
        <item>Substituting the values for price, \$62.25, and annual dividend, \$1.76, we find the percent yield for the stock to be $${Yld\%} = \frac{ \text{Annual Dividend} }{ \text{Share Price} } \times 100\% = \frac{\$1.76}{\$62.25} \times 100\% = 2.83\%$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

<example number="6.67" title="Stock Price Increases">
    <problem>

      <list type="ordered">

        <item>What was his return on investment for that one year?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Vincent spent \$21.87 per share to buy the stock. The total he spent on the stock was $$\$21.87 \times 100 = \$2,187.00$$ . When he sold the stock, the price was \$29.15, so he received $$\$29.15 \times 100 = \$2,915.00$$ . He made $$\$2,915.00 - \$2,187.00 = \$728.00$$ .</item>

title: Investing in a Mutual Fund
snippet: Investing in a Mutual Fund: Kaitlyn has analyzed her \$12,862.50 quarterly budget using the 50-30-20 budget philosophy, and sees she should be saving or paying down debt with \$2,572.50 per quarter. She decides to invest \$1,300 quarterly...
body_xml:
<example number="6.68" title="Investing in a Mutual Fund">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Kaitlyn has analyzed her \$12,862.50 quarterly budget using the 50-30-20 budget philosophy, and sees she should be saving or paying down debt with \$2,572.50 per quarter. She decides to invest \$1,300 quarterly a mutual fund that reports an average return of 11.62% over the 18-year life of the mutual fund. Assuming that this interest rate continues, and is compounded quarterly, how much will her mutual fund account be worth after 5 years?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Kaitlyn’s plan is an ordinary annuity, and so the future value of her account can be found using the formula $$FV = pmt \times \frac{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}{r/n}$$ , with a payment of \$1,300, a rate of 0.1162, number of compounding periods 4, after 5 years. Substituting these values into the formula and calculating, we find</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {FV} & = & {pmt \times \frac{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}{r/n}} \\ & = & {\$1,300 \times \frac{{(1.02905)}^{20} - 1}{0.02905}} \\ & = & {\$1,300 \times \frac{0.773084935178}{0.032905}} \\ & = & {\$1,300 \times 26.6122189784} \\ & = & {\$34,595.88} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Kaitlyn’s mutual fund will be worth \$34,595.88 after 5 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Investing in a Mutual Fund to Reach a Goal
snippet: Investing in a Mutual Fund to Reach a Goal: Kaitlyn wants to retire with \$1,500,000 in her mutual fund account. She will invest for 35 years. The mutual fund reports an average return of 11.62% over the 18-year-long life of the mutual...
body_xml:
<example number="6.69" title="Investing in a Mutual Fund to Reach a Goal">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Kaitlyn wants to retire with \$1,500,000 in her mutual fund account. She will invest for 35 years. The mutual fund reports an average return of 11.62% over the 18-year-long life of the mutual fund. Assuming that this interest rate continues, and is compounded quarterly, how much will she need to pay annually into her mutual fund to reach her goal?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Kaitlyn’s plan is an ordinary annuity, and so the payment to reach her goal can be found using the formula $$pmt = \frac{FV \times (r/n)}{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}$$ , with a $$FV$$ , or goal, of \$1,500,000, a rate of 0.1162, for 35 years. Substituting these values into the formula and calculating, we find</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {pmt} & = & \frac{FV \times (r/n)}{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{\$1,500,000 \times (0.1162/1)}{{(1 + 0.1162/1)}^{1 \times 35} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{\$174,300}{26.0558103113} \\ & = & {\$6,689.49} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Kaitlyn needs to invest \$6,689.49 per year (or \$557.46 per month) into the mutual fund to reach \$1,500,000 in 35 years.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.70" title="Return on Investment for a Bond">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Recall Example 6.62, in which Muriel purchased a \$3,000 bond with a maturity of 4 years at a fixed coupon rate of 5.5% paid annually. What was Muriel’s return on investment?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Each year, Muriel received \$165. She received this money four times, so earned a total of \$660. This represents $$FV$$ – $$P$$ , or just the earnings. Using that we find that the ROI is $$\text{ROI} = \frac{660}{3000} = 0.22$$ , or 22%.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Annual Return on Investment for a Bond
snippet: Annual Return on Investment for a Bond: Recall Example 6.70, in which Muriel purchased a \$3,000 bond with a maturity of 4 years at a fixed coupon rate of 5.5% paid annually. What was Muriel’s annual return on investment? Interpret this as...
body_xml:
<example number="6.71" title="Annual Return on Investment for a Bond">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Recall Example 6.70, in which Muriel purchased a \$3,000 bond with a maturity of 4 years at a fixed coupon rate of 5.5% paid annually. What was Muriel’s annual return on investment? Interpret this as compound interest.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Muriel earned a total of \$660. This represents $$FV$$ – $$P$$ , or just the earnings. The starting principal was \$3,000. The value at the end of 4 years was \$3,000 + \$660 = \$3,660. The time of the investment was 4 years. Using that we find that the annual return is $$\text{annual return} = \left( \frac{FV}{P} \right)^{(\frac{1}{t})} - 1 = \left( \frac{\$3,660}{\$3,000} \right)^{(\frac{1}{4})} - 1 = 1.22^{\frac{1}{4}} - 1 = 1.050969 = 0.050969$$ , or 5.10%. The 5.5% bond earned the equivalent of 5.10% compounded annually.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Return on Investment for Stock in Company ABC
snippet: Return on Investment for Stock in Company ABC: Haniah buys stock in the ABC company, investing a total of \$13,000. After 20 years, the stock is worth \$132,293.49, including reinvestment of dividends. What is Haniah’s return on...
body_xml:
<example number="6.72" title="Return on Investment for Stock in Company ABC">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Haniah buys stock in the ABC company, investing a total of \$13,000. After 20 years, the stock is worth \$132,293.49, including reinvestment of dividends.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>What is Haniah’s return on investment?</item>
        <item>What is Haniah’s annual return?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To calculate Hanniah’s return on investment, substitute \$13,000 for $$P$$ and \$132,293.49 for $$FV$$ in the formula $$\text{ROI} = \frac{FV - P}{P}$$ and calculate. Doing so we find Haniah’s return on investment to be $$\text{ROI} = \frac{FV - P}{P} = \frac{\$132,293.49 - \$13,000}{\$13,000} = 9.176422$$ , or 917.64%</item>
        <item>To calculate Haniah’s annual return, substitute \$13,000 for $$P$$ and \$132,293.49 for $$FV$$ in the formula $$\text{annual return} = \left( \frac{FV}{P} \right)^{(\frac{1}{t})} - 1$$ and calculate. Doing so we find her annual return to be $$\text{annual return} = \left( \frac{FV}{P} \right)^{(\frac{1}{t})} - 1 = \left( \frac{\$132,293.49}{\$13,000} \right)^{(\frac{1}{20})} - 1 = 0.1230$$ , or 12.3%</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Example 6.73
snippet: Example 6.73: Richard is saving for new siding for his home. He and his partner believe they will need \$37,500 in 10 years to pay for the siding. How much should they invest yearly in a mutual fund they believe will have an annual...

<example number="6.73">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Richard is saving for new siding for his home. He and his partner believe they will need \$37,500 in 10 years to pay for the siding. How much should they invest yearly in a mutual fund they believe will have an annual interest rate of 12%, compounded annually, in order to reach their goal?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The necessary annual payment is found using the function $$pmt = \frac{FV \times (r/n)}{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1}$$ with $$FV$$ = 37,500, $$r$$ = 0.12, and $$n$$ = 1. Substituting and calculating, we find the annual payment should be</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {pmt} & = & \frac{FV \times (r/n)}{{(1 + r/n)}^{n \times t} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{\$37,500 \times (0.12/1)}{{(1 + 0.12/1)}^{1 \times 10} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{\$4,500}{{(1.12)}^{10} - 1} \\ & = & \frac{\$4,500}{2.10584820834} \\ & = & {\$2,136.91} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Matching 401(k) Deposit: Alice signs up for her employer-based 401(k). The employer matches any 401(k) contribution up to 6% of the employee salary. Alice’s annual salary is \$51,600. What is the most money that Alice can deposit that will...
