snippet: Identifying Explanatory and Response Variables: For each of the following pairs of related datasets, identify which (if any) should be assigned the role of response variable and which should be assigned to be the explanatory variable. A...
body_xml:
<example number="8.44" title="Identifying Explanatory and Response Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following pairs of related datasets, identify which (if any) should be assigned the role of response variable and which should be assigned to be the explanatory variable.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>A person’s height and weight</item>
        <item>A professional basketball player’s salary and their average points scored per game (which is a measure of how good they are at basketball)</item>
        <item>The length and width of leaves on a tree</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>As people get taller, their weight tends to increase. But if a person goes on a diet and loses weight, we don’t expect them to also get shorter. So, weight depends on height. That means we’ll say that the response variable is weight and the explanatory variable is height.</item>
        <item>The more points a basketball player scores, the more money they should make. But if a basketball player gets a raise, we wouldn’t expect them to get better at basketball as a result. So, the response is salary and the explanatory is points per game.</item>
        <item>The way that the length and width of leaves are connected isn’t clear. It seems reasonable that as the width goes up, so would the length. But the other direction is also plausible: as the length goes up, so does the width. Without a clear dependence relationship, we’re free to declare either to be the response and the other to be the explanatory.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Finding the Equation of the Regression Line from Statistics: Suppose you have datasets x and y with the following statistics: x has mean 21 and standard deviation 4, y has mean 8 and standard deviation 2, and their correlation coefficient...
body_xml:
<example number="8.49" title="Finding the Equation of the Regression Line from Statistics">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose you have datasets $$x$$ and $$y$$ with the following statistics: $$x$$ has mean 21 and standard deviation 4, $$y$$ has mean 8 and standard deviation 2, and their correlation coefficient is −0.4. What’s the equation of the regression line?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: We’re given $$\overline{x} = 21$$ , $$s_{x} = 4$$ , $$\overline{y} = 8$$ , $$s_{y} = 2$$ , and $$r = - 0.4$$ . Let's start with the formula for the equation of the regression line:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y = r\left( \frac{s_{y}}{s_{x}} \right)(x - \overline{x}) + \overline{y}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Plugging in our values gives us:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y = - 0.4\left( \frac{2}{4} \right)(x - 21) + 8$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Our final regression line equation is:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y = - 0.2x + 12.2$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Applying the Equation of the Regression Line: The data in “MLB2019Off” gives offensive team stats for the 2019 Major League Baseball season. Use that dataset to answer the following questions: What is the equation of the regression line...
body_xml:
<example number="8.51" title="Applying the Equation of the Regression Line">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The data in “MLB2019Off” gives offensive team stats for the 2019 Major League Baseball season. Use that dataset to answer the following questions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>What is the equation of the regression line for runs (R) vs. hits (H)?</item>
        <item>How many runs would we expect a team to score if the team got 1500 hits in a season?</item>
        <item>Did the Kansas City Royals (KCR) overperform or underperform in terms of runs scored, based on their hit total? By how much?</item>
        <item>Write a sentence to interpret the slope of the regression line.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Using Google Sheets, we find that the regression line equation is $$y = 0.884x-456$$ , where $$y$$ is the number of runs scored and $$x$$ is the number of hits.</item>
        <item>Plugging 1500 into the equation of the regression line, we get $$0.884 \times 1500 - 456 = 870$$ . We would predict that a team with 1500 hits would score 870 runs.</item>
        <item>The Royals had 1356 hits, so we would predict their run total to be $$0.884 \times 1356 - 456 \approx 743$$ . They actually scored 691 runs, so they underperformed expectations by 52 runs $$\left( {743-691} \right)$$ .</item>
        <item>The slope gives us the predicted change in the response that corresponds to a one unit increase in the explanatory variable. So, we expect one additional hit to result in 0.884 more runs. Since 0.884 runs doesn’t really make sense, we can get a better interpretation by multiplying through by ten or one hundred: Ten additional hits will result in almost nine additional runs, or a hundred additional hits will yield on average just over 88 additional runs.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: More Applying the Equation of the Regression Line
snippet: More Applying the Equation of the Regression Line: The data in “WNBA2019” gives team statistics from the 2019 WNBA season. Use that dataset to answer these questions about team wins (W) and the proportion of team field goals made (FG%, the...
body_xml:
<example number="8.52" title="More Applying the Equation of the Regression Line">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The data in “WNBA2019” gives team statistics from the 2019 WNBA season. Use that dataset to answer these questions about team wins (W) and the proportion of team field goals made (FG%, the number of shots made divided by the number of shots attempted. Even though this column is labeled using a percent sign, the values are not expressed as percentages):</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>What is the equation of the regression line for wins vs. proportion of made field goals?</item>
        <item>How many wins would we expect for a team that makes 42% of its shots?</item>
        <item>Did the New York Liberty overperform or underperform in terms of wins, based on the team’s proportion of made field goals?</item>
        <item>Write a sentence to interpret the slope of the regression line.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Using Google Sheets, we get the equation $$y = 178.097x - 58.543$$ , where $$x$$ is the proportion of field goals made and $$y$$ is the number of wins.</item>
        <item>Since 42% corresponds to a proportion of 0.42, we’ll plug 0.42 into the regression equation for $$x$$ , which gives us $$178.097 \times 0.42 - 58.543 \approx 16.26$$ . We would predict that a team that makes 42% of its shots would win about 16 games.</item>
        <item>The New York Liberty made 41.4% of their shots, so we expect they would have $$178.097 \times 0.414 - 58.543 \approx 15.19$$ wins. In fact, they had only 10 wins, so they underperformed expectations by over 5 wins.</item>
        <item>Step 1: The slope gives us the expected increase in the response that corresponds to a one unit increase in the explanatory variable. If we simply go with that interpretation, we would get a sentence like “We expect an increase in proportion of field goals made of 1 would result in an additional 178 wins.” However, that sentence doesn't make much sense. Let's consider why. Step 2: First, proportions must be between 0 and 1, the proportion of made field goals can’t be increased by 1 and still make sense. Second, the total number of games played is only 34, so no team could get an additional 178 wins! So, we’ll have to change the units. Step 3: Since the proportions of made field goals are often expressed as a percentage, we could try to use that. If we express the slope as a fraction with 1 in the denominator (remember, the denominator represents the proportion of field goals made), then convert the denominator to a percentage and simplify, we get $$\frac{178.097}{1} = \frac{178.097}{100\%} \approx \frac{1.78}{1\%}$$ . Step 4: So, an increase in field goal percentage of 1% would result in an expected increase of 1.78 wins.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Reasonable Values for Length

<example number="9.3" title="Determining Reasonable Values for Length">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>What is a reasonable value for the length of a person’s thumb: 5 meters, 5 centimeters, or 5 millimeters?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Given that a meter is slightly longer than a yard, 5 meters is not a reasonable value for the length of a person’s thumb. Since a millimeter is 10 times smaller than a centimeter, which is approximately $$\frac{1}{2}$$ inch, 5 millimeters is not a reasonable estimate for the length of a person’s thumb. The correct answer is 5 centimeters.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting Metric Distances Using Multiplication
snippet: Converting Metric Distances Using Multiplication: The firehouse is 13.45 km from the library. How many meters is it from the firehouse to the library? When converting from a larger unit to a smaller unit, use multiplication. The conversion...

<example number="9.4" title="Converting Metric Distances Using Multiplication">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The firehouse is 13.45 km from the library. How many meters is it from the firehouse to the library?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>When converting from a larger unit to a smaller unit, use multiplication. The conversion factor from kilometer to the base unit of meters is 1,000.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$13.45 \times 1,000 = 13,450$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, the firehouse is 13,450 meters away from the firehouse.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting Metric Capacity Using Division

<example number="9.5" title="Converting Metric Capacity Using Division">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>How many liters is 3,565 milliliters?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>When converting from a smaller unit to a larger unit, use division. The conversion factor from milliliter to the base unit of liters is 1,000.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$3,565 \div 1,000 = 3.565$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, 3,565 milliliters is 3.565 liters.</paragraph>
    </solution>

<example number="9.6" title="Converting Metric Units of Mass to Solve Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Caroline and Aiyana are working on a chemistry experiment together and must perform calculations using measurements taken during the experiment. Due to miscommunication, Caroline took measurements in centigrams and Aiyana used milligrams. Convert Caroline’s measurement of 125 centigrams to milligrams.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>When converting from a larger unit to a smaller unit, use multiplication. The conversion factor from centigrams to the milligrams is 10.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$125 \times 10 = 1,250$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, the 125 centigrams are 1,250 milligrams.</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Converting Metric Units of Volume to Solve Problems
snippet: Converting Metric Units of Volume to Solve Problems: A bottle contains 500 mL of juice. If the juice is packaged in 24-bottle cases, how many liters of juice does the case contain? Step 1: Multiply the amount of juice in each bottle by the...
body_xml:
<example number="9.7" title="Converting Metric Units of Volume to Solve Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A bottle contains 500 mL of juice. If the juice is packaged in 24-bottle cases, how many liters of juice does the case contain?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Multiply the amount of juice in each bottle by the number of bottles.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$500{mL} \times 24 = 12,000{mL}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Divide by 1,000 to convert from milliliters to liters.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{12,000{mL}}{1,000} = 12L$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, there are 12 liters of juice in each case.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting Grams to Solve Problems
snippet: Converting Grams to Solve Problems: The nutrition label on a jar of spaghetti sauce indicates that one serving contains 410 mg of sodium. You have poured two servings over your favorite pasta before recalling your doctor’s advice about...
body_xml:
<example number="9.8" title="Converting Grams to Solve Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The nutrition label on a jar of spaghetti sauce indicates that one serving contains 410 mg of sodium. You have poured two servings over your favorite pasta before recalling your doctor’s advice about keeping your sodium consumption below 1 g per meal. Have you followed your doctor’s recommendation?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Multiply the number of servings by the amount of sodium in each serving.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$410{mg} \times 2 = 820{mg}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Divide by 1,000 to convert from milligrams to grams.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{820{mg}}{1,000} = 0.82g$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>You have followed doctor’s recommendation because 0.82 g is less than 1 gram.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Comparing Different Units
snippet: Comparing Different Units: A student carefully measured 0.52 cg of copper for a science experiment, but their lab partner said they need 6 mg of copper total. How many more centigrams of copper does the student need to add? Step 1: Convert...

<example number="9.9" title="Comparing Different Units">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A student carefully measured 0.52 cg of copper for a science experiment, but their lab partner said they need 6 mg of copper total. How many more centigrams of copper does the student need to add?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Convert these two measurements into a common unit. Since the question asks for the number of centigrams, convert 6 mg to centigrams, which is 0.6 cg.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Find the difference by subtracting $$0.6 - 0.52$$ which is 0.08 cg. This means the student must add another 0.08 cg of copper.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Reasonable Units for Area
snippet: Determining Reasonable Units for Area: Which unit of measure is most reasonable to describe the area of a sheet of paper: \text{km} ^{2} , \text{cm} ^{2} , or \text{mm} ^{2} ? In the U.S. Customary System of Measurement, the length and...
body_xml:
<example number="9.10" title="Determining Reasonable Units for Area">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Which unit of measure is most reasonable to describe the area of a sheet of paper: $$\text{km} ^{2}$$ , $$\text{cm} ^{2}$$ , or $$\text{mm} ^{2}$$ ?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>In the U.S. Customary System of Measurement, the length and width of paper is usually measured in inches. In the metric system centimeters are used for measures usually expressed in inches. Thus, the most reasonable unit of measure to describe the area of a sheet of paper is square centimeters. Square kilometers is too large a unit and square millimeters is too small a unit.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Reasonable Values for Area
snippet: Determining Reasonable Values for Area: You want to paint your bedroom walls. Which represents a reasonable value for the area of the walls: 100 cm2, 100 m2, or 100 km2? An area of 100 cm2 is equivalent to a surface of 10{cm} \times...
body_xml:
<example number="9.11" title="Determining Reasonable Values for Area">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>You want to paint your bedroom walls. Which represents a reasonable value for the area of the walls: 100 cm2, 100 m2, or 100 km2?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>An area of 100 cm2 is equivalent to a surface of $$10{cm} \times 10{cm},$$ which is much too small for the walls of a bedroom. An area of 100 km2 is equivalent to a surface of $$10{km} \times 10{km},$$ which is much too large for the walls of a bedroom. So, a reasonable value for the area of the walls is 100 m2.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Explaining Reasonable Values for Area
snippet: Explaining Reasonable Values for Area: A landscaper is hired to resod a school’s football field. After measuring the length and width of the field they determine that the area of the football field is 5,350 km2. Does their calculation make...

<example number="9.12" title="Explaining Reasonable Values for Area">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A landscaper is hired to resod a school’s football field. After measuring the length and width of the field they determine that the area of the football field is 5,350 km2. Does their calculation make sense? Explain your answer.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>No, kilometers are used to determine longer distances, such as the distance between two points when driving. A football field is less than 1 kilometer long, so a more reasonable unit of value would be m2. An area of 5,350 km2 can be calculated using the dimensions 53.5 by 100, which are reasonable dimensions for the length and width of a football field. So, a more reasonable value for the area of the football field is 5,350 m2.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting Units of Measure for Area Using Division
snippet: Converting Units of Measure for Area Using Division: A plot of land has an area of 237,500,000 m2. What is the area in square kilometers? Use division to convert from a smaller metric area unit to a larger metric area unit. To convert from...

<example number="9.13" title="Converting Units of Measure for Area Using Division">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A plot of land has an area of 237,500,000 m2. What is the area in square kilometers?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use division to convert from a smaller metric area unit to a larger metric area unit. To convert from m2 to km2, divide the value of the area by 1,000,000.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{237,500,000}{1,000,000} = 237.5$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The plot of land has an area of 237.5 km2.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <problem>
      <paragraph>A plot of land has an area of 0.004046 km2. What is the area of the land in square meters?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use multiplication to convert from a larger metric area unit to a smaller metric area unit. To convert from km2 to m2, multiply the value of the area by 1,000,000.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$0.004046 \times 1,000,000 = 4,046$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The plot of land has an area of 4,046 m2.</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Determining Area by Converting Units of Measure for Length First
snippet: Determining Area by Converting Units of Measure for Length First: A computer chip measures 10 mm by 15 mm. How many square centimeters is the computer chip? Step 1: Convert the measures of the computer chip into centimeters...

<example number="9.15" title="Determining Area by Converting Units of Measure for Length First">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A computer chip measures 10 mm by 15 mm. How many square centimeters is the computer chip?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Convert the measures of the computer chip into centimeters</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {10{mm}} & = & {1{cm}} \\ {15{mm}} & = & {1.5{cm}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Use the area formula to determine the area of the chip.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$1 \times 1.5 = 1.5$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The computer chip has an area of $$1.5$$ $$\text{cm} ^{ \text{2} }$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving for the Area of Complex Surfaces
snippet: Solving for the Area of Complex Surfaces: One side of a commercial building is 12 meters long by 9 meters high. There is a rolling door on this side of the building that is 4 meters wide by 3 meters high. You want to refinish the side of...
body_xml:
<example number="9.16" title="Solving for the Area of Complex Surfaces">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>One side of a commercial building is 12 meters long by 9 meters high. There is a rolling door on this side of the building that is 4 meters wide by 3 meters high. You want to refinish the side of the building, but not the door, with aluminum siding. How many square meters of aluminum siding are required to cover this side of the building?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Determine the area of the side of the building.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$12m \times 9m = 106{m}^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Determine the area of the door.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$4m \times 3m = 12{m}^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Subtract the area of the door from the area of the side of the building.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$106{m}^{2} - 12m^{2} = 92m^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, you need to purchase $$92m^{2}$$ of aluminum siding.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving for Area with Distance Measurements of Different Units
snippet: Solving for Area with Distance Measurements of Different Units: A national park has a land area in the shape of a rectangle. The park measures 2.2 kilometers long by 1,250 meters wide. What is the area of the park in square kilometers?...
body_xml:
<example number="9.17" title="Solving for Area with Distance Measurements of Different Units">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A national park has a land area in the shape of a rectangle. The park measures 2.2 kilometers long by 1,250 meters wide. What is the area of the park in square kilometers?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Use a conversion fraction to convert the information given in meters to kilometers.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$1,250m \times \frac{1{km}}{1,000m} = 1.25{km}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Multiply to find the area.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$2.2{km} \times 1.25{km} = 2.75{km}^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The park has an area of 2.75 km2.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving for Area Using Multiple Steps
snippet: Solving for Area Using Multiple Steps: A kitchen floor has an area of 15 m2. The floor in the kitchen pantry is 100 cm by 200 cm. You want to tile the kitchen and pantry floors using the same tile. How many square meters of tile do you...
body_xml:
<example number="9.18" title="Solving for Area Using Multiple Steps">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A kitchen floor has an area of 15 m2. The floor in the kitchen pantry is 100 cm by 200 cm. You want to tile the kitchen and pantry floors using the same tile. How many square meters of tile do you need to buy?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Determine the area of the pantry floor in square centimeters.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$100{cm} \times 200{cm} = 20,000{cm}^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Divide the area in cm2 by the conversion factor to determine the area in m2 since the other measurement for the kitchen floor is in m2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{20,000}{10,000} = 2$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The area of the kitchen pantry floor is 2 m2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Add the two areas of the pantry and the kitchen floors together.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$15m^{2} + 2m^{2} = 17m^{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, you need to buy 17 m2 of tile.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Reasonable Values for Volume
snippet: Determining Reasonable Values for Volume: A grandparent wants to send cookies to their grandchild away at college. Which represents a reasonable value for the volume of a box to ship the cookies: 3,375 km3, 3,375 m3, or 3,375 cm3? A volume...

<example number="9.19" title="Determining Reasonable Values for Volume">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A grandparent wants to send cookies to their grandchild away at college. Which represents a reasonable value for the volume of a box to ship the cookies:</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>3,375 km3,</item>
        <item>3,375 m3, or</item>
        <item>3,375 cm3?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>A volume of 3,375 km3 is equivalent to a rectangular prism with dimensions of $$15{km} \times 15{km} \times 15{km},$$ which is far too large for a shipping box. An area of 3,375 m3 is equivalent to a surface of $$15m \times 15m \times 15m,$$ which is also too large. A reasonable value for the volume of the box is 3,375 cm3.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Identifying Reasonable Values for Volume
snippet: Identifying Reasonable Values for Volume: A food manufacturer is prototyping new packaging for one of its most popular products. Which represents a reasonable value for the volume of the box: 2 dm3, 2 cm3, or 2 mm3? A decimeter is equal to...
body_xml:
<example number="9.20" title="Identifying Reasonable Values for Volume">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A food manufacturer is prototyping new packaging for one of its most popular products. Which represents a reasonable value for the volume of the box:</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>2 dm3,</item>
        <item>2 cm3, or</item>
        <item>2 mm3?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>A decimeter is equal to 10 centimeters. A box with a volume of 2 dm3 might have the dimensions $$1{dm} \times 1{dm} \times 2{dm}$$ , or $$10{cm} \times 10{cm} \times 20{cm}$$ , which is reasonable. A box with a volume of 2 cm3 or 2 mm3 would be too small.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Explaining Reasonable Values for Volume
snippet: Explaining Reasonable Values for Volume: A farmer has a hay loft. They calculate the volume of the hayloft as 64 cm3. Does the calculation make sense? Explain your answer. No. Centimeters are used to determine smaller distances, such as...

<example number="9.21" title="Explaining Reasonable Values for Volume">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A farmer has a hay loft. They calculate the volume of the hayloft as 64 cm3. Does the calculation make sense? Explain your answer.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>No. Centimeters are used to determine smaller distances, such as the length of a pencil. A hayloft is more than 64 centimeters long, so a more reasonable unit of value would be m2. A volume of 64 m3 can be calculated using the dimensions 4 meters by 4 meters by 4 meters, which are reasonable dimensions for a hayloft. So, a more reasonable value for the volume of the hayloft is 64 m3.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="9.22" title="Converting Like Units of Measure for Volume Using Multiplication">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A pencil case has a volume of 1,700 cm3. What is the volume in cubic millimeters?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use multiplication to convert from a larger metric volume unit to a smaller metric volume unit. To convert from cm3 to mm3, multiply the value of the volume by 1,000.</paragraph>

title: Converting Like Units of Measure for Volume Using Multi-Step Multiplication
snippet: Converting Like Units of Measure for Volume Using Multi-Step Multiplication: A shipping container has a volume of 33.2 m3. What is the volume in cubic centimeters? Use multiplication to convert a larger metric volume unit to a smaller...

<example number="9.23" title="Converting Like Units of Measure for Volume Using Multi-Step Multiplication">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A shipping container has a volume of 33.2 m3. What is the volume in cubic centimeters?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use multiplication to convert a larger metric volume unit to a smaller metric volume unit. To convert from m3 to cm3, first multiply the value of the volume by 1,000 to convert from m3 to dm3, and then multiply again by 1,000 to convert from dm3 to cm3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$33.2 \times 1,000 \times 1,000 = 33,200,000$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The shipping container has a volume of 32,200,000 cm3.</paragraph>
    </solution>

      <paragraph>A holding tank at the local aquarium has a volume of 22,712,000,000 cm3. What is the volume in cubic meters?</paragraph>

To convert from cm3 to m3, divide the value of the volume by 1,000 to first convert from cm3 to dm3, then divide again to convert from dm3 to m3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {{cm}^{3}{to dm}^{3}:\frac{22,712,000,000}{1,000} = 22,712,000} \\ {{dm}^{3}{to m}^{3}:\frac{22,712,000}{1,000} = 22,712} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>

title: Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume

<example number="9.25" title="Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A holding tank at the local aquarium has a volume of 22,712,000,000 cm3? What is the capacity of the holding tank in liters?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use division to convert from cubic centimeters to liters. To determine the equivalent volume in liters, convert from cm3 to L by dividing the value of the volume in cm3 by 1,000.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{22,712,000,000{cm}^{3}}{1,000} = 22,712,000L$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The holding tank holds 22,712,000 L of water.</paragraph>

title: Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume Using Multiplication
snippet: Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume Using Multiplication: An airplane used 150 m3 of fuel to fly from New York to Hawaii. How many liters of fuel did the airplane use? Because 1 liter is equivalent to 1 cubic decimeter, use...

<example number="9.26" title="Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume Using Multiplication">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>An airplane used 150 m3 of fuel to fly from New York to Hawaii. How many liters of fuel did the airplane use?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because 1 liter is equivalent to 1 cubic decimeter, use multiplication to convert from m3 to dm3. Multiply the value of the volume by 1,000 to convert from m3 to dm3. Because $$1{dm}^{3} = 1L$$ , the resulting value is equivalent to the number of liters used.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$150 \times 1,000 = 150,000{dm}^{3} = 150,000L$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The airplane used 150,000 liters of fuel.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume Using Multi-Step Division
snippet: Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume Using Multi-Step Division: How many liters can a pitcher with a volume of 8,000,000 mm3 hold? Use division to convert from a smaller metric volume unit to a larger metric volume unit. To...

<example number="9.27" title="Converting Different Units of Measure for Volume Using Multi-Step Division">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>How many liters can a pitcher with a volume of 8,000,000 mm3 hold?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use division to convert from a smaller metric volume unit to a larger metric volume unit. To convert from mm3 to dm3,</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Divide by 1,000 to convert from mm3 to cm3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Divide again by 1,000 to convert from cm3 to dm3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Use the unit value to express the volume in terms of liters.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{8,000,000{mm}^{3}}{1,000} & = & {8,000{cm}^{3}} \\ \frac{8,000{cm}^{3}}{1,000} & = & {8{dm}^{3} = 8 L} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The pitcher can hold 8 liters of liquid.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="9.28" title="Using Volume to Solve Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A cubic shipping carton’s dimensions measure $$2m \times 2m \times 2m$$ . A company wants to fill the carton with smaller cubic boxes that measure $$10{cm} \times 10{cm} \times 10{cm}$$ . How many of the smaller boxes will fit in each shipping carton?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Determine the volume of the shipping carton.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$2m \times 2m \times 2m = 8{m}^{3}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Use the appropriate conversion factor to convert the volume of the shipping carton from m3 to cm3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {8{m}^{3} \times 1,000 = 8,000{dm}^{3}} \\ {8,000{dm}^{3} \times 1,000 = 8,000,000{cm}^{3}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Determine the volume of the smaller boxes.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$10{cm} \times 10{cm} \times 10{cm} = 1,000{cm}^{3}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Divide the volume of the shipping carton, in cm3, by the volume of the smaller box, in cm3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{8,000,000{cm}^{3}}{1,000{cm}^{3}} = 8,000$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The shipping carton will hold 8,000 smaller boxes.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving Volume Problems with Different Units
snippet: Solving Volume Problems with Different Units: A carton of juice measures 6 cm long, 6 cm wide and 20 cm tall. A factory produces 28,800 liters of orange juice each day. How many cartons of orange juice are produced each day? Step 1: Find...
body_xml:
<example number="9.29" title="Solving Volume Problems with Different Units">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A carton of juice measures 6 cm long, 6 cm wide and 20 cm tall. A factory produces 28,800 liters of orange juice each day. How many cartons of orange juice are produced each day?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Find the volume of the carton in cubic centimeters.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$6{cm} \times 6{cm} \times 20{cm} = 720{cm}^{3}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Convert the volume in cm3 to liters.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {1{cm}^{3}} & = & {1{mL}} \\ {720{cm}^{3}} & = & {720{mL}} \\ \frac{720{mL}}{1,000} & = & {0.72 L} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Divide the number of liters of orange juice produced each day by the volume of each carton.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{28,800L}{0.72L} = 40,000$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The factory produces 40,000 cartons of orange juice each day.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving Complex Volume Problems
snippet: Solving Complex Volume Problems: A fish tank measures 60 cm long, 15 cm wide and 34 cm tall (Figure 9.11). The tank is 25 percent full. How many liters of water are needed to completely fill the tank? Step 1: Determine the volume of the...
body_xml: A fish tank measures 60 cm long, 15 cm wide and 34 cm tall (Figure 9.11). The tank is 25 percent full. How many liters of water are needed to completely fill the tank? Step 1: Determine the volume of the fish tank in cubic centimeters. $$60{cm} \times 15{cm} \times 34{cm} = 30,600{cm}^{3}$$ Step 2: Convert the volume in cm3 to volume in liters. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {1{cm}^{3}} & = & {1{mL}} \\ {30,600{cm}^{3}} & = & {30,600{mL}} \\ \frac{30,600{mL}}{1,000} & = & {30.6L} \end{array}$$ Step 3: Since the tank is 25 percent full, the tank is 75 percent empty. Convert 75 percent to its decimal equivalent. Multiply the total volume by 75 percent expressed in decimal form to determine how many liters of water are required to fill the tank. $$\begin{array}{rcl} {75\%} & = & 0.75 \\ {30.6 \times 0.75} & = & 22.95 \end{array}$$ So, 22.95 liters of water are needed to fill the tank.

title: Identifying Reasonable Units for Weight

title: Determining Reasonable Values for Weight
snippet: Determining Reasonable Values for Weight: Which of the following represents a reasonable value for the weight of three lemons? 250 g, 2,500 g, or 250 kg? Because a kilogram is about 2.2 pounds, we can eliminate 250 kg as it is way too...
body_xml:
<example number="9.32" title="Determining Reasonable Values for Weight">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Which of the following represents a reasonable value for the weight of three lemons?</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>250 g,</item>
        <item>2,500 g, or</item>
        <item>250 kg?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Because a kilogram is about 2.2 pounds, we can eliminate 250 kg as it is way too heavy. 2,500 grams is equivalent to 2.5 kilograms, or about five pounds, which is again, too heavy. So, a reasonable value for the weight of three lemons would be 250 grams.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Explaining Reasonable Values for Weight

<example number="9.33" title="Explaining Reasonable Values for Weight">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The blue whale is the largest living mammal on Earth. Which of the following is a reasonable value for the weight of a blue whale: 149 g, 149 kg, or 149 mt? Explain your answer.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>A reasonable value for the weight of a blue whale is 149 metric tons. Both 149 g and 149 kg are much too small a value for the largest living mammal on Earth.</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Converting Metric Units of Weight Using Multistep Division

<example number="9.34" title="Converting Metric Units of Weight Using Multistep Division">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>How many kilograms are in 24,300,000 milligrams?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use division to convert from a smaller metric weight unit to a larger metric weight unit. To convert from milligrams to kilograms,</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Divide the value of the weight in milligrams by 1,000 to first convert from milligrams to grams.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Divide by 1,000 again to convert from grams to kilograms.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{24,300,000{mg}}{1,000} & = & {24,300g} \\ \frac{24,300g}{1,000} & = & {24.3{kg}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, 24,300,000 milligrams are equivalent to 24.3 kilograms.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="9.35" title="Converting Metric Units of Weight Using Multiplication">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The average ostrich weighs approximately 127 kilograms. How many grams does an ostrich weigh?</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use multiplication to convert from a larger metric weight unit to a smaller metric weight unit. To convert from kilograms to grams, multiply the value of the weight by 1,000.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$127{kg} \times 1,000 = 127,000g$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The average ostrich weighs 127,000 grams.</paragraph>

title: Converting Metric Units of Weight Using Multistep Multiplication

title: Comparing Weights to Solve Problems
snippet: Comparing Weights to Solve Problems: The maximum weight for a child to safely use a car seat is 29 kilograms. If a child weighs 23,700 grams, can the child safely use the car seat? Step 1: Convert the child’s weight in grams to kilograms....

<example number="9.37" title="Comparing Weights to Solve Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The maximum weight for a child to safely use a car seat is 29 kilograms. If a child weighs 23,700 grams, can the child safely use the car seat?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Convert the child’s weight in grams to kilograms.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$23,700g \div 1,000 = 23.7{kg}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Compare the two weights.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$23.7{kg} < 29{kg}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Yes, the child can safely use the car seat.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving Multistep Weight Problems
snippet: Solving Multistep Weight Problems: A recipe for scones calls for 350 grams of flour. How many kilograms of flour are required to make 4 batches of scones? Step 1: Multiply the grams of flour need by 4 to determine the total amount of flour...

<example number="9.38" title="Solving Multistep Weight Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A recipe for scones calls for 350 grams of flour. How many kilograms of flour are required to make 4 batches of scones?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Multiply the grams of flour need by 4 to determine the total amount of flour needed.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$350g \times 4 = 1,400g$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Convert from grams to kilograms.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{1,400g}{1,000} = 1.4{kg}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, 1.4 kilograms of flour are needed to make four batches of scones.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving Complex Weight Problems
snippet: Solving Complex Weight Problems: The average tomato weighs 140 grams. A farmer needs to order boxes to pack and ship their tomatoes to local grocery stores. They estimate that this year’s harvest will yield 125,000 tomatoes. A box can hold...
body_xml:
<example number="9.39" title="Solving Complex Weight Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The average tomato weighs 140 grams. A farmer needs to order boxes to pack and ship their tomatoes to local grocery stores. They estimate that this year’s harvest will yield 125,000 tomatoes. A box can hold 12 kilograms of tomatoes. How many boxes does the farmer need?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Determine the total estimated weight of the harvested tomatoes.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$140g \times 125,000 = 17,500,000g$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Convert the total weight from grams to kilograms.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$17,500,000g \div 1,000 = 17,500{kg}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Divide the weight of the tomatoes by the weight each box can hold.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$17,500{kg} \div 12{kg} \approx 1,458$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, the farmer will need to order 1,458 boxes.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting Temperatures from Fahrenheit to Celsius
snippet: Converting Temperatures from Fahrenheit to Celsius: A recipe calls for the oven to be set to 392 °F. What is the temperature in Celsius? Use the formula in Table 9.3 to convert from Fahrenheit to Celsius. \begin{array}{rcl} C & = &...
body_xml:
<example number="9.40" title="Converting Temperatures from Fahrenheit to Celsius">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A recipe calls for the oven to be set to 392 °F. What is the temperature in Celsius?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the formula in Table 9.3 to convert from Fahrenheit to Celsius.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} C & = & {\frac{5}{9}(F - 32)} \\ C & = & {\frac{5}{9}(392 - 32)} \\ C & = & {\frac{5}{9}(360)} \\ C & = & 200 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, 392 °F is equivalent to 200 °C.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting Temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit
snippet: Converting Temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit: On a sunny afternoon in May, the temperature in London was 20 °C. What was the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit? Use the formula in Table 9.3 to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit....

<example number="9.41" title="Converting Temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>On a sunny afternoon in May, the temperature in London was 20 °C. What was the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the formula in Table 9.3 to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} F & = & {\frac{9}{5}C + 32} \\ F & = & {\frac{9}{5}(20) + 32} \\ F & = & {36 + 32} \\ F & = & 68 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The temperature was 68 °F.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Comparing Temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit
snippet: Comparing Temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit: A manufacturer requires a vaccine to be stored in a refrigerator at temperatures between 36 °F and 46 °F. The refrigerator in the local pharmacy cools to 3 °C. Can the vaccine be stored...
body_xml:
<example number="9.42" title="Comparing Temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A manufacturer requires a vaccine to be stored in a refrigerator at temperatures between 36 °F and 46 °F. The refrigerator in the local pharmacy cools to 3 °C. Can the vaccine be stored safely in the pharmacy’s refrigerator?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the formula in Table 9.3 to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} F & = & {\frac{9}{5}C + 32} \\ F & = & {\frac{9}{5}(3) + 32} \\ F & = & {5.4 + 32} \\ F & = & 37.4 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, compare the temperatures.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$36{}_{}^{} < 37.4{}_{}^{} < 46{}_{}^{}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Yes. 37.4 °F falls within the acceptable range to store the vaccine, so it can be stored safely in the pharmacy’s refrigerator.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

        <item>5 °C or</item>
        <item>–5 °C?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>

title: Using Estimation to Determine Reasonable Values for Temperatures
snippet: Using Estimation to Determine Reasonable Values for Temperatures: The average body temperature is generally accepted as 98.6 °F. What is a reasonable value for the average body temperature in degrees Celsius: 98.6 °C, 64.3 °C, or 34.3 °C?...
body_xml:
<example number="9.44" title="Using Estimation to Determine Reasonable Values for Temperatures">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The average body temperature is generally accepted as 98.6 °F. What is a reasonable value for the average body temperature in degrees Celsius:</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>98.6 °C,</item>
        <item>64.3 °C, or</item>
        <item>34.3 °C?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To estimate the average body temperature in degrees Celsius, subtract 30 from the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, and divide the result by 2.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{(98.6 - 30)}{2} = \frac{68.6}{2} = 34.3$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>A reasonable value for average body temperature is 34.3 °C.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Conversion to Determine Reasonable Values for Temperatures
snippet: Using Conversion to Determine Reasonable Values for Temperatures: Which is a reasonable temperature for storing chocolate: 28 °C, 18 °C, or 2 °C? Use the formula in Table 9.3 to determine the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit....
body_xml:
<example number="9.45" title="Using Conversion to Determine Reasonable Values for Temperatures">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Which is a reasonable temperature for storing chocolate:</paragraph>
      <list type="unordered">
        <item>28 °C,</item>
        <item>18 °C, or</item>
        <item>2 °C?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the formula in Table 9.3 to determine the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} F & = & {\frac{9}{5}C + 32} \\ F & = & {\frac{9}{5}(28) + 32 = 82.4} \\ F & = & {\frac{9}{5}(18) + 32 = 64.4} \\ F & = & {\frac{9}{5}(2) + 32 = 35.6} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>A temperature of 82.4 °F would be too hot, causing the chocolate to melt. A temperature of 35.6 °F is very close to freezing, which would affect the look and feel of the chocolate. So, a reasonable temperature for storing chocolate is 18 °C, or 64.4 °F.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Using Addition to Solve Temperature Problems: A scientist was using a liquid that was 35 °C. They needed to heat the liquid to raise the temperature by 6 °C. What was the temperature after the scientist heated it? Use addition to find the...

<example number="9.47" title="Using Addition to Solve Temperature Problems">

      <paragraph>A scientist was using a liquid that was 35 °C. They needed to heat the liquid to raise the temperature by 6 °C. What was the temperature after the scientist heated it?</paragraph>
    </problem>

title: Solving Complex Temperature Problems
snippet: Solving Complex Temperature Problems: The optimum temperature for a chemical compound to develop its unique properties is 392 °F. When the heating process begins, the temperature of the compound is 20 °C. For safety purposes the compound...
body_xml:
<example number="9.48" title="Solving Complex Temperature Problems">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The optimum temperature for a chemical compound to develop its unique properties is 392 °F. When the heating process begins, the temperature of the compound is 20 °C. For safety purposes the compound can only be heated 9 °C every 15 minutes. How long until the compound reaches its optimum temperature?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Determine the optimum temperature in degrees Celsius using the formula in Table 9.3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} C & = & {\frac{5}{9}\left( {F - 32} \right)} \\ C & = & {\frac{5}{9}(392 - 32)} \\ C & = & {\frac{5}{9}(360)} \\ C & = & 200 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: Subtract the starting temperature.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$200{}_{}^{} - 20{}_{}^{} = 180{}_{}^{}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: Determine the number of 15-minute cycles needed to heat the compound to its optimum temperature.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$180 \div 9 = 20$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4: Multiply the number of cycles needed by 15 minutes and convert the product to hours and minutes.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {15{minutes} \times 9 = 135{minutes}} \\ {135{minutes} = 2{hours}15{minutes}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, it will take 2 hours and 15 minutes for the compound to reach its optimum temperature.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Defining Lines
snippet: Defining Lines: For the following exercises, use this line (Figure 10.4). Define \overline{DE} . Define F . Define \overset{\leftrightarrow}{DF} . Define \overline{EF} . The symbol \overline{DE} , two letters with a straight line above,...
body_xml: For the following exercises, use this line (Figure 10.4). Define $$\overline{DE}$$ . Define $$F$$ . Define $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{DF}$$ . Define $$\overline{EF}$$ . The symbol $$\overline{DE}$$ , two letters with a straight line above, refers to the line segment that starts at point $$D$$ and ends at point $$E$$ . The letter $$F$$ alone refers to point $$F$$ . The symbol $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{DF}$$ , two letters with a line above containing arrows on both ends, refers to the line that extends infinitely in both directions and contains the points $$D$$ and $$F$$ . The symbol $$\overline{EF}$$ , two letters with a straight line above, refers to the line segment that starts at point $$E$$ and ends at point $$F$$ .

title: Determining the Best Route
snippet: Determining the Best Route: View the street map (Figure 10.6) as a series of line segments from point to point. For example, we have vertical line segments \overline{AB} , \overline{BC}, and \overline{CD} on the right. On the left side of...
body_xml: View the street map (Figure 10.6) as a series of line segments from point to point. For example, we have vertical line segments $$\overline{AB}$$ , $$\overline{BC},$$ and $$\overline{CD}$$ on the right. On the left side of the map, we have vertical line segments $$\overline{HI}$$ , $$\overline{FG.}$$ The horizontal line segments are $$\overline{HA}$$ , $$\overline{EI}$$ , $$\overline{IE}$$ , $$\overline{EB}$$ , $$\overline{FC}$$ , $$\overline{CF},$$ and $$\overline{GB}.$$ There are two diagonal line segments, $$\overline{AE}$$ and $$\overline{EF}.$$ Assume that each location is on a corner and that you live next door to the library. Let’s say that you want to stop at the grocery store on your way home from school. Come up with three routes you might take to do your errand and then go home. In other words, name the three ways by the line segments in the order you would walk, and which way do you think would be the most efficient route? How about stopping at the library after school? Name four ways you might travel to the library and which way do you think is the most efficient? Suppose you need to go to the post office and the dry cleaners on your way home from school. Name three ways you might walk to do your errands and end up at home. Which way do you think is the most efficient way to walk, get your errands done, and go home? From school to the grocery store and home: first way $$\overline{AH},\overline{HI},\overline{IE},\overline{EF},\overline{FG}$$ ; second way $$\overline{AB},\overline{BE},\overline{EI},\overline{IE},\overline{EF},\overline{FG}$$ ; third way $$\overline{AE},\overline{EI},\overline{IE},\overline{EF},\overline{FG}$$ . It seems that the third way is the most efficient way. From school to the library: first way $$\overline{AE},\overline{EF},\overline{FG}$$ ; second way $$\overline{AB},\overline{BC},\overline{CD},\overline{DG}$$ ; third way $$\overline{AB},\overline{BE},\overline{EF},\overline{FG}$$ ; fourth way $$\overline{AB},\overline{BC},\overline{CF},\overline{FG}$$ . The first way should be the most efficient way. From school to the post office or dry cleaners to home: first way $$\overline{AE},\overline{EF},\overline{FC},\overline{CD},\overline{DG}$$ ; second way $$\overline{AB},\overline{BE},\overline{EF},\overline{FC},\overline{CD},\overline{DG}$$ ; third way $$\overline{AB},\overline{BC},\overline{CF},\overline{FG}$$ . The third way would be the most efficient way.

title: Identifying Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
snippet: Identifying Parallel and Perpendicular Lines: Identify the sets of parallel and perpendicular lines in Figure 10.9. Drawing these lines on a grid is the best way to distinguish which pairs of lines are parallel and which are perpendicular....
body_xml: Identify the sets of parallel and perpendicular lines in Figure 10.9. Drawing these lines on a grid is the best way to distinguish which pairs of lines are parallel and which are perpendicular. Because they are on a grid, we assume all lines are equally spaced across the grid horizontally and vertically. The grid also tells us that the vertical lines are parallel and the horizontal lines are parallel. Additionally, all intersections form a $$90^{\circ}$$ angle. Therefore, we can safely say the following: $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{AB} \parallel \overset{\leftrightarrow}{CD}$$ , the line containing the points $$A$$ and $$B$$ is parallel to the line containing the points $$C$$ and $$D$$ . $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{EF} \parallel \overset{\leftrightarrow}{GH}$$ , the line containing the points $$E$$ and $$F$$ is parallel to the line containing the points $$G$$ and $$H$$ . $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{AB}\bot\overset{\leftrightarrow}{EF}$$ , the line containing the points $$A$$ and $$B$$ is perpendicular to the line containing the points $$E$$ and $$F$$ . We know this because both lines trace grid lines, and intersecting grid lines are perpendicular. We can also state that $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{AB}\bot\overset{\leftrightarrow}{GH}$$ ; the line containing the points $$A$$ and $$B$$ is perpendicular to the line containing the points $$G$$ and $$H$$ because both lines trace grid lines, which are perpendicular by definition. We also have $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{CD}\bot\overset{\leftrightarrow}{EF}$$ ; the line containing the points $$C$$ and $$D$$ is perpendicular to the line containing the points $$E$$ and $$F$$ because both lines trace grid lines, which are perpendicular by definition. Finally, we see that $$\overset{\leftrightarrow}{CD}\bot\overset{\leftrightarrow}{GH}$$ ; the line containing the points $$C$$ and $$D$$ is perpendicular to the line containing the points $$G$$ and $$H$$ because both lines trace grid lines, which are perpendicular by definition.

snippet: Solving for Angle Measurements and Supplementary Angles: Solve for the angle measurements in Figure 10.29. Step 1: These are supplementary angles. We can see this because the two angles are part of a horizontal line, and a horizontal line...
body_xml: Solve for the angle measurements in Figure 10.29. Step 1: These are supplementary angles. We can see this because the two angles are part of a horizontal line, and a horizontal line represents $$180^{\circ}.$$ Therefore, the sum of the two angles equals $$180^{\circ}.$$ Step 2: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {(32x - 7) + (5x + 2)} & = & 180 \\ {37x - 5} & = & 180 \\ {37x} & = & 185 \\ x & = & 5 \end{array}$$ Step 3: Find the measure of each angle: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {32x - 7} & = & {32(5) - 7} \\ & = & 153^{\circ} \\ {5x + 2} & = & {5(5) + 2} \\ & = & 27^{\circ} \end{array}$$ Step 4: We check: $$153^{\circ} + 27^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}.$$

title: Measuring Angles Formed by a Transversal
snippet: Measuring Angles Formed by a Transversal: In Figure 10.40 given that angle 2 measures 23^{\circ}, find the measure of the remaining angles and state the reason for your solution. m\measuredangle 2 = m\measuredangle 3 = 23^{\circ} by...
body_xml: In Figure 10.40 given that angle 2 measures $$23^{\circ},$$ find the measure of the remaining angles and state the reason for your solution. $$m\measuredangle 2 = m\measuredangle 3 = 23^{\circ}$$ by vertical angles, because $$\measuredangle 2$$ and $$\measuredangle 3$$ are the opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines. $$m\measuredangle 1 = 157^{\circ}$$ by supplementary angles to $$m\measuredangle 2$$ or $$m\measuredangle 3.$$ We see that $$\measuredangle 1$$ and $$\measuredangle 2$$ form a straight angle as does $$\measuredangle 1$$ and $$\measuredangle 3.$$ A straight angle measures $$180^{\circ},$$ so $$180^{\circ} - 23^{\circ} = 157^{\circ}.$$ $$m\measuredangle 4 = m\measuredangle 1 = 157^{\circ}$$ by vertical angles, because $$\measuredangle 4$$ and $$\measuredangle 1$$ are the two opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines. $$m\measuredangle 5 = m\measuredangle 1 = 157^{\circ}$$ by corresponding angles because they are the same angle formed by the transversal crossing two parallel lines, one exterior and one interior. $$m\measuredangle 8 = m\measuredangle 5 = 157^{\circ}$$ by vertical angles because $$\measuredangle 8$$ and $$\measuredangle 5$$ are the two opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines. $$m\measuredangle 7 = m\measuredangle 2 = 23^{\circ}$$ by alternate exterior angles because, like vertical angles, these angles are the opposite angles formed by the transversal intersecting two parallel lines. $$m\measuredangle 6 = m\measuredangle 7 = 23^{\circ}$$ by vertical angles because these are the opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines.

snippet: Finding Measures of Angles Inside a Triangle: Find the measure of each angle in the triangle shown (Figure 10.46). We know that the sum of the angles must equal 180^{\circ}. Step 1: As the sum of the interior angles equals 180^{\circ}, we...
body_xml: Find the measure of each angle in the triangle shown (Figure 10.46). We know that the sum of the angles must equal $$180^{\circ}.$$ Step 1: As the sum of the interior angles equals $$180^{\circ},$$ we can use algebra to find the measures: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x + (x + 17) + (3x - 62)} & = & 180 \\ {5x - 45} & = & 180 \\ {5x} & = & 225 \\ x & = & {\frac{225}{5} = 45} \end{array}$$ Step 2: Now that we have the value of $$x$$ , we can substitute 45 into the other two expressions to find the measure of those angles: $$\begin{array}{rcl} \left( {x + 17} \right) & = & {45 + 17 = 62^{\circ}} \\ {(3x - 62)} & = & {3(45) - 62 = 135 - 62 = 73^{\circ}} \end{array}$$ Step 3: Then, $$m\measuredangle x = 45^{\circ}$$ , $$m\measuredangle(x + 17) = 62^{\circ}$$ , and $$m\measuredangle(3x - 62) = 73^{\circ}.$$

title: Determining If Triangles Are Similar
snippet: Determining If Triangles Are Similar: Are the two triangles shown in Figure 10.56 similar? Step 1: We will look at the proportions within each triangle. In triangle \alpha (alpha), the side opposite the 57^{\circ} angle measures 7, and the...
body_xml: Are the two triangles shown in Figure 10.56 similar? Step 1: We will look at the proportions within each triangle. In triangle $$\alpha$$ (alpha), the side opposite the $$57^{\circ}$$ angle measures 7, and the side opposite the $$33^{\circ}$$ angle measures 4. Then, the measures of the corresponding sides in triangle $$\beta$$ (beta) measures 3.5 and 2, respectively. We have $$\frac{4}{7} = 0.5714 \frac{2}{3.5} = 0.5714.$$ This is the proportion $$\frac{4}{7} = \frac{2}{3.5}$$ . The scaling factor is 0.5714. Step 2: Let’s try another correspondence. In triangle $$\alpha$$ , the hypotenuse measures 8.06 and the side opposite the $$57^{\circ}$$ angle measures 7. In triangle $$\beta$$ , the hypotenuse measure 4.03 and the side opposite the $$57^{\circ}$$ angle measures 3.5. We have $$\frac{7}{8.06} = 0.8685 \frac{3.5}{4.03} = 0.8685.$$ Step 3: Now, let’s look at the proportions between triangle $$\alpha$$ and triangle $$\beta.$$ The side measuring 2 in triangle $$\beta$$ corresponds to the side measuring 4 in triangle $$\alpha$$ , the side measuring 3.5 in triangle $$\beta$$ corresponds to the side measuring 7 in triangle $$\alpha,$$ and the hypotenuse in triangle $$\beta$$ corresponds to the hypotenuse in triangle $$\alpha.$$ We have $$\frac{2}{4} = 0.5 \frac{3.5}{7} = 0.5 \frac{4.03}{8.06} = 0.5$$ Thus, the corresponding angles are equal and the proportions between each pair of corresponding sides equals 0.5. In other words, the scaling factor is 0.5. Therefore, the triangles are similar.

title: Proving Similarity
snippet: Proving Similarity: In Figure 10.57, is triangle \delta (delta) similar to triangle \varepsilon (epsilon)? Find the lengths of sides x and y as part of your answer. We can see that all three angles in triangle \delta are equal to the...
body_xml: In Figure 10.57, is triangle $$\delta$$ (delta) similar to triangle $$\varepsilon$$ (epsilon)? Find the lengths of sides $$x$$ and $$y$$ as part of your answer. We can see that all three angles in triangle $$\delta$$ are equal to the corresponding angles in triangle $$\varepsilon$$ . That is enough to determine similarity. However, we want to find the values of $$x$$ and $$y$$ to prove similarity. Step 1: We have to do is set up the proportions between the corresponding sides. We have the side that measures 2.375 in triangle $$\delta$$ corresponding to the side measuring 1.069 in triangle $$\varepsilon$$ . We have the hypotenuse/side in triangle $$\delta$$ measuring 6 corresponding to the hypotenuse/side labeled $$y$$ in triangle $$\varepsilon$$ . And, finally, the side labeled $$x$$ in triangle $$\delta$$ corresponds to the side measuring 2.475 in triangle $$\varepsilon.$$ Each proportion should be equal. We start with the proportion of the shorter sides. Thus $$\frac{1.069}{2.375} = 0.45$$ Step 2: We solve for $$y$$ using the first proportion. Set the two ratios equal to each other, cross-multiply, and solve for $$y$$ . We have: $$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{1.069}{2.375} & = & \frac{y}{6} \\ {(6)(1.069)} & = & {(2.375)(y)} \\ 6.414 & = & {2.375y} \\ \frac{6.414}{2.375} & = & {2.7 = y} \end{array}$$ So, $$y = 2.7$$ . Step 3: Checking that length in the proportion factor of 0.45, we have: $$\frac{y}{6} = \frac{2.7}{6} = 0.45$$ Step 4: Solving for $$x$$ , we will use the same proportion we used to solve for $$y$$ . We have: $$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{1.069}{2.375} & = & \frac{2.475}{x} \\ {1.069(x)} & = & {2.475(2.375)} \\ {1.069(x)} & = & 5.878 \\ x & = & {\frac{5.878}{1.069} = 5.5} \\ \frac{2.475}{x} & = & {\frac{2.475}{5.5} = 0.45} \end{array}$$ Step 5: We test the proportions. We have the following: $$\frac{2.7}{6} = \frac{2.475}{5.5} = \frac{1.069}{2.375} = 0.45$$ The proportions are all equal. Therefore, we have proven the property of similarity between triangle $$\delta$$ and triangle $$\varepsilon.$$

title: Applying Similar Triangles
snippet: Applying Similar Triangles: A person who is 5 feet tall is standing 50 feet away from the base of a tree (Figure 10.58). The tree casts a 57-foot shadow. The person casts a 7-foot shadow. What is the height of the tree? The bigger triangle...
body_xml: A person who is 5 feet tall is standing 50 feet away from the base of a tree (Figure 10.58). The tree casts a 57-foot shadow. The person casts a 7-foot shadow. What is the height of the tree? The bigger triangle includes a tree at side $$x$$ and the smaller triangle includes the person at the side labeled 5 ft. These two triangles are similar because the smaller triangle fits inside the larger triangle at the smallest angle. It would fit inside the larger triangle at either of the other two angles as well. That all angles are equal is one of the criteria for similar triangles, so we can solve using proportions: $$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{5}{7} & = & \frac{x}{57} \\ {5(57)} & = & {7x} \\ \frac{285}{7} & = & {x = 40.7} \end{array}$$ The tree is 40.7 feet tall.

title: Calculating the Sum of Interior Angles
snippet: Calculating the Sum of Interior Angles: Find the measure of an interior angle in a regular octagon using the formula, and then find the sum of all the interior angles using the sum formula. An octagon has eight sides, so n = 8 . Step 1:...
body_xml:
<example number="10.28" title="Calculating the Sum of Interior Angles">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the measure of an interior angle in a regular octagon using the formula, and then find the sum of all the interior angles using the sum formula.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>An octagon has eight sides, so $$n = 8$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1: Using the formula $$a = \frac{(n - 2)180^{\circ}}{8}$$ :</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} a & = & \frac{(8 - 2)180^{\circ}}{8} \\ & = & \frac{(6)180^{\circ}}{8} \\ & = & {135^{\circ}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, the measure of each interior angle in a regular octagon is $$135^{\circ}$$ .</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2: The sum of the angles inside an octagon, so using the formula:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} S & = & {(n - 2)180^{\circ}} \\ & = & {(8 - 2)180^{\circ}} \\ & = & {6(180)} \\ & = & {1,080^{\circ}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3: We can test this, as we already know the measure of each angle is $$135^{\circ}$$ . Thus, $$8(135^{\circ}) = 1,080^{\circ}$$ .</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Interior Angles
snippet: Calculating Interior Angles: Use algebra to calculate the measure of each interior angle of the five-sided polygon (Figure 10.70). Step 1: Let us find out what the total of the sum of the interior angles should be. Use the formula for the...
body_xml: Use algebra to calculate the measure of each interior angle of the five-sided polygon (Figure 10.70). Step 1: Let us find out what the total of the sum of the interior angles should be. Use the formula for the sum of the angles in a polygon with $$n$$ sides: $$S = (n - 2)180^{\circ}$$ . So, $$S = (5 - 2)180^{\circ} = 540^{\circ}$$ . Step 2: We add up all the angles and solve for $$x$$ : $$\begin{array}{rcl} {5(x + 7) + 120 + (6x + 25) + 5(2x + 5) + 5(3x - 5)} & = & 540 \\ {5x + 6x + 10x + 15x + 180} & = & 540 \\ {36x} & = & 360 \\ x & = & 10 \end{array}$$ Step 3: We can then find the measure of each interior angle: $$\begin{array}{l} {m\measuredangle A = 5(10 + 7) = 85^{\circ}} \\ {m\measuredangle B = 120^{\circ}} \\ {m\measuredangle C = 6(10) + 25 = 85^{\circ}} \\ {m\measuredangle D = 5(2*10 + 5) = 125^{\circ}} \\ {m\measuredangle E = 5(3*10 - 5) = 125^{\circ}} \end{array}$$

title: Calculating Circumference for the Real World
snippet: Calculating Circumference for the Real World: You decide to make a trim for the window in Figure 10.74. How many feet of trim do you need to buy? The trim will cover the 6 feet along the bottom and the two 12-ft sides plus the half circle...
body_xml: You decide to make a trim for the window in Figure 10.74. How many feet of trim do you need to buy? The trim will cover the 6 feet along the bottom and the two 12-ft sides plus the half circle on top. The circumference of a semicircle is ½ the circumference of a circle. The diameter of the semicircle is 6 ft. Then, the circumference of the semicircle would be $$\frac{1}{2}\pi d = \frac{1}{2}\pi(6) = 3\pi \text{ft} = 9.4 \text{ft} .$$ Therefore, the total perimeter of the window is $$6 + 12 + 12 + 9.4 = 39.4 \text{ft} .$$ You need to buy 39.4 ft of trim.

title: Creating a Translation
snippet: Creating a Translation: Suppose you have a hexagon on a grid as in Figure 10.81. Translate the hexagon 5 units to the right and 3 units up. The best way to do this is by translating the individual points A,B,C,D,E,F . Once translated, the...
body_xml: Suppose you have a hexagon on a grid as in Figure 10.81. Translate the hexagon 5 units to the right and 3 units up. The best way to do this is by translating the individual points $$A,B,C,D,E,F$$ . Once translated, the points become $$A^{\prime},B^{\prime},C^{\prime},D^{\prime},E^{\prime},F^{\prime}.$$

title: Applying a Rotation
snippet: Applying a Rotation: Figure 10.84 illustrates a tessellation begun with an equilateral triangle. Explain how this pattern is produced. A rotation to the right or to the left around the vertex by 60^{\circ}, six times, produces the...
body_xml: Figure 10.84 illustrates a tessellation begun with an equilateral triangle. Explain how this pattern is produced. A rotation to the right or to the left around the vertex by $$60^{\circ},$$ six times, produces the hexagonal shape. The sixth rotation brings the triangle back to its original position. Then, a reflection up and another one on the diagonal will reproduce the pattern. When a shape returns to its original position by a rotation, we say that it has rotational symmetry.

title: Applying the Glide Reflection
snippet: Applying the Glide Reflection: An obtuse triangle is reflected about the dashed line, and the two shapes are joined together. How does the tessellation shown in Figure 10.87 materialize? The new shape is reflected horizontally and joined...
body_xml: An obtuse triangle is reflected about the dashed line, and the two shapes are joined together. How does the tessellation shown in Figure 10.87 materialize? The new shape is reflected horizontally and joined with the original shape. It is then translated vertically and horizontally to make up the tessellation. Notice the blank spaces next to the vertical pattern. These areas are made up of the exact original shape rotated $$180^{\circ},$$ but with no line up the center. These rotated shapes are translated horizontally and vertically, and thus, the plane is tessellated with no gaps. This is an example of a glide reflection where the order of the transformations matters.

title: Applying More Than One Tessellation
snippet: Applying More Than One Tessellation: Show how this tessellation (Figure 10.88) can be achieved. This is a tessellation that has one color on the front of the trapezoid and a different color on the back. There is a translation on the...
body_xml: Show how this tessellation (Figure 10.88) can be achieved. This is a tessellation that has one color on the front of the trapezoid and a different color on the back. There is a translation on the diagonal, and a reflection vertically. These are two separate transformations resulting in two new placements of the trapezoid. We can call this a combination of two transformations or a glide reflection.

title: Tessellating the Plane
snippet: Tessellating the Plane: Do regular pentagons tessellate the plane by themselves (Figure 10.94)? We can see that regular pentagons do not tessellate the plane by themselves. There is a gap, a gap in the shape of a parallelogram. We conclude...
body_xml: Do regular pentagons tessellate the plane by themselves (Figure 10.94)? We can see that regular pentagons do not tessellate the plane by themselves. There is a gap, a gap in the shape of a parallelogram. We conclude that regular pentagons will not tessellate the plane by themselves.

title: Tessellating Octagons
snippet: Tessellating Octagons: Do regular octagons tessellate the plane by themselves (Figure 10.95)? Again, we see that regular octagons do not tessellate the plane by themselves. The gaps, however, are squares. So, two regular polygons, an...
body_xml: Do regular octagons tessellate the plane by themselves (Figure 10.95)? Again, we see that regular octagons do not tessellate the plane by themselves. The gaps, however, are squares. So, two regular polygons, an octagon and a square, do tessellate the plane.

title: Creating Your Own Tessellation
snippet: Creating Your Own Tessellation: Create a tessellation using two colors and two shapes. We used a parallelogram and an isosceles triangle. The parallelogram is reflected vertically and horizontally so that only every other corner touches....
body_xml: Create a tessellation using two colors and two shapes. We used a parallelogram and an isosceles triangle. The parallelogram is reflected vertically and horizontally so that only every other corner touches. The triangles are reflected vertically and horizontally and then translated over the parallelogram. The result is alternating vertical columns of parallelograms and then triangles (Figure 10.101).

title: Determining the Cost of Floor Tile
snippet: Determining the Cost of Floor Tile: Jennifer is planning to install vinyl floor tile in her rectangular-shaped basement, which measures 29 ft by 16 ft. How many boxes of floor tile should she buy and how much will it cost if one box costs...
body_xml:
<example number="10.43" title="Determining the Cost of Floor Tile">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Jennifer is planning to install vinyl floor tile in her rectangular-shaped basement, which measures 29 ft by 16 ft. How many boxes of floor tile should she buy and how much will it cost if one box costs \$50 and covers $$20 \text{ft} ^{2}?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The area of the basement floor is $$A = 29(16) = 464 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$ We will divide this area by $$20 \text{ft} .$$ Thus, $$\frac{464}{20} = 23.2.$$ Therefore, Jennifer will have to buy 24 boxes of tile at a cost \$1,200.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Area of a Parallelogram Park
snippet: Finding the Area of a Parallelogram Park: The boundaries of a city park form a parallelogram (Figure 10.110). The park takes up one city block, which is contained by two sets of parallel streets. Each street measures 55 yd long. The...
body_xml: The boundaries of a city park form a parallelogram (Figure 10.110). The park takes up one city block, which is contained by two sets of parallel streets. Each street measures 55 yd long. The perpendicular distance between streets is 39 yd. How much sod, sold by the square foot, should the city purchase to cover the entire park and how much will it cost? The sod is sold for \$0.50 per square foot, installation is \$1.50 per square foot, and the cost of the equipment for the day is \$100. Step 1: As sod is sold by the square foot, the first thing we have to do is translate the measurements of the park from yards to feet. There are 3 ft to a yard, so 55 yd is equal to 165 ft, and 39 yd is equal to 117 ft. Step 2: The park has the shape of a parallelogram, and the formula for the area is $$A = bh$$ : $$A = 165(117) = 19,305 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$ Step 3: The city needs to purchase $$19,305 \text{ft} ^{2}$$ of sod. The cost will be \$0.50 per square foot for the sod and \$1.50 per square foot for installation, plus \$100 for equipment: $$\begin{array}{rcl} {19,305(\$0.50) + 19,305(\$1.50)} & = & {\$9,652.5 + \$28,957.5 + \$100.00} \\ & = & {\$38,710.00} \end{array}$$

title: Finding the Area of a Trapezoid
snippet: Finding the Area of a Trapezoid: ABCD (Figure 10.112) is a regular trapezoid with \overline{AB}\left\| {\overline{CD}.} \right. Find the exact perimeter of ABCD , and then find the area. The perimeter is the measure of the boundary of the...
body_xml: $$ABCD$$ (Figure 10.112) is a regular trapezoid with $$\overline{AB}\left\| {\overline{CD}.} \right.$$ Find the exact perimeter of $$ABCD$$ , and then find the area. The perimeter is the measure of the boundary of the shape, so we just add up the lengths of the sides. We have $$P = 31 + 13.5 + 11 + 13.5 = 69 \text{in} .$$ Then, the area of the trapezoid using the formula is $$A = \frac{1}{2}(10)(11 + 31) = 210 \text{in} ^{2}$$ .

title: Finding the Area of a Rhombus
snippet: Finding the Area of a Rhombus: Find the measurement of the diagonal d_{1} if the area of the rhombus is 240 \text{cm} ^{2}, and the measure of d_{2} = 24 \text{cm} . Use the formula with the known values: \begin{array}{rcl} 240 & = &...

<example number="10.47" title="Finding the Area of a Rhombus">

      <paragraph>Find the measurement of the diagonal $$d_{1}$$ if the area of the rhombus is $$240 \text{cm} ^{2},$$ and the measure of $$d_{2} = 24 \text{cm} .$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the formula with the known values:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} 240 & = & \frac{d_{1}(24)}{2} \\ {240(2)} & = & {d_{1}(24)} \\ \frac{480}{24} & = & {d_{1} = 20} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

title: Finding the Area of a Rhombus
snippet: Finding the Area of a Rhombus: You notice a child flying a rhombus-shaped kite on the beach. When it falls to the ground, it falls on a beach towel measuring 36 \text{in} by 72 \text{in} . You notice that one of the diagonals of the kite...
body_xml: You notice a child flying a rhombus-shaped kite on the beach. When it falls to the ground, it falls on a beach towel measuring $$36 \text{in}$$ by $$72 \text{in} .$$ You notice that one of the diagonals of the kite is the same length as the $$36 \text{in}$$ width of the towel. The second diagonal appears to be 2 in longer. What is the area of the kite (Figure 10.114)? Using the formula, we have: $$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & \frac{d_{1}d_{2}}{2} \\ & = & {\frac{36(38)}{2} = 684 \text{in} ^{2}} \end{array}$$
